A positive Gowers manoeuvre signals hip girdle rather than distal weakness
Creatine kinase is the decisive first test and is grossly elevated
Genetic testing of the dystrophin gene confirms the diagnosis
Speech delay coexists in a substantial minority and is not a separate problem
explanation.pearls: Any boy not walking independently by 18 months, or any child with an unexplained transaminase rise on routine bloods, should have a creatine kinase measured, because a raised alanine aminotransferase of muscle origin is a common accidental route to the diagnosis.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness
BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Australian Institute of Musculoskeletal Science: Neuromuscular disorders in children

subtopic_detail: Habitual snoring with witnessed pauses in a healthy five year old with large tonsils and normal growth
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 5 year old girl whose parents say she snores loudly every night and sleeps with her mouth open and her neck arched back. Twice a week her father has watched her stop breathing for several seconds before she gasps and starts again.

Her kindergarten teacher has raised concerns about inattention and afternoon irritability, and she still naps most days. She was born at term, has no asthma, no allergic rhinitis and no syndromic features, and she is growing along the 50th centile for height and weight. Her tonsils meet close to the midline and her nasal airway is narrow.

data_table.Examination: Tonsils enlarged to grade 3 bilaterally with no exudate, hyponasal voice, mouth breathing at rest, nasal mucosa pink with no polyps or allergic crease, tympanic membranes normal, chest clear with no chest wall deformity, cardiovascular examination normal, body mass index on the 55th centile
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer to an otolaryngologist for consideration of adenotonsillectomy
options.rationale: An otherwise healthy child between two and twelve with habitual snoring, witnessed apnoeas and adenotonsillar hypertrophy can be referred for surgery on clinical grounds, and removal of the obstructing tissue is the definitive treatment with documented gains in behaviour and quality of life. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

options.text: Arrange overnight polysomnography before any referral is made
options.rationale: Formal sleep study is reserved for children under two, those with obesity, craniofacial or neuromuscular disease or Down syndrome, and cases where the history and the airway findings disagree. Insisting on it for a straightforward presentation adds months of waiting without changing the decision. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

options.text: Start an intranasal corticosteroid spray and review her in three months
options.rationale: Intranasal corticosteroid helps mild snoring driven by allergic rhinitis, and the near pair here is that rhinitis gives a pale boggy mucosa, an allergic crease and seasonal symptoms. Her mucosa is normal and she has witnessed apnoeas, which is beyond the reach of a nasal spray. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Provide sleep hygiene advice with a bedtime routine and review in a month
options.rationale: Behavioural sleep advice addresses settling difficulty and night waking, not an obstructed upper airway. A child who stops breathing in her sleep is not having a behavioural problem and the delay allows the daytime consequences to continue. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

options.text: Refer to a paediatrician for assessment of attention and behaviour first
options.rationale: Inattention here is a consequence of fragmented sleep, and assessing it before the airway risks a stimulant prescription for a reversible problem. Behavioural referral is appropriate if the symptoms persist once the obstruction has been treated. (Source: Australian Sleep Association: Paediatric sleep disordered breathing)
source_refs: Australian Sleep Association: Paediatric sleep disordered breathing

explanation.summary: Obstructive sleep apnoea affects between one and four per cent of Australian children and peaks between two and eight years when the tonsils and adenoids are largest relative to the airway. The presentation differs from adults, with daytime hyperactivity, inattention and irritability rather than sleepiness, so it is frequently mistaken for a primary behavioural disorder. Untreated disease causes growth faltering, learning difficulty, enuresis and in severe cases pulmonary hypertension. In the otherwise healthy preschool or school aged child, the Australian pathway accepts a clinical diagnosis and refers for adenotonsillectomy without waiting for a sleep study.
key_points: Habitual snoring with witnessed apnoeas is the core clinical picture
Daytime inattention rather than sleepiness is the childhood presentation
Polysomnography is for under twos, comorbidity, or a discordant history
Adenotonsillectomy is the definitive treatment for adenotonsillar disease
Untreated disease can cause growth faltering and pulmonary hypertension
explanation.pearls: A child under three years, or one with an oxygen saturation nadir below 80 per cent on any sleep study, should have the surgery performed in a centre with paediatric intensive care access because of the risk of postoperative respiratory compromise in the first night.

sources.label: Australian Sleep Association: Paediatric sleep disordered breathing

subtopic_detail: Fourteen months of waxing and waning blinking and throat clearing in a school aged boy with no functional impairment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 9 year old boy whose parents are worried about repeated hard blinking and a throat clearing noise that has been present on and off for 14 months. The movements come in runs for a few weeks, settle for a while, then return, and are worse when he is tired or excited before a football match.

He can hold them back for a minute or two when he concentrates, and then they come out in a burst. His teacher has not raised any concern, his marks are good and he has friends. He is not distressed by the movements himself, and his neurological examination is normal.

data_table.Examination: Frequent brief forceful eye blinking and intermittent throat clearing during the consultation, movements suppressible on request for about 90 seconds, no impairment of conscious state during the movements, cranial nerves normal, tone power and coordination normal, no chorea, gait normal, conjunctivae white with no discharge
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start risperidone at a low dose and review the response in six weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are reserved for tics causing pain, injury or significant social or educational impairment, none of which apply, and they carry weight gain, sedation and prolactin elevation in a growing child. Treating a well functioning child exposes him to harm for no measurable gain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start clonidine at night and titrate the dose over the next six weeks
options.rationale: Clonidine is a reasonable first pharmacological choice when tics do warrant treatment, particularly with coexisting attention difficulties, so the near pair question is whether any drug is indicated at all. Here the threshold of impairment has not been crossed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram to characterise the repeated movements
options.rationale: Electroencephalography is for events with impaired awareness, automatisms or a stereotyped unvarying pattern, since seizures are neither suppressible nor responsive to distraction. His movements can be held back voluntarily, which is not a feature of epilepsy. (Source: RCH CPG: Tics)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and measure copper studies
options.rationale: Imaging and copper studies belong to the child with a progressive movement disorder, dystonia, cognitive decline or abnormal neurological signs. A normal examination with a fluctuating fourteen month course is characteristic of a primary tic disorder. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Tic disorders)

options.text: Explain the natural history and arrange planned review in six months
options.rationale: A combination of motor and vocal tics for more than a year that waxes and wanes is expected to peak around ten to twelve years and then improve through adolescence, and when there is no functional impairment the evidence supports education and monitoring rather than drug treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Tics)

explanation.summary: Tics affect up to one in five school aged children at some point and the combination of multiple motor tics with at least one vocal tic for over a year defines the syndrome that carries Gilles de la Tourette's name. The defining features are a premonitory urge, brief voluntary suppressibility followed by a rebound, and a fluctuating course that typically worsens with fatigue, excitement or illness. Severity peaks around puberty and improves substantially in most by the late teens, which is why the first intervention is accurate information for the child, the family and the school. Comorbid attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive symptoms cause more impairment than the tics themselves and should be actively sought.
key_points: Suppressibility with rebound distinguishes tics from seizures and chorea
Motor plus vocal tics for over twelve months defines the syndrome
Waxing and waning severity with stress and fatigue is expected
Education and monitoring are first line when function is preserved
Screen for attention and obsessive compulsive symptoms at every review
explanation.pearls: Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics, built around habit reversal training, is the recommended first active treatment when impairment does appear, and it outperforms medication for tic severity without the metabolic cost of an antipsychotic.

subtopic_detail: Four months of bilateral evening leg pain in a well six year old who runs normally by day with a normal examination
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6 year old girl who has been waking in the evening crying with pain in both calves and the fronts of both thighs, three or four nights a week for four months. Her mother rubs her legs and she settles within twenty minutes and sleeps through the rest of the night.

She is up and running at school the next morning with no limp and has not missed a day. There is no fever, no weight loss, no night sweats and no bruising, and she plays netball each weekend. Her aunt has juvenile arthritis and her mother is anxious about that. Examination of both legs is entirely normal.

data_table.Examination: Height and weight tracking along the 60th centile, no pallor, no bruising or petechiae, no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly, no bone tenderness over the tibiae femora or spine, hips and knees with full painless range of movement, no joint swelling or warmth, normal gait and normal single leg hop on each side
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange a full blood count with a blood film and measure lactate dehydrogenase
options.rationale: Blood testing is indicated when pain wakes the child from established sleep, is unilateral or localised to bone, or comes with pallor, bruising, fever or weight loss. None of those are present and her daytime function is unaffected. (Source: RCH CPG: Growing pains)

options.text: Explain the pattern, advise simple analgesia and review if features change
options.rationale: Bilateral pain confined to the evening with complete freedom of movement and a normal examination the following day is the recognised benign pattern, and positive diagnosis with safety netting avoids a cascade of tests. The parents are told exactly which changes would prompt reassessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Growing pains)

options.text: Arrange radiographs of both femora and both tibiae to exclude a bony lesion
options.rationale: Radiographs are for focal bone tenderness, a palpable mass or a limp, since osteoid osteoma and osteosarcoma are localised rather than symmetrical. Symmetrical pain with no tenderness anywhere does not fit a structural lesion. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Limb pain in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Limb pain in children

options.text: Measure the serum 25 hydroxyvitamin D level and treat if it is below range
options.rationale: Vitamin D deficiency causes bone pain with proximal weakness, a waddling gait and sometimes deformity or fracture, and the near pair is that its pain persists through the day rather than resolving by morning. Testing without those features usually yields an incidental result that is then treated pointlessly. (Source: RACGP: Vitamin D testing)

options.text: Refer to a paediatric rheumatologist for assessment of inflammatory joint pain
options.rationale: Inflammatory joint disease shows morning stiffness with swelling or restricted movement of a specific joint, the opposite of the diurnal pattern here where mornings are her best time. The family history raises the possibility but her examination does not support it. (Source: RCH CPG: Growing pains)

explanation.summary: Benign nocturnal limb pain of childhood affects around a third of children between three and twelve years and is a positive diagnosis rather than a diagnosis of exclusion. The defining pattern is bilateral pain in the muscles of the legs, late in the day or in the evening, with the child entirely well and fully mobile between episodes and a normal examination. The features that move a child out of this category are pain that is unilateral, localised over bone, present in the morning, associated with limp, swelling, fever, weight loss or systemic upset, or that wakes the child repeatedly from deep sleep. Massage, stretching and simple analgesia are effective, and the condition resolves over months to a few years.
key_points: The pain is bilateral and muscular rather than over a specific bone
Symptoms appear in the evening and the child is well the next morning
Examination must be entirely normal to make the diagnosis
Limp, morning symptoms or systemic features demand investigation
Massage and simple analgesia with parental reassurance are sufficient
explanation.pearls: Pain that is reliably worst in the morning, or that has been present for weeks over a single bony point, should prompt a full blood count with film and a plain radiograph of that bone, because leukaemia can present with normal peripheral counts in about one in ten children.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Limb pain in children

subtopic_detail: Painless scrotal swelling in a ten month old that transilluminates, has an upper border you can palpate above it, and does not change with crying
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 10 month old boy whose mother noticed at bath time that his left side of the scrotum looks bigger than the right. It has been there for at least two months, is the same size in the morning and the evening, and does not change when he cries or strains.

He feeds well, opens his bowels daily, has never vomited and is thriving on the 60th centile. He does not seem to mind when she washes the area. On examination the swelling is soft and non-tender, you can feel normal cord above it, and it lights up when you shine a torch behind it. Both testes are descended and the scrotal skin is normal.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender left scrotal swelling measuring about 3 cm, transilluminates brightly, upper border easily palpable with normal spermatic cord above it, no impulse on crying, no reducibility, both testes palpable within the scrotum, abdomen soft and non-distended, groins without swelling or tenderness
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently to a paediatric surgeon for herniotomy on the next available list
options.rationale: Urgent repair is for an inguinal hernia, which extends into the groin, has no palpable upper border, and characteristically enlarges with crying and reduces when the child is relaxed. The near pair matters because a hernia in this age group carries a real risk of incarceration while this lesion does not. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions

options.text: Arrange a scrotal ultrasound with Doppler before deciding on any referral
options.rationale: Ultrasound is reserved for a swelling that fails to transilluminate, a testis that cannot be felt separately, or a suspicion of a mass or torsion. Imaging adds nothing when the clinical findings already define the lesion and both testes are palpable. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Scrotal swelling in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Scrotal swelling in children

options.text: Arrange aspiration of the fluid in the clinic and send it for cell count analysis
options.rationale: Aspiration is not part of paediatric practice because the fluid reaccumulates while the underlying processus remains patent, and the procedure risks injuring the testis. It also converts a benign observation problem into an invasive one. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions

options.text: Start a course of oral antibiotics and review the swelling again in one week
options.rationale: Antibiotics would treat epididymo-orchitis, which is painful, tender and often accompanied by fever, dysuria or scrotal erythema. A painless swelling in a well afebrile infant with normal overlying skin has no infective features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Reassure the parents and review him in the clinic after his second birthday
options.rationale: A swelling with a palpable upper border that does not vary in size is a non communicating collection around the testis, and the processus vaginalis closes spontaneously in most infants, so the great majority resolve by two years without any intervention. Surgery is considered only for persistence beyond that age. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions

explanation.summary: Fluid collecting within the tunica vaginalis is common in the first year of life and reflects incomplete obliteration of the processus vaginalis after testicular descent. The clinical task is to separate it from an inguinal hernia, which is the lesion that threatens the bowel and the testis, and the three discriminators are a palpable upper border, transillumination, and whether the swelling changes size with crying or through the day. A collection that fluctuates in size indicates a communication with the peritoneum and behaves more like a hernia, warranting earlier surgical opinion. Persistence beyond two years, rapid enlargement, or the appearance of a new collection in an older boy all justify referral, the last because it may signal an underlying testicular tumour or torsion of an appendage.
key_points: A palpable upper border places the swelling below the inguinal canal
Transillumination indicates fluid rather than bowel within the sac
Size that varies with crying indicates a patent communication
Most non communicating collections resolve before two years of age
A new collection in an older boy warrants ultrasound of the testis
explanation.pearls: A scrotal swelling that is larger at the end of the day and smaller after a night in the cot indicates a communicating processus and should be referred for repair rather than observed, because the same defect can admit bowel.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions

subtopic_detail: Two days of early morning vomiting and afternoon drowsiness in an afebrile child with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt in place since infancy
stem: A 6-year-old boy has vomited on waking for two mornings with headache. He was well between episodes yesterday but fell asleep this afternoon and is hard to rouse. He has a ventriculoperitoneal shunt inserted at four months.

data_table.Examination: GCS 13, neck supple, pupils equal and reactive, reduced upgaze, shunt reservoir refills slowly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Give intravenous ondansetron and observe in the short stay unit
options.rationale: Antiemetic treatment suits gastroenteritis, which would give diarrhoea, abdominal pain, fever or a sick contact, none of which are present. Treating the symptom here removes the only visible sign of a rising intracranial pressure while the pathology continues. (Source: RCH CPG: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt complications)

options.text: Lumbar puncture for cell count and culture after blood cultures
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture in suspected obstructive hydrocephalus risks downward herniation, and shunt infection is sampled by neurosurgical tap of the reservoir rather than by the lumbar route. His supple neck, normal temperature and clean shunt tract also argue against infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intranasal sumatriptan with outpatient neurology follow-up
options.rationale: Migraine is a diagnosis for a child with a normal conscious state between and during attacks, and it does not progressively reduce the level of consciousness over an afternoon. A first presentation of headache in a shunted child is never assumed to be primary. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

options.text: Urgent non-contrast head computed tomogram and call neurosurgery
options.rationale: Morning headache and vomiting with declining conscious state in a shunted child is shunt failure until proven otherwise, and the imaging that answers it is a rapid non-contrast head scan compared with previous studies for ventricular size, obtained alongside an immediate neurosurgical discussion. Reduced upgaze and a sluggishly refilling reservoir both support raised pressure. (Source: RCH CPG: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt complications)

options.text: Abdominal ultrasound for a collection around the distal catheter
options.rationale: An abdominal pseudocyst does cause distal shunt obstruction, but it presents with abdominal distension, pain or a palpable mass, and it is looked for after the head has been imaged. His abdomen is soft and the immediate threat is intracranial. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Hydrocephalus)

explanation.summary: Around a third of ventriculoperitoneal shunts fail within the first year and the cumulative risk of at least one revision through childhood approaches half. Obstruction is the commonest mode and presents with the classic features of raised intracranial pressure, which in children means headache and vomiting worst on waking, irritability, declining school performance, and eventually drowsiness, impaired upgaze and bradycardia with hypertension. Papilloedema is an unreliable sign because it takes time to develop and is often absent in an acute rise. The standard assessment pairs urgent imaging of the ventricles against a baseline study with a shunt series and early neurosurgical involvement, since definitive treatment is surgical revision.
key_points: Headache and vomiting on waking suggest raised intracranial pressure
Absent papilloedema does not exclude an acute pressure rise
Impaired upgaze reflects pressure on the dorsal midbrain
Compare ventricular size with a previous study, not with a normal range
Lumbar puncture is contraindicated when obstruction is suspected
explanation.pearls: A shunt reservoir that refills slowly after compression suggests proximal obstruction and one that is difficult to depress suggests distal obstruction, but neither finding is sensitive enough to exclude failure, so a normal reservoir examination never overrules a convincing history.

subtopic_detail: Alert four month old with profound axial hypotonia, absent reflexes, tongue fasciculations and paradoxical breathing who missed newborn screening
stem: A 4-month-old girl has never lifted her head and has stopped kicking her legs. She was born overseas and had no newborn screening test.

data_table.Examination: Alert and socially smiling, profound hypotonia with head lag, movement only at fingers and toes, reflexes absent, tongue fasciculations, paradoxical inspiratory chest movement
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 118 units per litre (less than 200), gas and glucose normal

lead_in: Which investigation will establish the diagnosis?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of brain and whole spine under anaesthesia
options.rationale: Central causes of hypotonia produce reduced alertness, a poor social response, dysmorphism or seizures, and often upper motor neurone signs. A socially engaged infant with absent reflexes has a lower motor neurone problem, and the anaesthetic itself is hazardous with her respiratory pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.text: Muscle biopsy of quadriceps with enzyme histochemistry and microscopy
options.rationale: Biopsy is directed at a congenital myopathy or muscular dystrophy, which is the near pair here, but those raise the creatine kinase or at least do not spare it entirely and do not produce tongue fasciculations. Genetic testing now precedes biopsy for this phenotype. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Spinal muscular atrophy)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Spinal muscular atrophy

options.text: Targeted genetic testing of the survival motor neurone gene
options.rationale: Alertness with a normal facial expression places the lesion below the brain, and areflexia with tongue fasciculations and a normal creatine kinase localises it to the anterior horn cell rather than to muscle or nerve. Deletion testing of the survival motor neurone gene confirms the diagnosis in the great majority and is the test that unlocks disease modifying therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.text: Repeat newborn screening for metabolic and endocrine disorders
options.rationale: Metabolic causes of hypotonia usually announce themselves with encephalopathy, acidosis, hypoglycaemia, organomegaly or a raised lactate, and her gas and glucose are normal. The screen is worth completing for public health reasons but it will not explain a pure motor picture. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.text: Repetitive nerve stimulation with acetylcholine receptor antibodies
options.rationale: Neuromuscular junction disease gives fatigable weakness with ptosis and ophthalmoplegia and characteristically preserves the deep tendon reflexes. Her reflexes are absent and her eye movements are full, which points away from the junction. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Spinal muscular atrophy)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Spinal muscular atrophy

explanation.summary: The floppy infant is sorted first into central and peripheral causes, and the single most useful bedside discriminator is the level of alertness and social interaction, because a baby who engages normally while lying motionless has a problem below the brain. Within the peripheral group, absent reflexes with tongue fasciculations and a normal creatine kinase indicate anterior horn cell degeneration, while a raised creatine kinase points to muscle and distal sensory loss points to nerve. Australian newborn bloodspot screening has included the survival motor neurone gene since 2022, so infants born here are usually identified presymptomatically, and a symptomatic presentation now most often means the child was born elsewhere or predates the program. Diagnosis is urgent because disease modifying therapies work best before motor neurones are lost, and respiratory and nutritional support must be organised in parallel.
key_points: Preserved alertness with profound weakness indicates a peripheral cause
Absent reflexes with tongue fasciculations localise to the anterior horn cell
A normal creatine kinase argues against a primary muscle disorder
Paradoxical breathing reflects intercostal weakness with a spared diaphragm
Genetic confirmation is urgent because treatment is time critical
explanation.pearls: Intercostal weakness with diaphragm sparing produces the bell shaped chest and inward chest movement on inspiration, and these infants decompensate abruptly during minor viral illness, so respiratory review and a cough assist plan should be arranged before the first winter.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness
BMJ Best Practice: Spinal muscular atrophy

subtopic_detail: Toddler with a harsh brassy cough and noisy breathing since infancy that worsens with crying and has not responded to eight weeks of inhaled therapy
stem: A 14-month-old boy has had noisy breathing since three months of age with a barking cough, loudest when he cries and absent in sleep. He has no eczema or family history of asthma. Salbutamol and eight weeks of inhaled corticosteroid changed nothing.

data_table.Examination: Monophonic expiratory wheeze over the trachea, chest clear when settled
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph normal, no right-sided arch

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a respiratory service for flexible bronchoscopy
options.rationale: A brassy cough with a central monophonic wheeze that varies with effort and settles in sleep describes dynamic collapse of a large airway, which is diagnosed by looking at the airway during spontaneous breathing. Flexible bronchoscopy both confirms the collapse and excludes an intraluminal lesion or extrinsic compression. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor and noisy breathing)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Stridor and noisy breathing

options.text: Increase inhaled corticosteroid and add a long-acting beta agonist
options.rationale: Escalating preventer therapy assumes asthma, which gives polyphonic wheeze scattered through both lung fields, atopy, and at least partial bronchodilator response. He has none of these and has already failed an adequate eight week trial. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

options.text: Arrange emergency rigid bronchoscopy for foreign body removal
options.rationale: An inhaled foreign body causes abrupt symptoms in a previously well child, usually with a witnessed choking episode and unilateral signs or hyperinflation on the film. Symptoms present since three months of age and a normal radiograph do not fit. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor and noisy breathing)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Stridor and noisy breathing

options.text: Start two weeks of oral amoxicillin with clavulanate
options.rationale: Extended antibiotics treat protracted bacterial bronchitis, the near pair for chronic cough in this age group, but that cough is wet and productive rather than brassy and it is not positional or effort dependent. A dry barking cough with a monophonic noise is mechanical. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Start a proton pump inhibitor with an oesophageal pH study
options.rationale: Reflux can aggravate airway symptoms and coexists with large airway collapse, but it is not the primary explanation for a noise that changes with respiratory effort and disappears in sleep. Treating it first leaves the structural question unanswered. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Tracheomalacia)

explanation.summary: Not every wheezing toddler has asthma, and the pattern of the noise is the key to the alternatives. Polyphonic wheeze scattered through both fields with a bronchodilator response indicates small airway disease, while a single pitched noise heard loudest centrally indicates one large airway that is narrowing. Dynamic collapse of the trachea or a main bronchus classically causes a brassy or barking cough, noise that worsens with crying, feeding and exertion and improves with rest, and complete failure to respond to inhaled therapy. The differential includes extrinsic compression by a vascular ring or a mediastinal mass, which is why the airway is examined directly and the arch anatomy is checked before the symptoms are attributed to a benign floppy trachea that will improve through the second and third years.
key_points: Monophonic central wheeze indicates a single large airway, not small airways
A brassy barking cough with effort dependent noise suggests dynamic collapse
Failure of an adequate preventer trial should prompt review of the diagnosis
Flexible bronchoscopy during spontaneous breathing shows the collapse
Exclude extrinsic vascular compression before accepting a benign cause
explanation.pearls: A toddler whose noisy breathing is worse when lying prone and better when lying on the side, and whose cough is brassy rather than wet, should be referred before a third preventer escalation, because inhaled corticosteroid has no effect on a collapsing airway and delays the structural diagnosis by months.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Stridor and noisy breathing

subtopic_detail: Head circumference crossing two centile lines between three and seven months with a full fontanelle in a developmentally normal infant
stem:
You are the general practitioner doing a 7 month check on a boy who was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. His mother has no concerns and he sits with a straight back, transfers a block between his hands and babbles.

His head circumference was on the 50th centile at birth and the 50th at three months, and today it plots on the 97th. His length and weight remain on the 50th. His anterior fontanelle feels full when he is sitting quietly and not crying, and the skull sutures feel slightly separated at the coronal suture. His eyes move fully in all directions and he fixes and follows. Both parents have head circumferences on the 50th centile for adults.

data_table.Examination: Head circumference on the 97th centile having tracked the 50th at birth and at three months, anterior fontanelle full but not tense at rest, slight separation of the coronal suture, scalp veins not distended, no setting sun sign with full upgaze, red reflexes present and symmetrical, tone and reflexes normal, sits unsupported and transfers objects, no organomegaly, no bruising
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Measure both parents' head circumferences and plot a repeat measurement monthly
options.rationale: Familial large head is a valid explanation for a head that is large but growing parallel to a centile line, and the parental measurements here are ordinary. A head that crosses centiles is describing a rate of growth, which no family history can normalise. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with sedation as the first study
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is the better test for posterior fossa detail and is appropriate once ultrasound is abnormal or the fontanelle has closed, so the near pair question is sequence rather than suitability. Starting here commits an infant to sedation for information a bedside study can provide. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly)

options.text: Arrange skull radiographs to assess the sutures for premature fusion and ridging
options.rationale: Premature suture fusion produces an abnormally shaped head with a palpable ridge and a head circumference that falls away rather than accelerates, because the skull cannot expand. His sutures are separated, which is the opposite finding. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Macrocephaly)

options.text: Reassure the parents that development is normal and repeat the plot in three months
options.rationale: Normal development is genuinely reassuring about the past but says nothing about a process still expanding, and infants compensate for raised pressure by enlarging the skull until they suddenly do not. Waiting three months risks presenting later with vomiting and impaired upgaze. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly)

options.text: Arrange a cranial ultrasound through the fontanelle within the next few days
options.rationale: Crossing two centile lines with a full fontanelle and separating sutures requires imaging rather than observation, and while the fontanelle remains open an ultrasound shows ventricular size and extra-axial fluid without radiation or sedation. It separates enlarged subarachnoid spaces from progressive ventricular dilatation, which need different follow up. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly)

explanation.summary: Head circumference is interpreted as a trajectory rather than as a single point, and the finding that demands action is crossing centile lines upward, particularly with signs of raised pressure such as a full fontanelle, separated sutures, distended scalp veins or impaired upgaze. The commonest benign explanation in this age group is enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces, which typically runs in families, presents with a rapidly enlarging but soft head, and resolves by two years with normal development. Progressive hydrocephalus from aqueduct stenosis, a posterior fossa lesion or a chronic subdural collection all present identically at the start, and a subdural collection additionally raises the question of inflicted injury. Cranial ultrasound through an open fontanelle is the practical first study in Australian primary care, with magnetic resonance imaging reserved for abnormal or equivocal findings.
key_points: Crossing upward through centile lines matters more than the absolute centile
A full fontanelle and separated sutures indicate raised intracranial pressure
Familial macrocephaly grows parallel to a centile line rather than crossing
Ultrasound through an open fontanelle avoids sedation and radiation
Normal development does not exclude an actively expanding process
explanation.pearls: Benign enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces carries a genuinely increased risk of subdural haemorrhage after trivial trauma, so a subdural collection found in an infant with this finding does not by itself resolve the question of inflicted injury and still warrants a full safeguarding assessment.

subtopic_detail: Six week old breastfed infant with a bulging fontanelle and bruising whose parents declined the birth injection, with prolonged clotting times and a normal platelet count
stem: A 6-week-old boy, fully breastfed, has been irritable and pale all day and had a one-minute focal seizure. His parents declined the injection offered after birth.

data_table.Examination: Pale, irritable, bulging fontanelle, oozing at the venepuncture site
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 78 g/L, platelets 388 x10^9/L, INR 6.4, APTT 92 seconds, fibrinogen 2.9 g/L, CRP 3 mg/L

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate intervention?

options.text: Platelet transfusion and urgent head computed tomography
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion treats thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction, and his count is squarely normal at 388. Transfusing platelets into a factor deficiency corrects nothing and delays the treatment that does. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management, paediatrics)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management, paediatrics

options.text: Intravenous vitamin K and urgent head computed tomography
options.rationale: A prolonged international normalised ratio and activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal platelet count and normal fibrinogen is the signature of deficient vitamin K dependent factors, and in a breastfed infant who received no prophylaxis this is late haemorrhagic disease with intracranial bleeding until imaged. Replacing the vitamin corrects the underlying defect within hours while the scan defines the bleed. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding

options.text: Intravenous cefotaxime and lumbar puncture once stable
options.rationale: Meningitis is the standard reflex for an irritable infant with a bulging fontanelle, but he is afebrile with a normal C reactive protein, and lumbar puncture with an international normalised ratio of 6.4 risks a spinal haematoma. The coagulation profile is the disconfirming finding that redirects the whole assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma alone and head computed tomography
options.rationale: Plasma is a useful adjunct for immediate factor replacement in life threatening bleeding and is given alongside the vitamin, so the near pair question is what corrects the deficiency rather than what fills the gap. Plasma alone wears off within hours because the liver still cannot carboxylate the factors. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management, paediatrics)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management, paediatrics

options.text: Skeletal survey and referral to the child protection unit
options.rationale: Inflicted injury must be considered in any infant with intracranial bleeding, and the assessment proceeds, but it does not precede treatment and it does not explain a grossly deranged coagulation profile with normal platelets. Correct the coagulopathy first and keep the safeguarding question open. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: Vitamin K dependent factors two, seven, nine and ten fall over the first weeks of life because placental transfer is poor, the gut is not yet colonised and breast milk contains very little vitamin K, which is why a single intramuscular dose is offered to every Australian newborn. The late form of the deficiency presents between two and twelve weeks, almost exclusively in breastfed infants who missed prophylaxis or who have unrecognised cholestasis, and roughly half of these infants present with intracranial haemorrhage. The laboratory signature is a markedly prolonged international normalised ratio and activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal platelet count and normal fibrinogen, which separates it from disseminated intravascular coagulation and from thrombocytopenic causes. Treatment is intravenous vitamin K with plasma or prothrombin complex for active major bleeding, alongside imaging and neurosurgical involvement.
key_points: Late presentation occurs between two and twelve weeks in breastfed infants
Prolonged clotting times with normal platelets and fibrinogen is the signature
Intracranial haemorrhage is the presentation in about half of late cases
Intravenous vitamin K corrects the defect, plasma only bridges it
Lumbar puncture is unsafe until the coagulopathy has been corrected
explanation.pearls: An infant with this presentation who has also had pale stools or prolonged jaundice needs a conjugated bilirubin measured on the same admission, because biliary atresia causes fat malabsorption and can produce the identical deficiency despite a correctly given birth dose.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding
National Blood Authority: Patient blood management, paediatrics

subtopic_detail: Unilateral absent red reflex found at the six week check in an infant with no ocular discharge or watering
stem:
You are the general practitioner performing the six week check on a boy born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. His mother says that in photographs taken over the last fortnight the middle of his left eye looks cloudy and pale, and that he does not seem to look at her with that eye.

His eyes are not sticky and do not water. The newborn examination on day one recorded red reflexes present and symmetrical. He is feeding well and gaining weight along the 50th centile, and there is no family history of childhood eye disease.

data_table.Examination: Red reflex absent on the left and present on the right, left pupil appears grey-white to the direct ophthalmoscope, no conjunctival injection or discharge, corneal diameters equal, eyes of equal size
data_table.Visual behaviour: Fixes and follows the examiner's face steadily when the left eye is covered, becomes distressed and turns away when the right eye is covered
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Repeat the red reflex examination at the four month health check
options.rationale: Deferring re-examination wastes the window in which occlusion amblyopia becomes irreversible, and an absent red reflex is never a finding to observe. The mother's account of a change since the newborn check makes progression rather than resolution the expectation. (Source: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions)
source_refs: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions

options.text: Refer to a community optometrist for refraction within three months
options.rationale: Refraction assesses focusing error in an eye with a clear media and does not address an opacity blocking the reflex. The near pair here is that optometric refraction is the right pathway for a squint with an intact red reflex, which is not this child. (Source: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions)
source_refs: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions

options.text: Arrange paediatric ophthalmology assessment within the next week
options.rationale: An absent red reflex in one eye requires ophthalmological assessment within days, both because a media opacity must be cleared early enough to allow the visual pathway to develop and because an intraocular tumour presents this way. Deprivation from a dense unilateral opacity produces dense amblyopia if the eye is not treated in the first months of life. (Source: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions)
source_refs: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions

options.text: Request TORCH serology and review the infant when results return
options.rationale: Congenital infection is one cause of a media opacity but serology takes days and does not change the immediate need for specialist examination. Investigating aetiology before securing the eye assessment inverts the order of priorities. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Congenital cataract)

options.text: Order a cranial ultrasound and review once the scan is reported
options.rationale: Cranial ultrasound images the brain and does not resolve the anterior segment or the retina to the standard needed here. A normal scan would falsely reassure while the visual deprivation continues. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Congenital cataract)

explanation.summary: The red reflex is the single most useful screening test of the paediatric eye in primary care, and it is performed at the newborn check, the six to eight week check and whenever a parent reports an abnormal appearance. An absent, dull or asymmetric reflex means light is not returning from the retina, which places a media opacity, a retinal detachment or an intraocular mass in the differential. The visual cortex is plastic only for the first months of life, so a dense unilateral opacity that is not cleared early leaves permanent amblyopia even if the opacity is later removed. Parental reports of an abnormal appearance in photographs are a genuinely useful history, because the camera flash reproduces the test under conditions the parent sees repeatedly.
key_points: An absent red reflex is a referral finding in its own right, not an observation finding
A normal newborn red reflex does not exclude an opacity developing later in infancy
Absent discharge and watering argue against nasolacrimal duct obstruction as the cause
Objection to occlusion of one eye implies the fellow eye is the seeing eye
Aetiological investigation must not delay the specialist eye assessment
explanation.pearls: Surgery for a dense unilateral congenital cataract gives the best visual outcome when performed between four and six weeks of age, which is why an absent red reflex found at the six week check is a same week referral rather than a routine one.

sources.label: RANZCO: Referral pathways for paediatric eye conditions
RACGP: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice

subtopic_detail: Angle of trunk rotation of eight degrees on forward bending in a thirteen year old girl eleven months after menarche
stem:
A 13 year old girl is brought to your general practice because her mother noticed that one shoulder sits higher than the other and that one side of her back sticks up when she bends forward to pick things up. She has no back pain, no night pain and no change in bowel or bladder function.

Her menarche was eleven months ago. On examination she is well grown, her skin shows no birthmarks or patches of altered pigmentation, her foot arches are normal on standing and reflexes are symmetrical with downgoing plantar responses. On the Adams forward bend test there is a right thoracic prominence, and a scoliometer placed over it reads 8 degrees.

data_table.Examination: Right thoracic rib prominence on forward bending with a scoliometer angle of trunk rotation of 8 degrees, shoulder heights unequal by approximately 2 cm, waist creases asymmetric, no midline skin lesion over the spine, no cafe au lait macules, normal pes planus free foot arches, power and reflexes normal and symmetrical in both legs
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Reassure and review her in twelve months with a repeat examination
options.rationale: A twelve month interval is far too long in a girl less than two years past menarche, when the residual growth spurt drives the majority of curve progression. Observation without a baseline radiograph also leaves the curve magnitude unknown. (Source: RCH CPG: Scoliosis)

options.text: Arrange a standing whole spine radiograph and refer to a spine clinic
options.rationale: A scoliometer angle of trunk rotation at or above 7 degrees is the accepted threshold for imaging, because it corresponds to a curve likely to be clinically significant, and management decisions depend on the Cobb angle measured on an erect film. Referral alongside imaging allows skeletal maturity and curve magnitude to be combined into a progression risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Scoliosis)

options.text: Refer for magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine before review
options.rationale: Spinal magnetic resonance imaging is reserved for features suggesting an underlying neural axis abnormality, such as a left thoracic curve, a midline skin lesion, a cavus foot, asymmetric reflexes or pain waking the child. None of those features is present here. (Source: RCH CPG: Scoliosis)

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for a scoliosis specific exercise program
options.rationale: Scoliosis specific exercises are an adjunct considered once a curve has been measured and staged, not a substitute for establishing the Cobb angle. Starting therapy without imaging risks missing a curve already in the bracing or surgical range. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis

options.text: Fit a thoracolumbosacral brace and review her again in three months
options.rationale: Bracing is indicated for a curve between about 25 and 40 degrees in a patient with remaining growth, so it cannot be prescribed before the Cobb angle is known. Bracing an unmeasured curve exposes the patient to a demanding treatment that may be unnecessary. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis

explanation.summary: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is a structural three dimensional deformity that produces rotation as well as lateral curvature, which is why the rib prominence on forward bending is the physical sign rather than the visible curve itself. Risk of progression is driven by the curve magnitude and the growth remaining, so skeletal maturity markers such as time since menarche and the Risser sign are as important as the Cobb angle. Curves under 25 degrees are usually observed, curves between about 25 and 40 degrees in a growing patient are braced, and curves beyond about 45 to 50 degrees are considered for surgery. Features pointing away from idiopathic disease include pain, a left thoracic curve, neurological signs and cutaneous markers, each of which redirects the workup towards imaging of the neural axis.
key_points: The scoliometer measures trunk rotation, and 7 degrees is the usual threshold for radiography
Progression risk is highest in the two years spanning the pubertal growth spurt
Management is decided on the Cobb angle from an erect whole spine film
Normal reflexes, normal foot arches and no skin lesions argue against a neural axis cause
A right thoracic curve is the expected pattern in idiopathic disease
explanation.pearls: A left sided thoracic curve in an adolescent is atypical for idiopathic scoliosis and should prompt magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine to look for a syrinx, a Chiari malformation or a cord tumour, even when the neurological examination is normal.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis

subtopic_detail: Bowed legs with a raised alkaline phosphatase in an eighteen month old who is still breastfed and has had very little sun exposure
stem: An 18-month-old girl has increasingly bowed legs since walking at 14 months. She is still breastfed, has never had a vitamin supplement, and is almost always indoors.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical genu varum; widening of both distal radial metaphyses; frontal bossing
data_table.Investigations: Calcium 2.12 mmol/L (2.20-2.60); phosphate 0.82 mmol/L (1.10-1.90); alkaline phosphatase 1180 U/L (110-320); parathyroid hormone raised; 25 hydroxyvitamin D 14 nmol/L (>50); renal function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Oral calcium carbonate alone, with no vitamin supplement
options.rationale: Calcium alone does not correct the substrate deficiency driving the secondary hyperparathyroidism, so the bone disease persists and the parathyroid hormone stays elevated. Calcium deficiency rickets with a normal vitamin D level is the situation in which calcium alone is appropriate. (Source: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents

options.text: Oral calcitriol 0.25 micrograms daily plus dietary calcium
options.rationale: Calcitriol bypasses renal hydroxylation and is reserved for renal disease or the rare hydroxylase defects, neither of which fits normal renal function with a profoundly low 25 hydroxyvitamin D. Its narrow therapeutic index makes hypercalcaemia a real hazard in nutritional deficiency. (Source: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents

options.text: Oral colecalciferol 400 units daily plus dietary calcium
options.rationale: Four hundred units is the daily dose used to prevent deficiency in an at risk infant, not to heal established rickets, and at this dose the radiological and biochemical abnormalities correct slowly if at all. The near pair here is prevention dosing against treatment dosing of the same drug. (Source: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents

options.text: No supplement, with repeat biochemistry and a bone survey
options.rationale: Untreated rickets continues to deform the growing skeleton and carries a risk of hypocalcaemic seizures and cardiomyopathy in young children. A skeletal survey adds radiation without altering the treatment that the biochemistry already indicates. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Oral colecalciferol 3000 units daily plus dietary calcium
options.rationale: Established nutritional rickets in a child over twelve months is treated with high dose colecalciferol for three months, together with an adequate calcium intake because healing bone consumes calcium rapidly. Treatment dosing is an order of magnitude above prevention dosing, and maintenance supplementation continues once the course is complete. (Source: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents

explanation.summary: Nutritional rickets remains common in Australian children whose skin is rarely exposed to sunlight, whether because of latitude, clothing practices, or prolonged indoor time, and exclusive or prolonged breastfeeding without supplementation compounds the risk because breast milk contains very little vitamin D. The biochemical signature is a low 25 hydroxyvitamin D with a raised alkaline phosphatase and a raised parathyroid hormone, with phosphate falling as parathyroid hormone drives renal phosphate loss and calcium held near the lower limit until decompensation. Normal renal function distinguishes nutritional disease from the rickets of chronic kidney disease, and a raised parathyroid hormone distinguishes it from X linked hypophosphataemia, where parathyroid hormone is normal or only slightly raised. Radiographs of the wrist show cupping, splaying and fraying of the metaphysis and are useful for confirming healing.
key_points: Alkaline phosphatase is the most sensitive routine marker of active rickets in a child
Secondary hyperparathyroidism explains the low phosphate and the near normal calcium
Normal renal function excludes renal osteodystrophy as the explanation
Treatment dosing of colecalciferol is far higher than prevention dosing
Calcium intake must be adequate during healing or hypocalcaemia can worsen
explanation.pearls: Alkaline phosphatase rises further in the first weeks of vitamin D treatment as the bone heals before it falls, so a rising value at the four week review is evidence of response rather than treatment failure.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand consensus: Vitamin D deficiency in infants children and adolescents
Australian Medicines Handbook: Children's Dosing Companion

subtopic_detail: Purulent conjunctivitis beginning on day nine of life with a negative gonococcal culture and a positive chlamydial nucleic acid test
stem:
You are the resident in the emergency department reviewing a nine day old boy whose mother says his eyes have been gluey and his eyelids puffy for three days, and that the discharge keeps coming back after she wipes it away. He was born at term at home, and his mother booked late in the pregnancy and had no antenatal screening swabs taken.

He is afebrile, feeding well and has gained weight since discharge. Both conjunctivae are injected with a copious yellow discharge and marked lid oedema, and the corneas are clear on fluorescein staining. A conjunctival swab shows no organisms on Gram stain and culture is negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, while nucleic acid amplification testing is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 beats per minute, blood pressure 68/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bilateral lid oedema with copious mucopurulent discharge, conjunctival injection without follicles, clear corneas on fluorescein staining, chest clear on auscultation with no cough, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Conjunctival swab Gram stain shows polymorphs with no organisms seen, culture negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, nucleic acid amplification test positive for Chlamydia trachomatis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Topical chloramphenicol ointment and review of the mother and her partner
options.rationale: Chloramphenicol has poor activity against this organism and topical therapy alone does not reach the nasopharyngeal reservoir, so up to a fifth of infants go on to develop a pneumonitis at four to twelve weeks. Chloramphenicol is a reasonable choice for ordinary bacterial conjunctivitis beyond the neonatal period. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral azithromycin for the infant and treatment of the mother and her partner
options.rationale: Systemic therapy is required because the organism colonises the nasopharynx as well as the conjunctiva, and oral azithromycin for the infant is the Australian regimen of choice. The infection is sexually transmitted, so the mother and her sexual partners must be treated and offered testing for other infections at the same time. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone for the infant and treatment of mother and partner
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is the treatment for gonococcal ophthalmia, which is excluded here by a negative Gram stain and culture, and it has no useful activity against this organism. Ceftriaxone also displaces bilirubin from albumin, which is an added reason to avoid it in the neonate without indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Topical erythromycin ointment and treatment of the mother and her partner
options.rationale: Erythromycin has the right spectrum but the wrong route, since topical delivery clears the eye while leaving the nasopharynx colonised and the pneumonitis risk untouched. The near pair here is that the same drug class given systemically would be an acceptable alternative regimen. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

options.text: Saline eye toilet alone and review of the mother and her partner in a week
options.rationale: Eye toilet is useful supportive care but does not eradicate an organism that causes scarring conjunctivitis and later respiratory disease if untreated. Saline alone is appropriate for the sticky eye of nasolacrimal duct obstruction, where there is watering without lid oedema or purulent discharge. (Source: RCH CPG: Conjunctivitis)

explanation.summary: Neonatal conjunctivitis is stratified by the day of onset and by the organism, because the treatment and the consequences differ sharply. Gonococcal disease presents within the first two to five days with hyperacute purulent discharge and threatens the cornea within hours, whereas chlamydial disease presents at the end of the first week to the middle of the second with a more indolent mucopurulent discharge and lid swelling. Chlamydial infection is acquired during passage through the birth canal and colonises the nasopharynx as well as the eye, which is why systemic rather than topical therapy is mandatory and why an afebrile infant with a staccato cough at six weeks may be the same infection presenting again. Any neonatal chlamydial or gonococcal infection is a sexually transmitted infection in the mother, so contact tracing and testing for co-infection are part of the management, not an optional extra.
key_points: Onset at the end of the first week points away from gonococcal disease
A negative Gram stain and culture for Neisseria excludes the hyperacute sight threatening cause
Topical therapy leaves the nasopharyngeal reservoir and the pneumonitis risk untreated
Maternal and partner treatment with contact tracing is part of the infant's management
Clear corneas on fluorescein staining exclude established corneal involvement
explanation.pearls: Chlamydial pneumonitis appears between four and twelve weeks of age as an afebrile infant with a staccato cough, tachypnoea and eosinophilia, and a history of a sticky eye in the second week of life is often the only clue linking the two presentations.

subtopic_detail: Refusal to weight bear in a four year old with a temperature of 38.7 degrees and a C reactive protein of 62
stem:
You are the emergency registrar assessing a 4 year old boy who has refused to stand since waking this morning and cries when his mother lifts him. He had a mild runny nose a week ago that has since settled, and there has been no injury.

He looks unwell and flushed. He lies with the right hip held flexed, abducted and externally rotated, and he resists any passive movement through more than about 10 degrees in any direction. There is no rash, no joint swelling elsewhere and no bony tenderness over the tibia or femoral shaft.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 152 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right hip held flexed abducted and externally rotated with guarding through a 10 degree arc, no effusion palpable at the knee, no overlying erythema or warmth over the thigh, no rash, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 17.4 x10^9/L (5.0 to 15.0), C reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 58 mm/h (less than 15), blood culture collected, hip radiograph shows no fracture and no femoral head abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Urgent orthopaedic referral for hip joint aspiration under anaesthesia
options.rationale: He meets four of the predictors used to separate septic arthritis from transient synovitis, which places the probability of infection high enough that the joint must be sampled. Aspiration under anaesthesia confirms the diagnosis and decompresses a joint whose cartilage and femoral head blood supply are at risk within hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain)

options.text: Oral ibuprofen and review in forty eight hours if he is not improving
options.rationale: Anti inflammatory treatment and review is the pathway for transient synovitis, which typically follows a viral illness in a child who is afebrile, still weight bears with a limp and has normal or near normal inflammatory markers. A temperature of 38.7 degrees with a C reactive protein of 62 and complete refusal to weight bear does not fit that pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain)

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin and review the response overnight
options.rationale: Antibiotics before aspiration reduce the yield of synovial culture and can leave the child on a prolonged empirical course without an organism or a drained joint. Antibiotics are started immediately after the sample is taken, not instead of taking it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange a hip radiograph and review once the film has been reported
options.rationale: A radiograph has already been taken and is normal, which is expected because plain films stay normal for the first one to two weeks of joint or bone infection. Repeating imaging that cannot exclude the diagnosis simply delays the definitive test. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain)

options.text: Arrange bone scintigraphy and review once the scan has been reported
options.rationale: Scintigraphy is a second line study when the site of infection is genuinely unclear, and it takes hours to arrange while adding radiation. Here the hip is clinically localised, so the sampling procedure is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Septic arthritis in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Septic arthritis in children

explanation.summary: The irritable hip in a young child sits on a spectrum from transient synovitis, which is self limiting, to septic arthritis, which destroys cartilage and can infarct the femoral head within days. The Kocher predictors of fever above 38.5 degrees, refusal to weight bear, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 and a white cell count above 12 stratify that risk, with the probability of infection rising steeply as the number of predictors increases, and Australian practice adds a C reactive protein above 20 as a further strong predictor. Ultrasound reliably shows an effusion but cannot distinguish an infected effusion from a sterile one, so it guides aspiration rather than replacing it. The hip is held flexed, abducted and externally rotated in both conditions because that position maximises capsular volume and minimises intracapsular pressure.
key_points: The position of comfort is common to both diagnoses and does not discriminate
Plain radiographs are normal early in septic arthritis and cannot exclude it
Ultrasound shows an effusion but cannot tell an infected joint from a sterile one
Synovial fluid must be obtained before antibiotics wherever possible
A preceding viral illness is compatible with either diagnosis
explanation.pearls: A child with an irritable hip who is afebrile, weight bears with a limp and has a C reactive protein below 20 can usually be managed as transient synovitis with review in 48 hours, whereas any one of fever above 38.5 degrees, complete refusal to weight bear, or a C reactive protein above 20 moves the child into the aspiration pathway.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Septic arthritis in children

subtopic_detail: Soiling most days in a six year old with a palpable abdominal faecal mass who passed meconium on the first day of life
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6 year old boy whose parents report that he is dirtying his underpants almost every day and that the smell has become a problem at school. They say he opens his bowels properly only once every week or so, and that when he does the stool is so large it blocks the toilet.

He passed his first bowel motion on the day he was born and grew normally through infancy. He is now withholding, standing on tiptoes and crossing his legs when he feels the urge. His abdomen is soft with a firm indentable mass palpable in the left iliac fossa and suprapubically. The perianal skin is normal, anal tone is normal on inspection with no fissure seen, and the lower limb neurological examination and back are normal.

data_table.Examination: Weight and height tracking the 50th centile, abdomen soft and non tender with a firm indentable faecal mass in the left iliac fossa extending suprapubically, normally sited anus with normal perianal sensation, no sacral dimple or hair tuft, normal power tone and reflexes in both legs
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: A phosphate enema daily until the impaction clears, then maintenance
options.rationale: Rectal treatment is distressing in a child who is already withholding and reinforces the aversion that drives the cycle, and repeated phosphate enemas carry a risk of electrolyte disturbance. Enemas are reserved for oral disimpaction that has failed. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: A lactulose maintenance dose with a high fibre diet and toilet sitting
options.rationale: Starting maintenance without clearing the impaction leaves soft stool to leak past the retained mass, so the soiling continues and the family concludes the treatment has failed. The near pair here is that this is exactly the right regimen once disimpaction is complete. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: An escalating oral macrogol regimen followed by a maintenance dose
options.rationale: The overflow soiling is caused by liquid stool passing around a retained faecal mass, so the mass must be cleared before any maintenance regimen can work, and an escalating oral macrogol course achieves this without rectal intervention. Maintenance then continues for months, because stopping as soon as the stools normalise is the commonest cause of relapse. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Referral for manual evacuation under anaesthesia, then maintenance
options.rationale: Manual evacuation under anaesthesia is a last resort for impaction resistant to oral and rectal treatment, and it exposes the child to an anaesthetic for a problem that usually resolves medically. It is not a first line intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Referral for anorectal manometry before any laxative is commenced
options.rationale: Manometry and rectal biopsy investigate an aganglionic segment, which is made unlikely by passage of meconium on the first day, normal growth and a rectum loaded with stool rather than empty. Investigating before treating delays relief in a child with a clear functional picture. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Constipation in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Constipation in children

explanation.summary: Faecal incontinence in a school aged child is usually overflow from chronic functional constipation rather than a behavioural problem, and framing it that way to the family is an important part of the consultation because blame is common and unhelpful. The cycle starts with a painful or frightening stool, leads to withholding, and produces a dilated rectum that loses the sensation of fullness so that soft stool leaks past the retained mass without the child noticing. Treatment has two distinct phases, disimpaction and then maintenance, and skipping the first phase is the commonest reason treatment appears to fail. Red flags that redirect the workup include delayed passage of meconium beyond 48 hours, ribbon stools with an empty rectum, faltering growth, a sacral dimple or hair tuft, and abnormal lower limb neurology.
key_points: Soiling in this setting is overflow incontinence, not deliberate behaviour
Disimpaction must precede maintenance or the soiling continues
Passage of meconium on day one makes an aganglionic segment unlikely
A normal back and normal lower limb neurology argue against a spinal cause
Maintenance is continued for months, and stopping early causes relapse
explanation.pearls: Warn the family before starting disimpaction that soiling usually gets worse for the first several days as the retained mass breaks up, because families who are not warned stop the macrogol at exactly the point it is starting to work.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Constipation in children

subtopic_detail: Escherichia coli sepsis with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in a nine day old whose urine gives positive reducing substances with a negative glucose oxidase strip
stem: A 9-day-old girl with lethargy and poor feeding has grown Escherichia coli from blood culture. She fed well until her mother's milk came in, then vomited after most feeds. Newborn screening is pending.

data_table.Examination: Lethargic, jaundiced to the abdomen, liver 3 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 268 micromol/L, conjugated 92 micromol/L, ALT 148 U/L, INR 1.9, glucose 2.4 mmol/L, urine reducing substances positive with a negative glucose oxidase strip

lead_in: What is the most appropriate feeding management?

options.text: Continue breastfeeding and start phototherapy
options.rationale: Phototherapy acts on unconjugated bilirubin and does nothing for a conjugated fraction of 92 micromol/L, and continuing lactose containing milk sustains the toxic metabolite load. A conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia always signals liver disease rather than the exaggerated physiological jaundice that phototherapy treats. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Stop lactose-containing feeds and give a soy formula
options.rationale: Positive urinary reducing substances with a negative glucose oxidase strip means a non glucose reducing sugar is present, which in a jaundiced neonate with coagulopathy and Gram negative sepsis points to galactose accumulation, and the specific treatment is immediate removal of dietary galactose. Waiting for the newborn screening result risks progressive liver failure, so the feed is changed on suspicion and the diagnostic samples are taken alongside. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic conditions)

options.text: Continue breastfeeding and start ursodeoxycholic acid
options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid is a bile flow agent used in established cholestatic disease and does not address a substrate that is actively injuring the liver while the feed continues. It would leave the galactose load in place. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Galactosaemia)

options.text: Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula
options.rationale: Extensively hydrolysed formulas break down the protein but most still contain lactose, so the offending sugar is delivered unchanged. The near pair here is that the hydrolysed formula is the right answer for cow's milk protein allergy, where the protein rather than the sugar is the problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic conditions)

options.text: Stop enteral feeds and give intravenous 10% dextrose
options.rationale: Dextrose corrects the hypoglycaemia but prolonged starvation of a septic neonate is not a sustainable plan, and a galactose free feed both removes the substrate and provides nutrition. Intravenous glucose is a useful adjunct rather than the definitive feeding decision. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic conditions)

explanation.summary: Classical galactosaemia presents in the first two weeks once milk feeding is established, because galactose from lactose accumulates as galactose 1 phosphate and injures the liver, kidney and brain. The triad that should trigger suspicion is a jaundiced unwell neonate with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia, and Gram negative sepsis, since Escherichia coli sepsis is characteristically associated with the condition through impaired neutrophil function. Newborn screening in Australia includes galactosaemia, but the result may not be back before the infant becomes unwell, so the diagnosis is made clinically and the feed is changed immediately rather than waiting. Even with prompt dietary treatment, long term outcomes include learning difficulties and primary ovarian insufficiency in girls, so treatment is not curative and follow up is lifelong.
key_points: Positive reducing substances with a negative glucose strip indicates a non glucose sugar
Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in a neonate always indicates liver disease
Gram negative sepsis is characteristically associated with this metabolic disorder
Dietary galactose is removed on suspicion rather than after confirmation
Hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy reflect hepatic involvement rather than sepsis alone
explanation.pearls: Galactose free soy formula is started on clinical suspicion, but the diagnostic red cell galactose 1 phosphate uridyltransferase assay must be taken before any red cell transfusion, because transfused donor enzyme masks the deficiency for up to three months.

subtopic_detail: A femoral shaft fracture in a non ambulant five month old with blue sclerae and a father who broke bones easily as a child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the emergency department to see a five month old boy brought in because he cries whenever his nappy is changed. His parents say he rolled off a low couch onto a carpeted floor the previous afternoon and seemed briefly upset but then settled.

He has not yet rolled over deliberately, does not sit unsupported and is not crawling. His father says he broke his own arm twice as a child and that his teeth chipped easily. On examination the sclerae have a blue-grey tinge, the left thigh is swollen and he resists movement of that leg. The radiograph shows a transverse fracture of the left femoral shaft and the radiologist notes no other fractures on that film.
