options.text: Bolus of 5 per cent glucose, then maintenance fluid
options.rationale: A glucose bolus delivers free water rapidly to a hypernatraemic brain and is the classic route to cerebral oedema and seizures during correction, and her glucose is normal so there is no metabolic indication for it. Where a bolus is needed for circulatory compromise it is given as isotonic sodium chloride. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on intravenous fluids)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on intravenous fluids

options.text: Lactation support with formula top ups at home tomorrow
options.rationale: Home management is appropriate for the well infant with modest weight loss and normal alertness, but this baby is lethargic with a sodium of 158 mmol/L and biochemical evidence of prerenal impairment. Feeding support is essential but must accompany admission rather than replace it. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on dehydration)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on dehydration

options.text: Admit for intravenous 0.9 per cent sodium chloride
options.rationale: Hypernatraemic dehydration is corrected with isotonic fluid so that the fall in serum sodium is gradual, aiming for no more than about 0.5 mmol/L per hour or 10 to 12 mmol/L per day, with four hourly electrolytes to steer the rate. Admission also allows skilled lactation support, which addresses the cause and protects the breastfeeding relationship. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on dehydration)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on dehydration
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on intravenous fluids

options.text: Admit for intensive phototherapy and intravenous fluid
options.rationale: Her bilirubin sits well below the treatment threshold for her age in hours, so phototherapy is not indicated, and making jaundice the target distracts from the sodium and the feeding problem. Jaundice in this setting is largely a consequence of poor intake and improves as hydration and feeding improve. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on neonatal jaundice

options.text: Septic screen with lumbar puncture and antibiotics
options.rationale: A septic screen is mandatory in a lethargic neonate when the cause is not evident, but here the lethargy is fully explained by a documented 13 per cent weight loss with hypernatraemia, she is afebrile with a normal C reactive protein, and the feeding history identifies the mechanism. Cultures and antibiotics remain a low threshold addition if she does not improve with rehydration. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on febrile and unwell neonates)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on febrile and unwell neonates

explanation.summary: Hypernatraemic dehydration in the first week of life is almost always a lactation problem rather than a disease of the infant, arising when attachment difficulties or nipple trauma limit milk transfer before the milk supply is established. Weight loss beyond about ten per cent of birthweight, fewer than four wet nappies a day after day four, and persistent dark stools beyond day four are the practical warning signs. The clinical picture is deceptive because intravascular volume is relatively preserved in hypernatraemia, so the infant can look less unwell than the sodium suggests, and doughy skin with irritability or lethargy is more typical than shock. Correction is deliberately slow, with isotonic fluid and frequent electrolyte monitoring, because rapid falls in serum sodium cause cerebral oedema and seizures. Skilled lactation support is part of the treatment and not an afterthought, since most mothers can continue to breastfeed successfully once attachment is corrected and supply is supported.
key_points: Weight loss over ten per cent with lethargy and reduced wet nappies in the first week points to inadequate milk transfer.
Hypernatraemia preserves intravascular volume, so the infant may look better than the biochemistry suggests.
Correction uses isotonic fluid with a target fall in sodium of no more than about 0.5 mmol/L per hour.
Hypotonic fluid or glucose boluses risk cerebral oedema and seizures during correction.
Lactation support addresses the underlying cause and preserves breastfeeding.
explanation.pearls: Serum sodium should be rechecked four hourly during correction, and if it is falling faster than about 0.5 mmol/L per hour the sodium content of the fluid is increased or the rate reduced rather than the fluid simply being stopped.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on dehydration
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on intravenous fluids
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on neonatal jaundice
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on febrile and unwell neonates

subtopic_detail: Recurrent bone pain at multiple sites with sterile biopsy cultures and no response to prolonged antibiotics in an eleven year old
stem: An 11-year-old girl had left clavicular pain and swelling nine months ago. Open biopsy was sterile; she completed six weeks of flucloxacillin and the pain returned once treatment stopped. She now has three weeks of right thigh pain, worst at night.

data_table.Investigations: CRP 11 mg/L, blood count and lactate dehydrogenase normal; lucent right femoral metaphyseal lesion with sclerotic margins

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Recommence intravenous antibiotics for another six weeks
options.rationale: Six weeks of appropriate antibiotics with sterile blood and biopsy cultures and a relapse on cessation is evidence against bacterial osteomyelitis rather than an argument for more of the same. Repeating the course commits her to line related risks while the underlying inflammatory process continues. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on bone and joint infection)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on bone and joint infection

options.text: Arrange whole body magnetic resonance imaging and rheumatology referral
options.rationale: Culture negative multifocal osteitis that relapses after antibiotics is the pattern of chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis, and whole body magnetic resonance imaging is the investigation that establishes multifocality by revealing clinically silent lesions, which both supports the diagnosis and provides a baseline for monitoring. Demonstrating symmetrical or clavicular and metaphyseal lesions without an infective focus moves care to rheumatology, where non steroidal anti inflammatory therapy is first line. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis

options.text: Perform a bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics
options.rationale: Marrow examination is the correct move when there are cytopenias, blasts on the film, a raised lactate dehydrogenase, systemic symptoms or a soft tissue mass, whereas her counts, film and lactate dehydrogenase are unremarkable and a lesion was already biopsied nine months ago. Malignancy remains in the differential and is addressed by biopsy of a representative lesion if imaging is atypical, rather than by marrow sampling first. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis

options.text: Request a technetium bone scan to map skeletal involvement
options.rationale: Scintigraphy does detect additional lesions but delivers ionising radiation and is less sensitive than whole body magnetic resonance imaging for marrow oedema, particularly in the vertebrae where collapse is the complication that changes management. It is the fallback when magnetic resonance imaging is unavailable or not tolerated. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone daily for the next four weeks
options.rationale: Corticosteroid will suppress symptoms in several of the conditions on this differential, including malignancy, and so obscures the diagnosis before it has been made. In established chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis the first line agent is a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug, with corticosteroid, bisphosphonate or tumour necrosis factor blockade reserved for refractory or spinal disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis, historically called chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis when multiple sites are involved, is an autoinflammatory bone disease of children with a median onset around ten years of age. It characteristically affects the metaphyses of long bones, the clavicle, the pelvis and the vertebrae, produces pain that is often worse at night, and is accompanied by only modest elevation of inflammatory markers. The diagnostic difficulty is that each individual lesion mimics subacute bacterial osteomyelitis or a bone tumour, so children commonly receive prolonged antibiotics before the multifocal, culture negative, relapsing pattern is recognised. Whole body magnetic resonance imaging is central because clinically silent lesions are present in most children and their distribution, particularly symmetrical metaphyseal or clavicular involvement, supports the diagnosis while also identifying vertebral lesions at risk of collapse. Treatment begins with non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs, which control around half of cases, with bisphosphonates favoured for spinal disease and tumour necrosis factor inhibitors for refractory disease, and associated conditions such as palmoplantar pustulosis, severe acne and inflammatory bowel disease are sought.
key_points: Relapse after an adequate antibiotic course with sterile cultures is the observation that redirects the diagnosis away from bacterial osteomyelitis.
Clavicular and metaphyseal lesions with night pain and modestly raised inflammatory markers are the typical pattern.
Whole body magnetic resonance imaging reveals clinically silent lesions, confirms multifocality and identifies vertebral involvement.
Biopsy remains necessary for unifocal or atypical disease because malignancy cannot be excluded on imaging alone.
Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are first line, with bisphosphonates for spinal lesions and biologics for refractory disease.
explanation.pearls: Vertebral involvement is the reason whole body imaging is preferred over targeted scans, because vertebra plana from an undetected spinal lesion causes permanent deformity and is the finding that moves treatment straight to a bisphosphonate such as pamidronate rather than a trial of naproxen.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on bone and joint infection

subtopic_detail: Both feet turning inwards when running in a four year old who sits between his heels with a normal neurological examination
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a four year old boy whose parents are worried that both feet turn inwards when he runs and that he trips more than other children at kindergarten. They have been told by a relative that he needs special boots.

He walked at thirteen months, has no pain, and keeps up with his friends at the playground. His parents say he always sits on the floor between his heels with his knees together.

data_table.Examination: Both patellae point inwards on walking, hip internal rotation 80 degrees with external rotation 15 degrees bilaterally in the prone position, thigh foot angle neutral on both sides, lateral borders of both feet straight with no forefoot deviation, tone power and reflexes normal in both legs with downgoing plantar responses, symmetrical leg lengths, no joint swelling
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer him to an orthopaedic surgeon to be assessed for a derotation osteotomy of both femurs before he starts school next year
options.rationale: Femoral derotation osteotomy is a major procedure reserved for severe rotational deformity that persists beyond about eight to ten years with genuine functional or cosmetic disability. Offering it to a four year old with a condition that resolves on its own in the great majority is disproportionate. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

options.text: Reassure the parents that this is physiological femoral anteversion and review only if it persists beyond the age of eight
options.rationale: Increased hip internal rotation with correspondingly reduced external rotation, a neutral thigh foot angle and straight lateral foot borders localises the rotation to the femur, and femoral anteversion peaks around four to six years and then remodels spontaneously in almost all children. Habitual W sitting is a consequence of the anteversion rather than its cause. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

options.text: Prescribe a night time derotation brace to be worn until the rotational profile of both of his legs has normalised
options.rationale: Braces, corrective shoes and twister cables have all been shown not to alter the natural history of rotational variants and they disturb sleep and self image for no benefit. Bracing retains a role in structural conditions such as developmental dysplasia of the hip and idiopathic scoliosis. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

options.text: Refer him for serial casting of both feet to correct the inward deviation of the forefoot that is causing his gait
options.rationale: Serial casting treats metatarsus adductus, in which the lateral border of the foot is curved and the forefoot deviates medially, and his feet have straight lateral borders. The level of the rotation is determined by examining the hip, the thigh foot angle and the foot separately. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and spine to look for a neurological cause of his in-toeing and his tripping
options.rationale: Spastic diplegia is the important neurological mimic of in-toeing, but it produces increased tone, brisk reflexes, upgoing plantar responses and usually a history of delayed walking, none of which are present. Imaging is warranted when the rotational deformity is asymmetrical or when the neurological examination is abnormal. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

explanation.summary: In-toeing is one of the commonest reasons for orthopaedic referral in early childhood and is almost always one of three physiological rotational variants, each of which has a characteristic age of presentation and a specific examination finding that localises it. Metatarsus adductus presents in infancy with a curved lateral foot border, internal tibial torsion presents in the toddler years with an internally rotated thigh foot angle, and femoral anteversion presents between about three and six years with markedly increased hip internal rotation and reduced external rotation. The rotational profile examination, performed with the child prone, separates these in a few minutes without any imaging. All three remodel spontaneously with growth, and no orthosis, shoe modification or exercise program has been shown to change the outcome, so the intervention is explanation and reassurance with a defined review point. The findings that should prompt further assessment are asymmetry, pain, an abnormal neurological examination, or persistence with functional disability into later childhood.
key_points: The rotational profile examination localises in-toeing to the foot, the tibia or the femur.
Increased internal with reduced external hip rotation indicates femoral anteversion.
A curved lateral foot border indicates metatarsus adductus rather than a rotational problem above it.
Braces, corrective shoes and exercises do not alter the natural history of any of these variants.
Asymmetry, pain or abnormal tone and reflexes are the findings that justify further assessment.
explanation.pearls: Measure hip rotation with the child prone and the knees flexed to 90 degrees, because total hip rotation stays roughly constant at around 90 to 100 degrees throughout childhood and it is the shift of that arc towards internal rotation, rather than the absolute internal rotation figure, that identifies femoral anteversion.

sources.label: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric lower limb variants
BMJ Best Practice: Gait abnormalities in children

subtopic_detail: Three weeks of pale greasy stools and weight loss in a preschooler after a childcare outbreak of loose motions
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a three year old girl whose mother reports three weeks of loose, pale, foul smelling motions that float, with a lot of wind and a swollen tummy. She has lost 0.8 kg over that time.

Four other children at her childcare centre have had similar prolonged loose motions in the past month. There has been no blood in the stool, no fever and no vomiting. She has eaten bread and cereal daily since she was seven months old without any previous bowel trouble, and her growth had tracked the 50th centile until this illness.

data_table.Examination: Mildly distended soft abdomen, no organomegaly, no mouth ulcers, no perianal disease, no rash, no clubbing, mucous membranes moist
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), albumin 38 g/L (35 to 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send a faecal specimen for protozoal nucleic acid amplification testing before starting any antimicrobial treatment
options.rationale: Prolonged non bloody steatorrhoea with flatulence, bloating and weight loss following a childcare cluster is the classic picture of giardiasis, and faecal nucleic acid amplification testing is far more sensitive than a single microscopy specimen. Confirming the organism before treating avoids committing a child to nitroimidazole therapy for what may prove to be a different diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start oral metronidazole empirically for three days and review her symptoms and weight in the clinic in two weeks
options.rationale: Empirical treatment is reasonable only when testing is unavailable, and here it would remove the chance to confirm an organism that must be notified and traced back to the childcare centre. Treatment is correct once the diagnosis is established, and single dose tinidazole is the preferred Australian regimen in children who can take it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Request coeliac serology with a total immunoglobulin A level and arrange gastroenterology review for possible biopsy
options.rationale: Coeliac disease produces exactly this stool description and weight loss, but it does not arrive abruptly three weeks ago in a child who has eaten gluten uneventfully for over two years, nor does it cluster among four other children at the same centre. It becomes the priority if the stool testing is negative and symptoms persist. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Chronic diarrhoea in children)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Chronic diarrhoea in children

options.text: Advise a two week trial of a strictly lactose free diet and review whether the stool frequency and bloating improve
options.rationale: Secondary lactose intolerance does follow gastroenteritis and can cause bloating and loose stools, but it does not cause progressive weight loss over three weeks and it does not explain the fatty floating stools. A dietary trial here delays a diagnosis that requires specific treatment and public health follow up. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Chronic diarrhoea in children)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Chronic diarrhoea in children

options.text: Arrange an abdominal ultrasound to look for a structural cause of her distension and her three weeks of loose stools
options.rationale: Imaging has no role in a well child with a soft abdomen, no organomegaly and normal inflammatory markers, and a normal scan would falsely reassure everyone. Ultrasound earns its place when there is an abdominal mass, organomegaly or a suspicion of intussusception. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Chronic diarrhoea in children)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Chronic diarrhoea in children

explanation.summary: Giardia duodenalis is the commonest protozoal cause of persistent diarrhoea in Australian children and spreads readily by the faecal oral route in childcare centres, where asymptomatic carriage sustains outbreaks. The organism blunts the small bowel villi and causes fat malabsorption, which is why the stools are pale, greasy and offensive rather than watery, and why weight loss appears within weeks. Faecal nucleic acid amplification testing has largely replaced the three specimen microscopy request because cyst shedding is intermittent and a single microscopy sample misses around half of cases. Treatment in Australia is a nitroimidazole, with tinidazole as a single dose being the usual first choice in children old enough to swallow it, and household contacts are treated only if symptomatic. Giardiasis is notifiable in most jurisdictions, which matters here because identifying the organism triggers exclusion and hygiene measures at the centre.
key_points: Pale greasy floating stools with flatulence and weight loss point to small bowel malabsorption, not colitis.
A childcare cluster with prolonged non bloody diarrhoea strongly suggests giardiasis.
Faecal nucleic acid amplification testing outperforms single specimen microscopy because cyst shedding is intermittent.
Long standing uneventful gluten exposure with abrupt onset argues against coeliac disease as the cause.
Confirming the organism triggers public health exclusion measures at the childcare centre.
explanation.pearls: Children with giardiasis should be excluded from childcare until they have had no loose stool for 24 hours, and a single 50 mg per kg dose of tinidazole to a maximum of 2 g cures around 90 per cent, which is why persistent symptoms after treatment should prompt a test for post infectious lactose intolerance rather than a second course.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Chronic diarrhoea in children

subtopic_detail: Screaming and thrashing an hour and a half after falling asleep in a preschooler who has no memory of it next day
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a four year old girl whose parents describe frightening episodes three or four nights a week. About ninety minutes after she falls asleep she sits up screaming, pushes them away and thrashes about with her eyes wide open, appearing terrified and not recognising them.

Each episode lasts around five minutes and she then settles back to sleep. In the morning she is cheerful and remembers nothing about it. Her father had similar episodes as a boy. She does not snore and has no daytime sleepiness.

data_table.Examination: Growth along the 50th centile, development age appropriate with fluent sentences, tonsils not enlarged on inspection, no dysmorphic features, neurological examination normal with normal tone power and reflexes, no skin stigmata of a neurocutaneous syndrome
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure her parents, advise safety measures in the bedroom and explain that the episodes settle without treatment
options.rationale: Arousal from the deepest non rapid eye movement sleep in the first third of the night, with unresponsiveness during the event and complete amnesia afterwards in a child with a family history, is a night terror, and these resolve spontaneously through childhood. Parents are advised not to wake or restrain the child and to make the bedroom and stairs safe. (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children

options.text: Arrange an overnight sleep electroencephalogram to look for frontal lobe seizures arising out of sleep
options.rationale: Sleep related hypermotor seizures are the key mimic but are stereotyped, brief, often occur several times in one night and typically leave the child aware or rousable afterwards. An electroencephalogram is warranted for stereotyped repetitive events, daytime episodes or any developmental regression. (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children

options.text: Commence low dose clonazepam at bedtime and review the frequency of the episodes in the clinic after four weeks
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines suppress deep non rapid eye movement sleep and are occasionally used for parasomnias, but they are not justified for a benign self limiting condition in a preschooler. They are reserved for episodes that are dangerous or that persist and disrupt the family severely despite all behavioural measures. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer her for polysomnography and adenotonsillectomy assessment on the basis that sleep disordered breathing is triggering the episodes
options.rationale: Obstructive sleep apnoea does fragment sleep and can provoke parasomnias, which is why it is asked about, but she does not snore, has no daytime sleepiness and has normal sized tonsils. A sleep study is indicated when snoring, witnessed apnoea or daytime symptoms are present alongside the parasomnia. (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children

options.text: Refer her to a child psychologist on the basis that these episodes represent anxiety dreams requiring trauma focused assessment
options.rationale: Nightmares occur in the second half of the night during rapid eye movement sleep, the child wakes fully, is consolable and recalls the dream, all of which are the opposite of what is described here. Psychological assessment is appropriate for recurrent distressing nightmares, particularly after a traumatic event. (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children

explanation.summary: Night terrors are a disorder of arousal from slow wave sleep and affect a substantial minority of preschool and early primary school children, with a strong familial tendency. They are separated from nightmares by four features: timing in the first third of the night rather than the second half, profound unresponsiveness and inconsolability during the event rather than a child who wakes and seeks comfort, marked autonomic arousal with sweating, tachycardia and dilated pupils, and complete amnesia the next morning. The important differential is sleep related hypermotor epilepsy, suggested by highly stereotyped brief events, clustering several times in a single night, or a persisting abnormality on waking. Sleep deprivation, irregular bedtimes, fever and untreated obstructive sleep apnoea all increase the frequency of arousal parasomnias, so addressing those is the practical intervention along with safety proofing the sleeping environment. Parents should be told explicitly not to wake or restrain the child, since doing so prolongs and intensifies the episode.
key_points: Night terrors arise from slow wave sleep in the first third of the night with complete amnesia afterwards.
Nightmares occur later in the night, the child wakes fully, is consolable and remembers the dream.
Stereotyped brief events clustering several times a night suggest sleep related seizures.
Sleep deprivation, irregular bedtimes, fever and sleep disordered breathing increase frequency.
Parents should not wake or restrain the child, and the sleeping environment is made safe.
explanation.pearls: Scheduled awakenings, in which the parent rouses the child briefly about fifteen to thirty minutes before the usual time of the event for a week or two, reduce night terror frequency substantially and are worth offering to exhausted families before any medication is considered.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children

subtopic_detail: Flattening at the back of the head in a five month old with the ear on the flattened side sitting forward of the other
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a five month old girl whose parents are distressed about the shape of her head. They say the back right side looks squashed and that it has become more obvious over the past two months, and they have read that a helmet may be needed.

She was born at term, rolls both ways, has good head control and has no feeding difficulty. She sleeps on her back and spends much of the day in a rocker.

data_table.Examination: Flattening of the right occiput with the right ear displaced anteriorly relative to the left and mild fullness of the right forehead, giving a parallelogram outline when viewed from above, no ridging palpable over any suture, no mastoid bulge behind either ear, anterior fontanelle soft and open, head circumference tracking the 50th centile, full passive neck rotation to both sides

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise counter positioning with supervised tummy time and cot repositioning, and review her head shape in two months
options.rationale: An anteriorly displaced ear with ipsilateral forehead fullness produces the parallelogram of deformational plagiocephaly, which responds to repositioning because the skull is still growing rapidly at five months. Most cases improve substantially with conservative measures and need nothing further. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Refer her urgently to the craniofacial service on the basis that a fused lambdoid suture is the likeliest explanation
options.rationale: Lambdoid synostosis is the near pair that must be excluded, but it pushes the ear on the affected side posteriorly and produces a mastoid bulge with a trapezoid rather than parallelogram outline, and neither feature is present. The direction the ear is displaced is the single most useful bedside discriminator. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the skull with three dimensional reconstruction to assess all of the cranial sutures
options.rationale: Computed tomography delivers a substantial radiation dose to a developing brain and is not needed when the clinical pattern is diagnostic of a positional deformity. It is reserved for cases where synostosis is genuinely suspected on examination and a craniofacial team requests it. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Refer her now for a moulding helmet orthosis to be fitted, because the deformity has been progressing over recent months
options.rationale: Helmet therapy is expensive, demanding for families and has not been shown in randomised comparison to outperform repositioning for mild to moderate deformity. It is considered only for severe deformity that has failed an adequate trial of repositioning, usually between five and eight months of age. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Refer her to physiotherapy for treatment of an underlying tightness of the neck muscles driving the positional preference
options.rationale: Torticollis commonly drives plagiocephaly and physiotherapy is then essential, but this infant has full passive rotation in both directions and no palpable muscle mass, so there is no restriction to treat. The presence or absence of a passive rotation deficit decides whether physiotherapy is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

explanation.summary: Deformational plagiocephaly became common after supine sleeping was correctly promoted to reduce sudden unexpected death in infancy, and it reflects external moulding of a soft skull rather than any abnormality of the sutures. Viewed from above the head forms a parallelogram, because the occipital flattening pushes the ipsilateral ear and forehead forward, whereas true lambdoid synostosis restricts growth and pulls the ipsilateral ear backwards with a compensatory mastoid bulge, giving a trapezoid. That single distinction spares almost every infant a computed tomography scan. Conservative management works because the skull grows fastest in the first year, so the earlier repositioning begins the more correction is achieved. Parents need explicit reassurance that the condition does not affect brain growth or development, since much of their distress comes from fearing that it does.
key_points: Parallelogram head shape with the ear displaced forward indicates a positional deformity.
Trapezoid shape with the ear displaced backwards and a mastoid bulge suggests lambdoid synostosis.
Palpable sutural ridging and a falling or rising head circumference are red flags for synostosis.
Repositioning and tummy time are first line and most effective before six months of age.
Always check passive neck rotation, since coexisting torticollis requires physiotherapy.
explanation.pearls: Assess the head from directly above the vertex rather than from the front, because the anterior or posterior position of the ear relative to its fellow is the finding that separates deformational plagiocephaly from lambdoid synostosis and it is almost invisible from any other angle.

subtopic_detail: Blotchy pink rash appearing on the trunk of a well eleven month old on the day a three day high fever settled
stem: An eleven-month-old boy has a pink blotchy rash that appeared this morning on his trunk and has spread to his neck. He had a temperature to 39.5 degrees C for three days, which broke overnight. He is now playing happily.

data_table.Examination: Blanching pink maculopapular rash on trunk and neck, sparing the face; afebrile, no conjunctival injection or coryza, no lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain a self limiting viral exanthem and give return advice
options.rationale: A high fever for three days that defervesces as a blanching truncal rash appears in a well infant is the defining sequence of roseola infantum, caused by human herpesvirus 6. The diagnosis is clinical, the illness is self limiting and testing changes nothing. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Notify public health and send measles serology
options.rationale: Measles is the notifiable mimic worth considering in any febrile child with a rash, but its rash appears while the fever is still high and is preceded by cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, none of which are present here. The temporal relationship of rash to fever is the discriminator between the two. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Measles)

options.text: Admit for blood cultures and intravenous antibiotics
options.rationale: A child who is playing, afebrile and has a blanching rash without petechiae has no features of invasive bacterial infection, and admission would expose him to unnecessary cannulation and antibiotics. Non blanching lesions, toxicity or an ill appearance would change this decision immediately. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Request a full blood count and film to exclude malignancy
options.rationale: Leukaemia can present with fever and skin lesions, but those lesions are petechiae or bruises rather than a blanching exanthem, and it is accompanied by pallor, lymphadenopathy or organomegaly, all absent here. Bleeding into the skin rather than a blanching rash is what should trigger a film. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Start oral amoxicillin and review the rash in two days
options.rationale: There is no bacterial focus and the illness has already resolved spontaneously, so antibiotics offer only adverse effects and resistance. Amoxicillin given to a child with undiagnosed infectious mononucleosis also provokes a florid rash that muddies the picture further. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Roseola infantum, also called exanthem subitum or sixth disease, is caused predominantly by human herpesvirus 6 and affects children between about six months and two years. Its signature is three to five days of high fever in a child who remains reasonably well, followed by abrupt defervescence and the emergence of a blanching pink rash that starts on the trunk and spreads centrifugally while the child is now afebrile. That sequence is diagnostic and separates it from measles, where the rash appears at the fever peak after a prodrome, and from scarlet fever, where the rash is sandpapery with perioral pallor and a strawberry tongue. Roseola is a common cause of febrile convulsion during the fever phase, which is worth mentioning to parents who have witnessed one. No treatment or exclusion is required and the rash fades within a few days without desquamation.
key_points: Rash appearing as the fever breaks is the defining feature of roseola infantum.
The child is characteristically well once afebrile, which supports the diagnosis.
Measles rash appears during high fever after cough, coryza and conjunctivitis.
No investigation or antibiotic is required for a well child with a blanching exanthem.
Any non blanching element or ill appearance overrides the diagnosis and demands sepsis assessment.
explanation.pearls: Human herpesvirus 6 accounts for roughly a third of first febrile convulsions in children under two, so a brief convulsion during the fever phase of roseola does not itself indicate a more serious illness or warrant lumbar puncture in an otherwise well child over twelve months.

subtopic_detail: Refusal to use one arm in a toddler after being lifted by the hand, with no swelling and no bony tenderness
stem:
You are the emergency department resident seeing a two year old girl brought in by her father twenty minutes after he lifted her by the hand up a kerb as she stumbled. He and her older brother both saw it happen. She cried immediately and has not used the left arm since.

She is now settled on her father's lap, playing with a toy in her right hand, and holds the left arm slightly bent at the elbow with the palm turned down against her body. She has no other injuries and there are no concerns about her care at home.

data_table.Examination: Left arm held in slight flexion and pronation, no swelling, deformity or bruising anywhere on the limb, no tenderness over the clavicle, humerus, forearm or wrist, mild discomfort on attempted supination at the elbow, hand warm and pink with a normal radial pulse, moves fingers normally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a reduction manoeuvre at the elbow and observe her for return of normal use of the arm before discharge
options.rationale: A typical traction mechanism with the arm held pronated and no swelling, deformity or bony tenderness is a pulled elbow, and either supination with flexion or hyperpronation restores function within minutes. Reduction is both the treatment and the confirmation of the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Request radiographs of the elbow and forearm first and arrange reduction only once a fracture has been formally excluded
options.rationale: Radiographs are normal in a pulled elbow because the radial head subluxation reduces or is not visible, so they add radiation and delay without changing management. Imaging is indicated when the history is atypical, when there is swelling, deformity or focal bony tenderness, or when a reduction attempt fails. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Apply a broad arm sling for comfort and arrange review in the fracture clinic within forty eight hours for reassessment
options.rationale: Immobilising the arm leaves a readily treatable subluxation in place and condemns the child to two more days of not using the limb. A sling is appropriate for an undisplaced fracture awaiting review, not for a condition curable at the bedside in seconds. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Refer her to the orthopaedic registrar for assessment of the elbow and definitive management of the arm she is not using
options.rationale: Reduction of a pulled elbow is a core emergency department skill and specialist referral is an unnecessary escalation. Orthopaedic involvement is warranted only after two failed reduction attempts or where imaging shows a fracture. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Undertake a skeletal survey and make a child protection notification before any attempt is made to treat the affected arm
options.rationale: A limb injury in a toddler always warrants a safeguarding thought, but here the mechanism is classical, independently witnessed, consistent with the findings and there are no other injuries or care concerns. An inconsistent or changing history, or bruising in unusual sites, would make this the priority. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: Pulled elbow, or radial head subluxation, occurs when longitudinal traction on a young child's extended pronated arm allows the annular ligament to slip over the radial head and become trapped in the radiocapitellar joint. It peaks between one and four years because the radial head is not yet fully developed and the ligament is lax, and it becomes rare after five. The child characteristically refuses to use the arm and holds it pronated and slightly flexed, but is otherwise comfortable and shows no swelling, which is what separates it from a fracture. Both hyperpronation and supination with flexion are effective, with hyperpronation succeeding slightly more often and causing less distress, and a palpable click at the radial head predicts success. Recurrence happens in around a quarter of children, so parents should be advised to lift the child under the arms rather than by the hands.
key_points: The mechanism is axial traction on a pronated extended arm, often lifting a child by the hand.
Absence of swelling, deformity and bony tenderness is what permits reduction without imaging.
Hyperpronation or supination with flexion both reduce the subluxation within minutes.
Return of spontaneous use within about fifteen minutes confirms the diagnosis.
Image the elbow if the history is atypical, if there is focal tenderness or if two attempts fail.
explanation.pearls: If the child is not using the arm within fifteen to thirty minutes of a technically satisfactory reduction, obtain elbow radiographs rather than repeating the manoeuvre a third time, because an occult supracondylar or proximal radial fracture is then the more likely explanation.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation

subtopic_detail: Drooling and refusal to drink in a toddler forty five minutes after swallowing strongly alkaline dishwasher powder
stem: A 2-year-old boy was found beside an open dishwasher with powder around his mouth 45 minutes ago; the container confirms a strongly alkaline detergent. He vomited once and has since drooled continuously and refused water.

data_table.Examination: Continuous drooling with pooled saliva, erythema of the tongue and palate with a white buccal plaque, no stridor or hoarseness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Nil by mouth with intravenous fluids and endoscopy at 12 to 24 hours
options.rationale: Drooling, vomiting and refusal to drink after an alkaline ingestion together predict significant oesophageal injury, and endoscopy between twelve and twenty four hours grades that injury when the burn has declared itself but before the tissue is at its most friable. Grading determines feeding, stricture surveillance and prognosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Give a single dose of activated charcoal and observe
options.rationale: Charcoal does not bind corrosives, obscures the mucosal view at endoscopy and risks a devastating aspiration into an already injured airway. It is reserved for ingestions of adsorbable toxins presenting within an hour with a protected airway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Encourage milk or water to dilute the alkali and observe
options.rationale: Dilution has no proven benefit beyond the first few minutes and provokes vomiting, which re exposes the oesophagus to the corrosive on the way back up. Small volumes of water may be offered immediately after ingestion, not forty five minutes later in a child who is drooling. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion

options.text: Give diluted lemon juice to neutralise the alkali now
options.rationale: Neutralisation is an exothermic reaction that adds a thermal burn to a chemical one, and it has no place in modern management. This is the classic anti pattern that the history of corrosive injury was written to abolish. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion

options.text: Commence high-dose oral corticosteroids to prevent stricture
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have never been shown to prevent stricture after corrosive injury and they mask the fever and peritonism that signal perforation. Their limited remaining role is decided by the endoscopic grade in specialist hands, not empirically before the oesophagus has been seen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

explanation.summary: Alkaline corrosives cause liquefactive necrosis, which penetrates deeply and continues to injure tissue after contact, whereas acids cause coagulative necrosis that tends to be more superficial in the oesophagus. Dishwasher and laundry detergents are among the commonest strongly alkaline agents in Australian homes and account for a large share of paediatric corrosive exposures. The presence of oral burns is an unreliable guide to what lies below, since serious oesophageal injury occurs with a normal mouth and an inflamed mouth may sit above a normal oesophagus, so the clinical triad of drooling, vomiting and dysphagia is used instead to select children for endoscopy. Timing matters because endoscopy before twelve hours may underestimate a burn that has not yet declared itself, while after about forty eight hours the wall is maximally friable and perforation risk rises. Long term, the concerns are stricture formation over subsequent weeks and a lifelong increase in oesophageal carcinoma risk.
key_points: Alkalis cause liquefactive necrosis that penetrates deeply and keeps injuring after contact.
Oral burns neither confirm nor exclude oesophageal injury.
Drooling, vomiting and refusal to drink together predict significant injury and select for endoscopy.
Charcoal, induced emesis, dilution beyond the first minutes and neutralisation are all contraindicated.
Endoscopy at twelve to twenty four hours grades the burn and guides feeding and stricture follow up.
explanation.pearls: Stridor, hoarseness or drooling with respiratory distress after a corrosive ingestion mandates airway assessment by an anaesthetist before anything else, because supraglottic oedema can progress over hours and a delayed intubation in a swollen corrosive injured airway is extremely difficult.

sources.label: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion

subtopic_detail: Profuse purulent discharge from both eyes with marked lid swelling on the third day of life after an unbooked pregnancy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the postnatal ward to see a baby girl on her third day of life. The midwife reports that both eyes began weeping yesterday evening and that this morning there is thick yellow discharge that reaccumulates within minutes of being wiped away.

Her mother arrived in labour without any antenatal care and no antenatal screening bloods or swabs were taken. The baby is feeding, has a normal temperature and has passed urine and meconium normally.

data_table.Examination: Marked bilateral eyelid oedema requiring gentle retraction to open the lids, profuse purulent discharge reaccumulating immediately, intense conjunctival injection and chemosis, corneas appear clear on the limited view obtained, no vesicles on the lids or scalp, anterior fontanelle soft, tone normal, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Take conjunctival swabs for culture and nucleic acid testing, give parenteral ceftriaxone and start hourly saline eye irrigation
options.rationale: Hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis with marked lid oedema in the first five days is gonococcal until proven otherwise, and it perforates the cornea within twenty four to forty eight hours if untreated. Parenteral third generation cephalosporin with frequent saline irrigation and urgent ophthalmology review is the standard Australian response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take conjunctival swabs for culture and nucleic acid testing and commence topical chloramphenicol drops two hourly to both eyes
options.rationale: Topical therapy alone does not clear gonococcal infection and does not treat the concurrent mucosal colonisation of the nasopharynx and rectum that drives relapse. Topical treatment is adequate for the non gonococcal bacterial conjunctivitis that presents later and without this degree of lid oedema. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take conjunctival swabs for culture and nucleic acid testing and commence a two week course of oral erythromycin for the baby
options.rationale: Oral erythromycin treats neonatal chlamydial infection, which is the near pair here, but chlamydia characteristically appears between the fifth and fourteenth days with a less purulent discharge and far less lid swelling. Chlamydia also needs treating if the testing confirms it, but it is not the organism that threatens this cornea today. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Gonorrhoea)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Gonorrhoea

options.text: Take conjunctival swabs for culture and nucleic acid testing and observe with regular saline cleaning and review the eyes tomorrow
options.rationale: Observation is appropriate for the sticky eye of nasolacrimal duct obstruction, where the conjunctiva stays white and the lids are not swollen. Applying it to a hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis risks corneal perforation and permanent blindness within a day. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take conjunctival swabs for viral testing and commence intravenous aciclovir with topical antiviral therapy to both affected eyes
options.rationale: Neonatal herpes simplex can involve the eye but produces a serous rather than frankly purulent discharge, usually with skin vesicles or dendritic corneal ulceration. Aciclovir becomes the priority if vesicles appear or if the baby develops encephalopathy or hepatitis. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Gonorrhoea)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Gonorrhoea

explanation.summary: Ophthalmia neonatorum means conjunctivitis in the first month of life, and the organism is predicted with reasonable accuracy by the day of onset and the character of the discharge. Neisseria gonorrhoeae presents between day one and day five with hyperacute profuse pus and dramatic lid oedema, and is the only cause that penetrates an intact corneal epithelium, which is why it can perforate the globe within two days. Chlamydia trachomatis is commoner overall but appears from day five to fourteen with a mucopurulent discharge and threatens the lungs rather than the cornea. The absence of antenatal screening is the single most important risk factor in this vignette, since Australian antenatal care would ordinarily have detected and treated maternal infection. Both mother and her sexual partners require testing and treatment, and both infections are notifiable.
key_points: Onset on days one to five with profuse pus and lid oedema indicates gonococcal infection.
Gonococcus can penetrate intact corneal epithelium and perforate the globe within forty eight hours.
Chlamydial ophthalmia presents from day five to fourteen and is treated with oral erythromycin.
Parenteral cephalosporin plus frequent saline irrigation is required, not topical therapy alone.
Test and treat the mother and her partners, and notify both infections.
explanation.pearls: Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis requires oral rather than topical treatment because around half of affected infants are also colonised in the nasopharynx and go on to develop an afebrile staccato cough pneumonitis between four and twelve weeks of age.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Gonorrhoea

subtopic_detail: Displaced elbow fracture in a school aged child whose hand stays warm and pink with no palpable radial pulse
stem: A 6-year-old boy fell onto an outstretched hand an hour ago. Radiographs show a completely displaced extension type supracondylar humeral fracture.

data_table.Examination: Deformity above the elbow, hand warm and pink, radial pulse impalpable and undetectable on Doppler, cannot make the circle sign with thumb and index finger, sensation intact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate theatre for closed reduction and percutaneous wire fixation
options.rationale: In a completely displaced supracondylar fracture the brachial artery is usually tented or kinked by the proximal fragment rather than transected, so reduction itself is the vascular intervention and it must not wait. The inability to make the circle sign indicates an anterior interosseous nerve palsy, which is a further indication for urgent operative reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus

options.text: Above elbow backslab and fracture clinic review within forty eight hours
options.rationale: Outpatient management is appropriate for undisplaced fractures with cortical contact, not for a completely displaced fracture with an absent pulse and a nerve deficit. Delaying reduction here allows progressive swelling that makes both reduction and vascular recovery harder. (Source: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus

options.text: Urgent computed tomography angiogram of the limb before any reduction
options.rationale: Angiography delays the reduction that usually restores flow and rarely alters the operative plan, since the injury site is already known from the fracture. It has a role only if the hand remains poorly perfused after a satisfactory reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus

options.text: Vascular surgery referral for brachial artery exploration before manipulation
options.rationale: Exploration before reduction operates on an artery whose problem is mechanical displacement, and most such arteries are found kinked rather than divided. Vascular involvement is warranted when the hand remains white and pulseless after the fracture has been reduced and stabilised. (Source: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus

options.text: Closed reduction under sedation in the emergency department with a backslab
options.rationale: A completely displaced supracondylar fracture is inherently unstable and redisplaces in plaster, so reduction without wire fixation fails and risks a cubitus varus deformity. Emergency department reduction is appropriate only as an emergency manoeuvre for a critically ischaemic limb when theatre is genuinely unavailable. (Source: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric supracondylar fractures)
source_refs: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric supracondylar fractures

explanation.summary: Supracondylar humeral fracture is the commonest elbow fracture of childhood and peaks between five and seven years, almost always from a fall onto an outstretched hand producing an extension type injury. The proximal fragment displaces anteriorly into the antecubital fossa, where it threatens the brachial artery and the median nerve with its anterior interosseous branch. The pink pulseless hand is the classic dilemma: perfusion is maintained by collateral flow around the elbow, and because the artery is usually kinked rather than cut, prompt reduction and stabilisation restores the pulse in most children. Anterior interosseous nerve injury produces weakness of the flexor pollicis longus and the index flexor digitorum profundus, so the child cannot make an O shape with thumb and index finger, and it recovers spontaneously in the great majority over weeks to months. A genuinely white pulseless hand is a surgical emergency of a different order and goes straight to theatre with vascular surgery on standby.
key_points: Extension type displacement drives the proximal fragment towards the brachial artery and median nerve.
A pink pulseless hand reflects collateral perfusion and is treated by urgent reduction and fixation.
Inability to make the circle sign indicates anterior interosseous nerve palsy.
Angiography and vascular exploration are reserved for persistent ischaemia after reduction.
Completely displaced fractures need percutaneous wires because plaster alone allows redisplacement.
explanation.pearls: Document the anterior interosseous nerve with the circle sign specifically, because it is a pure motor nerve with no sensory territory and a palsy present before reduction is entirely missed unless thumb interphalangeal and index distal interphalangeal flexion are tested individually.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus
Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric supracondylar fractures
BMJ Best Practice: Supracondylar humeral fracture

subtopic_detail: Six months of pain around the navel in a thriving nine year old with normal screening bloods whose parents want a scan
stem: A 9-year-old girl has six months of periumbilical pain on school mornings, easing at weekends and in holidays, never waking her at night. Her parents have asked for a scan.

data_table.Examination: Growth on the 50th centile, mild periumbilical tenderness only
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and CRP normal, negative coeliac serology with normal IgA, faecal calprotectin 22 micrograms/g

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange an abdominal ultrasound to complete the assessment
options.rationale: Ultrasound in a thriving child with normal screening tests has a very low yield and frequently turns up incidental findings that generate further anxiety and further tests. Imaging is indicated for a palpable mass, organomegaly, or pain with vomiting or urinary symptoms. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain

options.text: Diagnose functional abdominal pain and agree a graded school return
options.rationale: Functional abdominal pain is diagnosed positively on a characteristic history with normal growth, a normal examination and no alarm features, not by exhausting investigations. Naming the diagnosis, explaining gut and brain signalling and restoring school attendance are the interventions that actually change the outcome. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain

options.text: Refer for endoscopy with duodenal biopsies to exclude inflammation
options.rationale: Endoscopy under general anaesthetic cannot be justified with negative coeliac serology, a normal calprotectin and no weight loss or bleeding. It becomes appropriate when there is dysphagia, haematemesis, persistent vomiting or unexplained weight loss. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain

options.text: Trial a proton pump inhibitor for eight weeks and review
options.rationale: Acid suppression has no role in periumbilical pain without heartburn or epigastric burning, and prescribing it medicalises the problem while implying an organic disease that has not been found. A trial would be reasonable for genuine dyspeptic symptoms localised to the epigastrium. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain

options.text: Advise strict wheat and lactose exclusion for six weeks
options.rationale: Broad exclusion diets in children risk nutritional inadequacy and entrench illness behaviour around food, and the evidence for them in functional pain is weak. Any dietary manipulation should be short, targeted and dietitian supervised rather than open ended self imposed restriction. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Functional gastrointestinal disorders)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Functional gastrointestinal disorders

explanation.summary: Functional abdominal pain affects up to one in ten school aged children and is the commonest cause of recurrent abdominal pain in this age group. It is a positive diagnosis resting on a typical history, normal growth, a normal examination and the absence of alarm features such as weight loss, nocturnal waking with pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, persistent vomiting, dysphagia, unexplained fever or a family history of inflammatory bowel disease. Pain that is worse on school days and absent in holidays points strongly to a functional disorder with a school related trigger, and school avoidance is often the most disabling consequence rather than the pain itself. Continuing to investigate a child who meets these criteria reinforces the family's belief that a serious disease is being missed and makes the pain harder to treat. Management combines explanation of the gut and brain axis, restoration of normal function, and psychological therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy or gut directed hypnotherapy where symptoms persist.
key_points: Functional abdominal pain is diagnosed positively, not by exclusion after exhaustive testing.
Normal growth with a normal examination and normal screening tests is highly reassuring.
Alarm features include weight loss, nocturnal pain, bleeding, vomiting and a family history of inflammatory bowel disease.
Symptoms worse on school days and absent in holidays suggest a school related trigger.
Cognitive behavioural therapy and gut directed hypnotherapy have the best evidence for persistent symptoms.
explanation.pearls: A faecal calprotectin below 50 micrograms per gram has a negative predictive value above 95 per cent for paediatric inflammatory bowel disease, which is why a normal result in a thriving child without bleeding makes endoscopy very hard to justify.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Functional gastrointestinal disorders
NICE: Coeliac disease recognition and assessment

subtopic_detail: Eight weeks of daily rattly cough in a thriving preschooler with a clear chest and a normal chest radiograph
stem: A four-year-old boy has eight weeks of daily wet, rattly cough, present through the day. Two courses of oral salbutamol and four weeks of an inhaled corticosteroid made no difference. There was no choking episode beforehand.

data_table.Examination: Wet cough audible in the room, chest clear, no clubbing, growth on the 75th centile
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph normal, sweat chloride 18 mmol/L, immunoglobulins normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Two to four weeks of amoxicillin with clavulanate
options.rationale: A wet cough lasting longer than four weeks in a thriving child with a normal examination and radiograph, unresponsive to bronchodilator and inhaled steroid, defines protracted bacterial bronchitis, and the diagnosis is confirmed by resolution on a prolonged course of amoxicillin with clavulanate. Treating it properly matters because repeated untreated episodes progress to bronchiectasis. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children

options.text: Increase the inhaled corticosteroid and add a beta agonist
options.rationale: Asthma produces a dry cough with wheeze and variability, and this child has a consistently wet cough that has already failed both a bronchodilator and four weeks of inhaled steroid. Escalating asthma therapy in a child who has not responded to it is a common and harmful anti pattern. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.text: High resolution computed tomography of the chest
options.rationale: Computed tomography delivers a significant radiation dose and is not the first step when a therapeutic trial will both treat and diagnose the commonest cause. It is indicated when the wet cough fails to resolve after two adequate antibiotic courses or recurs repeatedly. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children

options.text: Flexible bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage
options.rationale: Bronchoscopy is invasive and requires general anaesthesia, and there was no choking episode and no focal radiographic or auscultatory finding to suggest a retained foreign body. It is reserved for treatment failure, recurrent episodes or a genuine suspicion of an airway lesion. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children

options.text: Reassure as post viral cough, review in eight weeks
options.rationale: Post viral cough is dry and settles within three to four weeks, whereas a wet cough persisting beyond four weeks is abnormal and demands an explanation. Watchful waiting here allows a treatable neutrophilic airway infection to continue damaging the airway wall. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children

explanation.summary: Protracted bacterial bronchitis is the commonest cause of chronic wet cough in Australian preschool children and results from persistent neutrophilic airway infection, typically with non typeable Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae or Moraxella catarrhalis, growing within a biofilm on the airway wall. The defining triad is a wet cough of more than four weeks, absence of any pointer to an alternative diagnosis, and resolution on an appropriate antibiotic course. The character of the cough is the most useful single discriminator, because asthma and post viral cough are dry while protracted bacterial bronchitis is consistently wet, and this explains the complete failure of asthma therapy in such children. Two weeks of amoxicillin with clavulanate resolves the cough in most, with a further two weeks for those who do not respond fully. This matters because recurrent or inadequately treated episodes sit on a continuum that leads through chronic suppurative lung disease to established bronchiectasis, a pathway of particular importance in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children.
key_points: A wet cough beyond four weeks in a child is never normal and needs a diagnosis.
Failure to respond to bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids argues strongly against asthma.
Protracted bacterial bronchitis is confirmed by resolution on two to four weeks of amoxicillin with clavulanate.
Normal growth, clear chest and normal radiograph do not exclude the diagnosis.
Recurrent untreated episodes progress towards chronic suppurative lung disease and bronchiectasis.
explanation.pearls: Refer for bronchoscopy and high resolution computed tomography if a child needs more than two courses of antibiotics in twelve months for wet cough, because recurrent protracted bacterial bronchitis at that frequency carries a substantial risk of established bronchiectasis on imaging.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children
National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook
BMJ Best Practice: Chronic cough in children

subtopic_detail: Toddler treated as gastroenteritis who has an enlarged liver and a gallop and deteriorates after an initial fluid bolus
stem: A three-year-old girl has two days of vomiting without diarrhoea, treated as gastroenteritis this morning. She arrived mottled, and after a 10 mL/kg sodium chloride bolus her breathing has worsened. Paediatric intensive care is four hours away.

data_table.Examination: Liver 4 cm below costal margin, gallop rhythm, new bibasal crackles
data_table.Investigations: Radiograph cardiomegaly; ECG low voltage QRS

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Further 20 mL/kg sodium chloride bolus over ten minutes
options.rationale: Repeated rapid boluses are correct for septic or hypovolaemic shock but are actively harmful when the shock is cardiogenic, because a failing ventricle sits on the descending limb of the Starling curve and further preload worsens pulmonary oedema. The crackles and hepatomegaly that appeared after the first bolus are the warning that this pathway is wrong. (Source: RCH CPG: Myocarditis)

options.text: Withhold fluid, urgent echocardiography, retrieval for inotropes
options.rationale: Hepatomegaly, a gallop rhythm, new basal crackles and cardiomegaly with low voltage complexes identify cardiogenic shock from acute myocarditis, in which the priority is to stop giving volume and start careful inotropic support with expert retrieval advice. Any further fluid must be given in small aliquots of no more than 5 to 10 mL/kg with reassessment after each. (Source: RCH CPG: Myocarditis)

options.text: Blood cultures, ceftriaxone and fluid to 60 mL/kg total
options.rationale: The paediatric sepsis pathway is the correct default for an undifferentiated shocked child, and covering for sepsis remains reasonable, but driving the fluid component to 60 mL/kg in the face of clear cardiac failure will cause pulmonary oedema. The sepsis pathway itself directs clinicians to reassess for cardiac dysfunction after each bolus for precisely this reason. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.text: Immunoglobulin now, then transfer to the paediatric ward
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin is sometimes used in fulminant paediatric myocarditis but the evidence is weak and it does nothing for the immediate haemodynamic emergency in front of you. It is a decision for the receiving intensive care team after echocardiography, not a substitute for circulatory support and retrieval. (Source: RCH CPG: Myocarditis)

options.text: Rapid sequence intubation, then continued volume resuscitation
options.rationale: Induction agents and positive pressure ventilation abolish sympathetic drive and reduce preload, and intubating a child in uncorrected cardiogenic shock without inotropic support first frequently precipitates arrest. If intubation becomes necessary it should follow the commencement of inotropes and be performed by the most experienced operator available. (Source: RCH CPG: Myocarditis)

explanation.summary: Acute myocarditis in young children is usually viral and characteristically masquerades as gastroenteritis, respiratory infection or sepsis, because vomiting, lethargy and poor feeding are its commonest presenting complaints and chest pain is rare below school age. The features that betray it are hepatomegaly, a gallop rhythm and respiratory signs that worsen rather than improve after fluid, together with cardiomegaly on the chest radiograph and low voltage complexes with repolarisation change on the electrocardiogram. Recognising this matters enormously because the standard shock response of repeated 20 mL/kg boluses is precisely the wrong treatment and can precipitate fulminant decompensation. Management is small cautious fluid aliquots if any, early inotropic support, avoidance of intubation until the circulation is supported, and urgent involvement of a paediatric retrieval service, since mechanical circulatory support may ultimately be required. Outcomes in children who survive the acute phase are surprisingly good, with many recovering normal ventricular function.
key_points: Vomiting and lethargy without diarrhoea should raise doubt about a diagnosis of gastroenteritis.
Hepatomegaly with a gallop rhythm and new basal crackles indicates cardiogenic rather than septic shock.
Low voltage complexes with cardiomegaly on the radiograph support acute myocarditis.
Fluid boluses beyond 5 to 10 mL/kg aliquots worsen cardiogenic shock and must be withheld.
Start inotropes and involve paediatric retrieval before contemplating intubation.
explanation.pearls: Palpate for the liver edge in every shocked child before the second fluid bolus, because a liver more than 2 cm below the costal margin in a toddler is the earliest and most reliable bedside sign that the shock is cardiogenic and that further volume will make things worse.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management
BMJ Best Practice: Myocarditis in children

subtopic_detail: Bruising over the cheek with a torn upper lip frenulum in a four month old who cannot yet roll
stem: A 4-month-old boy has a facial bruise. His parents say he rolled off the change table onto carpet, but the parent-held record shows he has not yet rolled.

data_table.Examination: Bruise on the left cheek and the left ear helix, torn upper lip frenulum, no other marks
data_table.Investigations: INR 1.0, APTT 31 seconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for skeletal survey, neuroimaging and fundoscopy, and notify child protection
options.rationale: Bruising in an infant who is not independently mobile, bruising of the ear and a torn frenulum are each high specificity markers of inflicted injury, and together they mandate admission for occult injury screening and a statutory report. Admission also provides a place of safety while the assessment proceeds. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Arrange an outpatient skeletal survey and discharge him home today
options.rationale: Deferring the survey sends the child back to the environment in which the injury occurred and loses the paired imaging and clinical assessment that occult fracture detection depends on. Timing of the statutory report cannot wait on imaging logistics. (Source: Queensland Health: Child protection guideline)

options.text: Order a skeletal survey and clotting profile, reassuring if normal
options.rationale: Normal investigations do not exclude inflicted injury, because most abusive head trauma and many soft tissue injuries leave no radiological trace. Making the report conditional on abnormal imaging inverts the threshold, which is reasonable suspicion rather than proof. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Photograph the bruises and repeat the coagulation screen next week
options.rationale: A normal coagulation screen has already been obtained and repeating it a week later neither explains the frenulum tear nor protects the child in the interval. Bleeding disorders cause bruising in unusual sites but do not tear a frenulum in a baby who cannot bring objects forcefully to his mouth. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Accept the history, give head injury advice and arrange a home visit
options.rationale: The history is not consistent with the injuries, since a baby who has never rolled cannot generate the mechanism described and carpet does not tear a frenulum. Accepting an implausible history is the commonest single failure in these presentations. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: Bruising in an infant who is not yet independently mobile is the single most useful red flag in child protection paediatrics, because babies who cannot roll, crawl or cruise do not sustain accidental bruises. The sites here compound that concern, since the ear and the cheek are protected areas rarely struck in falls, and a torn upper lip frenulum in a pre mobile baby is strongly associated with forced feeding or a direct blow. The history is discrepant in two ways, describing a developmental milestone the child has not reached and a mechanism that cannot produce an intraoral injury. Management is admission for a skeletal survey, neuroimaging and dilated fundoscopy to find occult fractures and intracranial or retinal haemorrhage, together with a statutory notification made on suspicion rather than on proof. A normal coagulation screen makes an inherited bleeding disorder unlikely but never substitutes for the protection assessment.
key_points: Any bruise in an infant who cannot independently move demands explanation and usually investigation.
Ear, neck, torso and intraoral injuries are high specificity sites for inflicted trauma.
A history describing a milestone the child has not reached is a discrepant history.
Occult injury screening in an infant includes skeletal survey, neuroimaging and fundoscopy.
Statutory notification is triggered by reasonable suspicion, not by confirmed investigation results.
explanation.pearls: A skeletal survey in a child under two is repeated at eleven to fourteen days, because healing periosteal reaction makes rib and metaphyseal fractures visible that were invisible on the first films, and omitting the repeat films is a recognised source of missed diagnosis.

subtopic_detail: Toe walking with calf hypertrophy and a creatine kinase of 12400 in a four year old boy
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a four year old boy whose parents are worried that he walks on his toes and cannot keep up with his older cousins. He falls more than other children at kindergarten and his teacher has noticed he pushes on his thighs to get up from sitting on the floor.
