He walked at eighteen months and says short sentences that his family understand. His calves look bulky compared with his thighs. You arranged blood tests at the last visit and the results are now available.

data_table.Examination: Waddling gait with toe walking, bulky firm calves, proximal weakness with a positive Gowers manoeuvre, reflexes present at the knees and reduced at the ankles, no fasciculation and no sensory deficit
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 12400 units per litre (60-305), alanine aminotransferase 180 units per litre (10-40), aspartate aminotransferase 210 units per litre (10-45), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to an orthopaedic surgeon for serial casting of the ankles to correct the toe walking and to improve his gait pattern
options.rationale: Casting treats idiopathic toe walking, in which strength and creatine kinase are normal, and here it would immobilise a boy whose weakness is progressive. Periods of immobilisation accelerate loss of ambulation in dystrophinopathy. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

options.text: Refer him for an open muscle biopsy of the quadriceps for dystrophin immunostaining before any other investigation is undertaken
options.rationale: Biopsy is now reserved for the minority whose genetic testing is uninformative, since it needs a general anaesthetic and adds little when a deletion is found. Ordering it first exposes the child to an avoidable procedure. (Source: Muscular Dystrophy Australia: Diagnosis pathway)

options.text: Repeat the liver enzymes and arrange a liver ultrasound, since the raised transaminases suggest an underlying hepatic disorder in this child
options.rationale: Transaminases are released from damaged skeletal muscle as well as from liver, and chasing them here is the classic diversion that delays neuromuscular diagnosis by months. A gamma glutamyl transferase would be normal and would settle the question. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

options.text: Reassure the parents that this is a normal variant of gait in preschool children and repeat the creatine kinase measurement in six months
options.rationale: Toe walking with proximal weakness and a creatine kinase in the thousands is never a normal variant, and delay costs the window in which corticosteroids best preserve ambulation. Idiopathic toe walkers have normal strength and can stand from the floor without their hands. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

options.text: Refer to a paediatric neurology service for genetic testing of the dystrophin gene with genetic counselling for the family
options.rationale: Genetic analysis for deletions, duplications and then sequence variants confirms the diagnosis non invasively in the great majority of boys and is the entry point to corticosteroid therapy, cardiac and respiratory surveillance and variant specific treatments. It also allows carrier testing of female relatives. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

explanation.summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy presents in boys between two and five years with delayed motor milestones, toe walking, a waddling gait and difficulty rising from the floor, and calf pseudohypertrophy reflects replacement of muscle by fat and connective tissue. A creatine kinase in the thousands to tens of thousands is the screening test, and transaminases are commonly raised from muscle rather than liver, a finding that regularly sends children down a hepatology pathway first. Confirmation is genetic, using multiplex ligation dependent probe amplification for deletions and duplications followed by sequencing, with muscle biopsy reserved for genetically uninformative cases. Early diagnosis matters because corticosteroids prolong ambulation, and cardiac and respiratory surveillance begins well before symptoms. A positive Gowers manoeuvre in a preschool boy should prompt a creatine kinase on the same day.
key_points: Calf pseudohypertrophy with proximal weakness in a boy suggests a dystrophinopathy.
Creatine kinase is the screening test and is typically above ten thousand units per litre.
Raised transaminases in this setting usually come from muscle, and a normal gamma glutamyl transferase confirms it.
Genetic testing has replaced biopsy as the first confirmatory test.
Corticosteroids and cardiorespiratory surveillance begin early, so delay has a real cost.
explanation.pearls: Girls are not exempt: manifesting carriers can present with calf hypertrophy, cramps and a creatine kinase of several thousand, and every female relative identified through cascade testing needs cardiac surveillance because cardiomyopathy can occur without any skeletal muscle weakness.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

subtopic_detail: Vomiting and poor weight gain at five weeks with sodium 122 and potassium 7.1
stem: A 5-week-old boy has four days of forceful milky vomiting after feeds and is hungry again straight afterwards. He is drowsy but rousable with reduced skin turgor.

data_table.Examination: Sunken fontanelle, delayed capillary refill; deeply pigmented scrotum and areolae
data_table.Investigations: Na 122 mmol/L; K 7.1 mmol/L; chloride 112 mmol/L; bicarbonate 12 mmol/L; glucose 2.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Steroid profile, then intravenous hydrocortisone with saline and dextrose
options.rationale: Hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, acidosis and hypoglycaemia in a shocked infant is a salt wasting crisis until proven otherwise, and glucocorticoid replacement with volume and glucose is both diagnostic and lifesaving. The sample taken beforehand preserves the diagnosis for later confirmation. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia)

options.text: Cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin after cultures, with a fluid bolus
options.rationale: Sepsis is a reasonable parallel concern in a collapsed infant and cultures with empirical cover are appropriate, but antibiotics alone will not reverse a crisis driven by absent cortisol and aldosterone. The electrolyte triad points away from sepsis as the sole explanation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Fluid bolus and correction of the alkalosis before theatre
options.rationale: The classical metabolic picture of gastric outlet obstruction is a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis, and this child has the mirror image with a low bicarbonate, a high chloride and a high potassium. Adding potassium to a baby with a level above seven would be dangerous. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia)

options.text: Insulin and dextrose with nebulised salbutamol for the potassium
options.rationale: Shifting potassium treats a number rather than the disease driving it, and in mineralocorticoid deficiency the potassium climbs straight back once the infusion stops. These measures are adjuncts reserved for arrhythmia or extreme levels while definitive hormone and salt replacement is being given. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Steroid profile, then oral fludrocortisone and salt once feeds stay down
options.rationale: Oral therapy cannot be absorbed reliably by a shocked vomiting infant, and fludrocortisone alone does not provide the glucocorticoid activity needed to support blood pressure and glucose in crisis. It becomes part of long term maintenance once the child is stable. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia)

explanation.summary: Salt wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia presents in the second to fifth week of life, and boys are the ones who present in crisis because they have no ambiguity of the genitalia to prompt earlier diagnosis. The combination of hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis and hypoglycaemia is close to specific, and hyperpigmentation from high adrenocorticotrophic hormone is a useful bedside clue. The trap in this vignette is the forceful milky vomiting of a five week old boy, which points to gastric outlet obstruction, but that condition produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis, so the biochemistry disconfirms it outright. Treatment is intravenous hydrocortisone with sodium chloride and dextrose after a sample is taken for seventeen hydroxyprogesterone, renin and cortisol, since delaying steroid for the result risks cardiac arrest. Newborn screening for this condition is not performed in all Australian jurisdictions, so clinical recognition remains essential.
key_points: Low sodium with high potassium, acidosis and hypoglycaemia in an infant means adrenal crisis until excluded.
Gastric outlet obstruction gives the opposite biochemistry, a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis.
Boys with salt wasting disease have normal genitalia and therefore present later and sicker.
Take the diagnostic sample first, then give hydrocortisone without waiting for the result.
Hydrocortisone in stress doses supplies the mineralocorticoid effect needed acutely.
explanation.pearls: Hyperkalaemia in adrenal crisis resolves with hydrocortisone and saline, so calcium gluconate is reserved for electrocardiographic changes, and the commonest iatrogenic error is adding potassium to maintenance fluids after the initial correction because the number has fallen quickly.

subtopic_detail: Systolic murmur with weak femoral pulses at the six week check in a thriving infant
stem: A baby girl is seen for her six week check. She feeds well and has gained 900 g since birth.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/54 mmHg right arm, SpO2 98% right hand, 96% right foot
data_table.Examination: Soft systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge radiating to the back, brachial pulses normal, femoral pulses not palpable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral furosemide with paediatric cardiology review within the week
options.rationale: There is no hepatomegaly, tachypnoea or feeding sweat to indicate failure, and diuresis in a baby dependent on preload for systemic perfusion can precipitate collapse. Medication is not a substitute for defining the anatomy. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

options.text: Reassure that this is an innocent murmur, reviewing at immunisation
options.rationale: Innocent murmurs are never accompanied by absent femoral pulses, and radiation through to the back is not a feature of a venous hum or a Still murmur. Reassurance here risks presentation in shock when the arterial duct finishes closing. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

options.text: Same day paediatric assessment with four limb blood pressures and echocardiography
options.rationale: Absent femoral pulses with a murmur radiating to the back is aortic obstruction until disproved, and the diagnosis must be made before ductal tissue completes its closure and precipitates collapse. Four limb pressures and echocardiography define the lesion and its severity. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease)

options.text: Electrocardiogram and chest radiograph today, reviewing her when back
options.rationale: Both tests can be normal in early coarctation and neither changes the immediate decision, so they add delay without adding safety. Imaging that answers the question is echocardiography performed by a service that can act on it. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease)

options.text: Routine paediatric cardiology referral, returning sooner if feeding worsens
options.rationale: A routine wait of weeks straddles exactly the period in which critical obstruction declares itself, and parents cannot reliably detect the transition until the infant is already shocked. Urgency is set by the pulse finding, not by how well the baby currently looks. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

explanation.summary: Coarctation of the aorta is the congenital lesion most often missed at the newborn and six week checks, because a baby with a patent arterial duct can perfuse the lower body normally and look entirely well. As the duct closes over the first weeks the obstruction is unmasked, and the infant who was thriving presents collapsed with acidosis and absent pulses. Palpation of the femoral pulses at every routine check is therefore the single highest yield part of the cardiovascular examination in infancy, and a murmur radiating to the interscapular area strengthens the suspicion. Pre and post ductal saturation difference may be small or absent once the duct has largely closed, so a normal pulse oximetry screen does not exclude the diagnosis. Referral for same day paediatric assessment with four limb blood pressures and echocardiography is the correct pathway, and prostaglandin is given if the infant decompensates.
key_points: Absent or weak femoral pulses in an infant means aortic obstruction until echocardiography says otherwise.
A thriving well baby does not exclude coarctation while the arterial duct remains open.
A murmur radiating to the back is a specific and easily missed clue.
Newborn pulse oximetry screening misses many coarctations.
Electrocardiogram and chest radiograph are frequently normal early and should not delay referral.
explanation.pearls: Compare the right arm and either leg blood pressure rather than left arm and leg, because an aberrant or coarcted left subclavian origin can make the left arm pressure falsely low, and a gradient above twenty mmHg between right arm and leg supports the diagnosis.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

subtopic_detail: Cyanotic episodes triggered by crying with rapid recovery and a normal electrocardiogram at fifteen months
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a fifteen month old girl who has had six frightening episodes over three months. Each begins when she is upset, after a fall or when a toy is taken away.

Her mother describes a long silent cry, then the lips turning blue, then a few seconds of limpness before she comes round and wants a cuddle. She is back to normal within a minute and has never been sleepy afterwards. She is fully immunised, her development is normal and an electrocardiogram arranged by the general practitioner was reported as normal with a normal corrected QT interval.

data_table.Examination: Alert and interactive, pale conjunctivae, no dysmorphic features, normal cardiac examination with no murmur, normal tone and power with age appropriate gait, developmental milestones appropriate
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram normal with normal corrected QT interval

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram to look for an epileptiform focus that could explain the recurrent episodes of limpness and colour change
options.rationale: The episodes are consistently provoked by an emotional or painful trigger and recovery is immediate without a postictal phase, which is not the pattern of epilepsy. An electroencephalogram in this setting is more likely to produce an incidental finding than an answer. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

options.text: Arrange a sleep deprived electroencephalogram with video recording and review her in the neurology clinic when the report is available
options.rationale: Adding sleep deprivation and video increases the sensitivity of a test that is not indicated, since the diagnosis here is clinical and the trigger is stereotyped. The delay also leaves a treatable contributor unaddressed. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

options.text: Arrange an echocardiogram to exclude a structural cardiac cause for the cyanosis and the transient loss of postural tone during the episodes
options.rationale: Structural disease severe enough to cause cyanotic episodes would give an abnormal cardiac examination or persisting symptoms between events rather than colour change confined to crying. The normal examination and electrocardiogram make this a low yield test. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

options.text: Send a full blood count with ferritin, since correcting iron deficiency reduces the frequency of these episodes in a substantial proportion of children
options.rationale: Iron deficiency is common in children with these spells and treating it reduces their frequency, making it the one investigation that changes management. The pale conjunctivae in this child strengthen the case for testing. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

options.text: Send a venous blood gas with lactate and an ammonia level during a well period to screen for an underlying metabolic disorder causing the events
options.rationale: Metabolic decompensation presents with intercurrent illness, poor feeding and developmental regression rather than brief episodes tied to frustration. Sampling between episodes in a thriving child with normal development adds nothing. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Breath holding attacks)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Breath holding attacks

explanation.summary: Breath holding spells affect around five per cent of children between six months and five years and are diagnosed on the history alone, with a provoking event, a cry, apnoea in expiration, colour change and then brief limpness or stiffening. The cyanotic type follows anger or frustration, while the pallid type follows a minor knock and reflects a vagally mediated asystolic pause. Rapid recovery without a postictal state separates them from seizures, although a brief anoxic convulsion at the end of a long spell does not change the diagnosis. Iron deficiency with or without anaemia is over represented in affected children, and iron supplementation reduces the frequency of spells, which makes a full blood count with ferritin the only routine test worth doing beyond an electrocardiogram. Parents need explicit reassurance that the episodes are involuntary, that the child is not manipulating them and that the condition resolves by school age.
key_points: Diagnosis rests on a stereotyped trigger, a cry, colour change and immediate recovery.
An electrocardiogram excludes long QT syndrome, particularly in pallid episodes.
Full blood count and ferritin are the only other routine tests required.
Iron replacement reduces spell frequency even when haemoglobin is normal.
Absence of a postictal phase distinguishes these events from epileptic seizures.
explanation.pearls: Advise parents to lay the child flat on their side during a spell rather than picking them up or shaking them, because the upright posture prolongs cerebral hypoperfusion and recovery, and warn them that a short stiffening jerk at the end of a spell is anoxic rather than epileptic and needs no anticonvulsant.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Breath holding attacks

subtopic_detail: Breech presentation at term as the only risk factor for hip dysplasia in a newborn with a normal examination
stem:
You are the resident on the postnatal ward reviewing a two day old girl before discharge. She was born at thirty nine weeks by caesarean section for a persistent breech presentation and has fed well since birth.

There is no family history of hip problems and the pregnancy was otherwise unremarkable with normal liquor volume. Her mother asks whether anything needs to be arranged for the hips because a friend's baby was put in a harness.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical thigh creases, full and equal abduction of both hips, no clunk on Ortolani or Barlow testing, legs of equal length on Galeazzi testing, spine and feet normal, neurological examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for her hips?

options.text: Arrange a pelvic radiograph now to assess the acetabular index and refer to the orthopaedic clinic if the femoral head appears displaced
options.rationale: The femoral head is unossified in the newborn, so radiography cannot assess it and only becomes useful from about four to six months of age. It also delivers gonadal irradiation for no diagnostic return. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Refer her for fitting of a Pavlik harness now on the basis of the breech presentation and review her in the orthopaedic clinic in six weeks
options.rationale: A harness treats dysplasia that has been demonstrated, not a risk factor alone, and unnecessary abduction bracing carries a risk of avascular necrosis. The decision to treat follows the ultrasound. (Source: Healthy Hips Australia: Clinical information)

options.text: Reassure her mother that the normal newborn examination excludes the condition and arrange no imaging beyond the routine child health checks
options.rationale: Clinical examination misses dysplastic hips that are located and stable at birth, which is precisely why risk factor based imaging exists. A normal examination lowers but does not remove the risk conferred by breech presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Arrange a hip ultrasound at around six weeks of age and continue routine clinical examination of the hips at each scheduled review
options.rationale: Breech presentation in the third trimester warrants imaging even when the examination is normal, and ultrasound at six weeks to four months avoids the false positives of scanning newborn physiological laxity. Clinical examination continues because dysplasia can appear later. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Arrange a hip ultrasound before discharge from the postnatal ward and refer to orthopaedics if any measurement falls outside the normal range
options.rationale: Scanning in the first weeks detects physiological immaturity that resolves spontaneously, generating harnesses and reviews that the child never needed. The window that balances sensitivity against false positives opens at about six weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

explanation.summary: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is screened for clinically at every newborn and infant check, but clinical examination alone misses a substantial proportion of dysplastic hips that are neither dislocated nor dislocatable. Australian practice therefore adds selective ultrasound for defined risk factors, of which breech presentation in the third trimester and a first degree family history are the strongest. Timing matters in both directions, because scanning in the first weeks captures physiological laxity that would have resolved and leads to overtreatment, while a pelvic radiograph is uninterpretable until the femoral head begins to ossify at around four to six months. Ultrasound at six weeks to four months is the compromise that Australian guidelines adopt. Treatment with an abduction harness is reserved for hips shown to be dysplastic or unstable, and late presentation after walking age usually requires operative reduction.
key_points: Breech presentation and a family history are the risk factors that trigger selective imaging.
A normal newborn hip examination does not exclude dysplasia.
Ultrasound is performed at about six weeks, not in the first days of life.
Radiography is uninformative until femoral head ossification at four to six months.
Harness treatment follows demonstrated dysplasia rather than risk factors alone.
explanation.pearls: Limited or asymmetrical hip abduction is the most reliable sign after three months of age, by which time Ortolani and Barlow testing has usually become negative because the soft tissues have tightened around a dislocated hip.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
BMJ Best Practice: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

subtopic_detail: Unimmunised ten month old exposed to measles two days ago in a hospital waiting room
stem: A ten-month-old boy sat in an emergency department waiting room two days ago at the same time as a person later confirmed to have measles. His parents have declined all immunisations. He is well today.

data_table.Examination: Alert and playful; no rash, conjunctivitis or Koplik spots

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Normal human immunoglobulin today, with his first vaccine brought forward
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin is the option when vaccine cannot be used or when more than seventy two hours have elapsed, and it also blunts the response to vaccine given afterwards for several months. Choosing it here forfeits the durable protection available from the vaccine. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles)

options.text: Measles mumps and rubella vaccine today, extra to the two doses due at twelve months
options.rationale: Vaccine given within seventy two hours of exposure can prevent or attenuate disease and is preferred to immunoglobulin in a healthy infant. A dose before the first birthday does not count towards the schedule because maternal antibody may blunt it. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles)

options.text: No action now, with isolation advice and review if fever develops
options.rationale: Watchful waiting forgoes an intervention that works when given inside the seventy two hour window and leaves a susceptible infant at risk of pneumonia and encephalitis. Isolation advice is necessary but is not sufficient on its own. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Measles SoNG)
source_refs: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Measles SoNG

options.text: Measles serology today, vaccinating only if immunoglobulin G is negative
options.rationale: Waiting for serology consumes the narrow window in which prophylaxis works, and a positive result in an infant may reflect residual maternal antibody rather than protection. Post exposure decisions are made on exposure history and age. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Measles)

options.text: Defer vaccination to twelve months as scheduled, with oral vitamin A
options.rationale: Vitamin A reduces mortality in children with established measles rather than preventing infection after exposure, so it does not substitute for prophylaxis. Deferring to the routine schedule ignores the current exposure. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Measles SoNG)
source_refs: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Measles SoNG

explanation.summary: Measles is among the most transmissible infections known, with airborne spread persisting in a room for up to two hours after the case has left, so shared waiting room air counts as a genuine exposure. For a susceptible immunocompetent contact aged six months or older, measles mumps and rubella vaccine given within seventy two hours of first exposure can prevent or modify disease and is preferred to immunoglobulin. Normal human immunoglobulin is used instead when the exposure was more than seventy two hours but within six days, when the contact is under six months, pregnant or significantly immunocompromised, and it delays subsequent vaccination for months. A dose of vaccine given before twelve months of age does not count towards the routine schedule, because circulating maternal antibody can neutralise the vaccine virus, so two further doses are still required. Public health units coordinate contact tracing, and any suspected case needs urgent notification with airborne precautions on arrival at a health service.
key_points: Vaccine within seventy two hours is the preferred prophylaxis for a healthy contact aged six months or over.
Immunoglobulin covers exposures beyond seventy two hours and up to six days, and vulnerable contacts.
A dose before twelve months does not replace either scheduled dose.
Serology should not delay prophylaxis after a defined exposure.
Measles remains airborne in a room for up to two hours after the case leaves.
explanation.pearls: Vitamin A is given to children with measles admitted to hospital or with severe disease, in two daily doses with a third dose after several weeks, because deficiency worsens outcomes even in high income settings where it is easily overlooked.

sources.label: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Measles SoNG

subtopic_detail: Secondary prevention after a first episode of acute rheumatic fever in a remote community child
stem: A nine-year-old boy in a remote Northern Territory community has a confirmed first episode of acute rheumatic fever. His streptococcal infection has been treated and his arthritis has settled. His mother asks about home.

data_table.Examination: Soft apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla; joints settled
data_table.Investigations: ESR 62 mm/h; CRP 28 mg/L; ECG first degree atrioventricular block; mild mitral regurgitation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing plan?

options.text: Twice daily oral phenoxymethylpenicillin for five years with dose aids
options.rationale: Daily oral penicillin is the fallback when injections are genuinely refused, because adherence over years is poor and breakthrough recurrences are more frequent than with the injectable form. Convenience aids do not close that gap. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Annual echocardiography and dental review, treating sore throats promptly
options.rationale: Treating only symptomatic pharyngitis misses the many streptococcal infections that are silent or occur in the skin, so recurrences continue. Surveillance detects damage rather than preventing it. (Source: RHDAustralia: ARF and RHD guideline)

options.text: Continue naproxen and add a low dose corticosteroid to protect the valve
options.rationale: Anti inflammatory treatment relieves arthritis but has never been shown to alter valve outcome, and corticosteroids are reserved for severe carditis with heart failure. Neither prevents the recurrence that drives progressive disease. (Source: RHDAustralia: ARF and RHD guideline)

options.text: Four weekly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin, with registration
options.rationale: Regular long acting penicillin injections are the only intervention shown to prevent recurrent episodes and progression to established valve disease, and registration ensures recall when the family travels. Echocardiography tracks the valve lesion that determines the duration of prophylaxis. (Source: RHDAustralia: ARF and RHD guideline)

options.text: Ten days of oral phenoxymethylpenicillin, reviewing if symptoms recur
options.rationale: A treatment course eradicates the triggering organism but does nothing about the next streptococcal infection, and recurrence is what destroys valves. Primary treatment and secondary prophylaxis are different tasks with different durations. (Source: RHDAustralia: ARF and RHD guideline)

explanation.summary: Acute rheumatic fever remains common in remote parts of northern Australia and carries one of the highest rates of rheumatic heart disease in the world, so recognition and secondary prevention are core Australian practice. Diagnosis uses the Jones criteria with a lowered threshold in high incidence settings, where monoarthritis, polyarthralgia and subclinical carditis on echocardiography all count. Once the diagnosis is made, the intervention that changes the natural history is secondary prophylaxis with four weekly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin, because each recurrence adds valve damage. Notification and entry onto the jurisdictional control register ensures recall, coordinates delivery across clinics when families move, and tracks echocardiographic severity. Duration depends on age and valve status, continuing for a minimum of ten years or until a defined age, and longer when significant valve disease is present.
key_points: Four weekly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin is the standard secondary prophylaxis.
Oral penicillin is a second choice used only when injections are refused.
Register notification supports recall and continuity when families move between communities.
Diagnostic criteria are deliberately relaxed in high incidence populations.
Anti inflammatory treatment relieves symptoms but does not protect the valves.
explanation.pearls: Mixing the benzathine injection with lidocaine markedly reduces injection pain without reducing penicillin levels, and pain is the commonest reason young people disengage from a program they need to continue for a decade.

subtopic_detail: Microcytic anaemia in a toddler drinking one and a half litres of cow milk each day
stem: A 2-year-old girl looks pale but is otherwise well, with no bruising or blood in her stool. She drinks about 1.5 L of cow milk daily and eats little meat or vegetables.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no organomegaly or petechiae
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L (110-140), MCV 62 fL, RDW 19%, ferritin 6 micrograms/L, CRP normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reduce milk to 500 mL daily, start oral iron and recheck in four weeks
options.rationale: Excessive cow milk displaces iron rich foods, impairs iron absorption and can cause occult gut blood loss, so dietary change and replacement therapy are both required. A four week recheck confirms a response before committing to a full course. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Send coeliac serology and defer iron until results return
options.rationale: Coeliac disease is worth considering when iron deficiency is unexplained, but here the history supplies an ample explanation and the child has no gastrointestinal symptoms or growth faltering. Deferring treatment prolongs a deficiency that affects neurodevelopment. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Refer to haematology for haemoglobin electrophoresis first
options.rationale: A low ferritin with a high red cell distribution width points to deficiency rather than thalassaemia trait, in which ferritin is normal and the cell size is disproportionately small for the degree of anaemia. Electrophoresis performed while iron deplete can also be misleading. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Admit for packed red cell transfusion then start oral iron
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise or cardiac failure, and a playful child who has adapted to slowly developing anaemia does not need it. Rapid transfusion in chronic anaemia risks circulatory overload. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Advise more red meat and vegetables alone, recheck in three months
options.rationale: Diet alone cannot replenish depleted stores at a useful rate once the ferritin has fallen this low, particularly in a fussy toddler. Dietary advice is an essential adjunct to replacement rather than an alternative. (Source: RACGP: Iron deficiency anaemia in children)
source_refs: RACGP: Iron deficiency anaemia in children

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional deficiency in Australian toddlers and excessive cow milk intake is the usual mechanism, acting through displacement of iron rich solids, inhibition of absorption by calcium and casein, and low grade enteric blood loss. The blood picture shows a microcytic hypochromic anaemia with a high red cell distribution width and a low ferritin, which separates it from thalassaemia trait where ferritin is normal and the red cell count is preserved. Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so a normal value with a raised C reactive protein does not exclude deficiency. Management combines limiting milk to about 500 mL daily with oral iron and a recheck at four weeks, looking for a haemoglobin rise that confirms both the diagnosis and adherence. Treatment continues for about three months after the haemoglobin normalises so that stores are replenished, because neurodevelopmental effects of early deficiency may not be fully reversible.
key_points: Cow milk above about 500 mL daily in a toddler is a leading cause of iron deficiency.
A low ferritin with a high red cell distribution width distinguishes deficiency from thalassaemia trait.
Ferritin rises with inflammation, so interpret it alongside C reactive protein.
Recheck at four weeks to confirm a response before continuing a full course.
Continue iron for about three months beyond normalisation to refill stores.
explanation.pearls: Give oral iron with a vitamin C source and away from milk, and warn families that stools turn black and that teeth can stain temporarily, because these unexpected effects are a common reason treatment is abandoned in the first fortnight.

sources.label: RACGP: Iron deficiency anaemia in children
BMJ Best Practice: Iron deficiency anaemia

subtopic_detail: Fever twelve days after chemotherapy with a neutrophil count of 0.3 in a well looking child
stem: A 6-year-old girl with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and a central venous line, twelve days past her last chemotherapy block, has a fever of 38.5 degrees C. She looks well with no localising symptoms.

data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 0.3 x10^9/L, platelets 62 x10^9/L, CRP 42 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Take blood cultures and await the C-reactive protein result
options.rationale: No laboratory marker reliably separates the child who will become septic from the child who will not, and every hour of delay increases mortality. Risk stratification tools are applied after the first dose, not instead of it. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia)

options.text: Give oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and review tomorrow in the day unit
options.rationale: Oral regimens are used only in carefully selected low risk children within a defined program, and a neutrophil count this low in the early recovery phase excludes that pathway. Discharge also removes the observation that early deterioration requires. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia)

options.text: Give paracetamol and observe for four hours before deciding
options.rationale: Antipyretics mask the one sign being used to monitor her and defer the intervention that changes outcome. Fever in neutropenia is treated as an emergency regardless of how the child looks at presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia)

options.text: Arrange a chest radiograph and urine culture, then treat any focus found
options.rationale: A focus is found in only a minority of episodes, so requiring one before treating guarantees delay in most children. Imaging is arranged when symptoms point to a site, after antibiotics have been given. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take blood cultures from the line and peripherally, then give antibiotics
options.rationale: Time to first antibiotic is the modifiable factor most strongly linked to survival in this group, and a well appearance offers no protection because a neutropenic child can decompensate within hours. Cultures are taken alongside rather than before the antibiotic. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia)

explanation.summary: Fever with neutropenia in a child receiving chemotherapy is a medical emergency in which the interval between arrival and the first antibiotic dose is the strongest modifiable determinant of outcome, and Australian services audit a target of sixty minutes. The well appearance of the child is a trap rather than reassurance, because neutropenic patients mount few localising signs and can progress from playful to shocked within hours, particularly with gram negative bacteraemia. Blood cultures are taken from each lumen of a central device and from a peripheral vein where possible, but collection must not delay treatment. Empirical therapy covers pseudomonas, usually with an antipseudomonal beta lactam, with an aminoglycoside or a glycopeptide added for shock, known resistant colonisation or a suspected line infection. Investigations for a focus follow the first dose and are directed by symptoms, since no source is identified in most episodes.
key_points: Aim for the first intravenous antibiotic within sixty minutes of arrival.
A well appearance and normal examination do not permit delay.
Cultures are taken from the central device and peripherally, without delaying therapy.
Empirical cover must include pseudomonas.
Inflammatory markers cannot be used to decide whether to treat.
explanation.pearls: A single temperature of 38.5 degrees Celsius, or two readings of 38 degrees Celsius an hour apart, defines fever in this setting, and the perianal region must be inspected but never examined digitally because instrumentation of neutropenic mucosa can seed a bacteraemia.

subtopic_detail: Glucose surveillance at two hours of age in a large for gestational age infant of a diabetic mother
stem: A boy born two hours ago at 39 weeks weighs 4.35 kg. His mother had insulin-treated gestational diabetes. He breastfed within the first half hour and no glucose has been measured.

data_table.Examination: Pink, warm and asleep in the cot, plethoric, no jitteriness, strong suck

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his glucose?

options.text: Measure the glucose before the next feed and support frequent feeding
options.rationale: Infants of diabetic mothers have hyperinsulinaemia and are screened routinely, with the first sample taken before a feed at two to four hours of age rather than in the immediate postnatal nadir. Feeding support in the interval is part of the same pathway. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Measure the glucose only if he becomes jittery or feeds poorly
options.rationale: Symptom triggered testing misses the substantial proportion of affected babies who are asymptomatic until they seize, which is precisely why risk factor based screening exists. Clinical signs are neither sensitive nor specific in the newborn. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Measure the glucose now and transfer for intravenous dextrose if low
options.rationale: A sample in the first hour or two captures the physiological nadir that all newborns pass through and generates unnecessary intervention. Escalation to intravenous dextrose follows failure of feeding and buccal gel rather than a single early value. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Give a formula top up after each breastfeed and measure daily
options.rationale: Routine supplementation undermines breastfeeding without addressing the monitoring requirement, and daily sampling is far too infrequent for the first twenty four hours. Supplementation is reserved for documented low values or inadequate feeding. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Clinical information)

options.text: Give buccal dextrose gel now and measure the glucose at six hours
options.rationale: Dextrose gel is treatment for a documented low value alongside a feed, and prophylactic use in an unscreened baby is not established practice. Deferring the first measurement to six hours leaves the highest risk window unmonitored. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Infants of mothers with diabetes are hyperinsulinaemic at birth because fetal islet hypertrophy persists after the maternal glucose supply is cut off, and macrosomia is the visible marker of that exposure. Australian pathways screen these babies along with those who are small or large for gestational age, preterm or unwell, taking the first capillary glucose before a feed at around two to four hours of age. Sampling earlier than this captures the normal postnatal nadir and prompts intervention that the baby does not need, while waiting for symptoms misses the many infants who remain asymptomatic until they have a seizure. Management escalates from early and frequent feeding, to buccal dextrose gel given with a feed for values below the threshold, to intravenous dextrose when values remain low or the baby is symptomatic. Screening continues through several pre feed measurements until values are consistently satisfactory.
key_points: Macrosomia in a diabetic pregnancy signals fetal hyperinsulinaemia and hypoglycaemia risk.
The first glucose is taken before a feed at about two to four hours, not immediately after birth.
Asymptomatic hypoglycaemia is common, so symptom triggered testing is unsafe.
Buccal dextrose gel with a feed is the first line treatment for a low value.
Screening continues over several pre feed samples before it can be stopped.
explanation.pearls: Persisting hypoglycaemia beyond the first two or three days, or a glucose requirement above eight milligrams per kilogram per minute, is no longer explained by maternal diabetes and calls for a formal hypoglycaemia screen with insulin, cortisol and ketones drawn while the glucose is low.

subtopic_detail: Jitteriness and poor feeding on day three in the baby of a mother on methadone maintenance
stem: A three-day-old girl born at 38 weeks is unsettled between feeds. Her mother is on a stable methadone program. The midwives report a high pitched cry, difficulty settling after feeds and three loose stools today. She is breastfeeding with some difficulty attaching.

data_table.Examination: Tremulous when disturbed, settles when swaddled, increased limb tone, excoriation over the nose, afebrile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral morphine now and wean it over the following week
options.rationale: Pharmacological treatment is reserved for babies whose scores cross a defined threshold on repeated assessments, because many settle with environmental measures alone. Treating early commits the pair to a longer admission without benefit. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

options.text: Replace breastfeeding with formula and observe for 48 hours
options.rationale: Breastfeeding is encouraged for women on stable opioid substitution because the amount transferred is small and feeding reduces the severity and duration of withdrawal. Stopping it abruptly can worsen symptoms. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Clinical information)

options.text: Give naloxone to clarify whether the symptoms are opioid related
options.rationale: Naloxone precipitates acute withdrawal and seizures in an opioid exposed newborn and is contraindicated in this setting. There is no diagnostic role for it here. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

options.text: Full septic screen with intravenous antibiotics pending cultures
options.rationale: Sepsis must be considered when a newborn deteriorates, but this baby is afebrile with normal perfusion and a clinical picture explained by the known exposure. Reflex septic screening separates mother and baby and undermines feeding. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

options.text: Withdrawal scoring with supportive care, medicating above threshold
options.rationale: Scoring on a validated tool at set intervals is what distinguishes an unsettled baby from one who needs opioid replacement, and swaddling, low stimulus care and frequent feeds resolve many cases without medication. Treatment decisions follow consecutive scores rather than a single impression. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

explanation.summary: Neonatal abstinence syndrome after intrauterine opioid exposure typically appears within the first three days for heroin and later, up to about a week, for methadone because of its longer half life. Assessment uses a structured scoring tool such as the Finnegan or its modified versions, applied at consistent intervals after feeds, and the decision to medicate rests on consecutive scores above threshold rather than on a single observation. Non pharmacological care is the foundation of treatment and includes rooming in, swaddling, minimal handling and light, frequent feeding, and dedicated units achieve lower medication rates with these measures. When medication is needed, oral morphine is the usual first agent, with phenobarbital added for polydrug exposure. Breastfeeding is supported for women on stable opioid substitution because it reduces the severity and duration of withdrawal, and naloxone is contraindicated because it precipitates abrupt withdrawal and seizures.
key_points: Methadone exposed babies may not show peak withdrawal until several days after birth.
Structured repeated scoring drives the decision to medicate.
Rooming in, swaddling and frequent feeds reduce the need for medication.
Breastfeeding is encouraged on stable opioid substitution therapy.
Naloxone is contraindicated because it precipitates acute withdrawal.
explanation.pearls: Score after a feed rather than during a period of hunger, because a hungry baby scores as irritable and excessively sucking, and inconsistent timing of scoring is the commonest reason infants are started on morphine they do not need.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

subtopic_detail: Six cafe au lait macules with axillary freckling in a seven year old with a normal examination
stem: A 7-year-old boy has had increasing brown skin patches over two years. He is well and progressing normally at school, with no headaches or visual complaints. His father has similar patches.

data_table.Examination: Six flat light brown macules over 5 mm on the trunk and limbs, axillary freckling, no cutaneous nodules, no scoliosis, normal neurological examination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing plan?

options.text: Genetic testing of the responsible gene before any surveillance
options.rationale: Molecular testing is useful for atypical presentations and reproductive counselling but is not needed when clinical criteria are met, and awaiting it delays surveillance. A negative result would not overturn a clinical diagnosis. (Source: Genetics Services Australia: Neurofibromatosis)

options.text: Annual ophthalmology, blood pressure and spine review, plus genetics
options.rationale: The skin findings meet the diagnostic criteria in a child with an affected parent, and annual surveillance targets the complications that matter, namely optic pathway glioma, hypertension from renal artery or adrenal disease, and scoliosis. Genetics involvement supports family counselling. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits today
options.rationale: Routine neuroimaging of asymptomatic children is not recommended, because incidental findings are common and lesions that matter declare themselves through visual or endocrine change. Imaging is triggered by abnormal ophthalmological assessment or new symptoms. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

options.text: Skin biopsy of one pigmented lesion to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: The diagnosis is clinical and a biopsy of a pigmented macule adds nothing to criteria that are already satisfied. It also subjects a child to a procedure whose result cannot change management. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

options.text: Reassure that these are inherited birthmarks and review as needed
options.rationale: Six macules of this size with axillary freckling is a recognised diagnostic combination rather than a benign familial pattern, and the father is most likely affected too. Discharging the child forfeits surveillance during the years when optic glioma presents. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

explanation.summary: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is diagnosed clinically when two or more criteria are present, and the combination most often seen in a young child is six or more cafe au lait macules over five millimetres with skinfold freckling in the axillae or groin. Other criteria include two or more neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma, two or more Lisch nodules, optic pathway glioma, a characteristic bony lesion such as sphenoid dysplasia or tibial pseudarthrosis, and an affected first degree relative. Cutaneous neurofibromas usually appear around puberty, so their absence in a seven year old is expected and does not argue against the diagnosis. Surveillance is annual and clinical, covering vision and ophthalmological assessment for optic pathway glioma, blood pressure for renal artery stenosis and phaeochromocytoma, growth and puberty for hypothalamic involvement, the spine for scoliosis, and learning and behaviour, which are the commonest day to day problems. Routine imaging of asymptomatic children is not recommended.
key_points: Two or more diagnostic criteria establish the diagnosis clinically.
Six or more cafe au lait macules with skinfold freckling is the usual childhood combination.
Cutaneous neurofibromas typically appear around puberty and are not expected earlier.
Annual surveillance covers vision, blood pressure, growth, spine and learning.
Routine brain imaging in asymptomatic children is not indicated.
explanation.pearls: Measure the blood pressure at every visit, because hypertension in a child with this condition is renal artery stenosis or phaeochromocytoma until proven otherwise rather than essential hypertension, and it is easily missed when the cuff is skipped in a well looking child.

subtopic_detail: One white pupil and one red pupil across several recent phone photographs in a thriving nine month old
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a nine month old girl in a general clinic. Her mother has brought her phone and shows you six photographs taken over the past two months, in which one pupil looks white while the other glows orange red.

The baby was born at term, feeds well and is tracking along the fiftieth centile for weight and length. She fixes on faces, follows a rolling ball across the room and reaches accurately for a small toy with either hand. There is no family history of childhood eye disease and no squint noticed by either parent.

data_table.Examination: Red reflex absent on the right and present on the left, no proptosis, no orbital swelling, corneal light reflex symmetrical, cover test reveals no shift on either side, anterior segments clear to penlight examination
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent referral to a paediatric ophthalmologist for examination under anaesthesia within one week
options.rationale: An absent red reflex in one eye is an urgent finding at any age and needs dilated examination under anaesthesia by a paediatric ophthalmologist, because the differential includes a tumour in which delay changes both survival and eye preservation. Normal visual behaviour does not soften the urgency, since a child with one working eye behaves normally. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.text: Reassure the mother that asymmetric camera flash is common and review the child at her twelve month health check
options.rationale: Off axis flash can produce a false white pupil in a single photograph, but a reflex that is reproducibly absent on direct examination is not a photographic artefact. Reassurance without examination findings to support it is the main route by which these presentations are delayed. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.text: Request an outpatient orbital ultrasound and review the result at a routine clinic appointment in six weeks
options.rationale: Imaging is arranged by the ophthalmology service as part of a staging assessment, not as a filter before referral, and a six week routine loop wastes the interval that matters most. Ordering the scan first also risks a normal report being read as permission to stop. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.text: Refer to a community optometrist for refraction and occlusion therapy to prevent amblyopia in the affected eye
options.rationale: Occlusion therapy treats amblyopia once a structural cause has been excluded, and applying it first would treat a consequence while leaving the cause unexamined. Optometrists cannot perform the dilated examination under anaesthesia that this finding requires. (Source: RANZCO: Paediatric vision screening)

options.text: Arrange a screening magnetic resonance scan of the brain and orbits before making any ophthalmology referral
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging has a role in assessing optic nerve and intracranial extension but follows the ophthalmic examination rather than preceding it, and in this age group it needs anaesthesia of its own. Sequencing it first adds a delay without changing the immediate pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

explanation.summary: The red reflex examination is part of every newborn check and every subsequent well child review in Australia, and its whole purpose is to detect opacity or mass in the visual axis before vision or life is threatened. An absent or asymmetric reflex carries a differential of retinoblastoma, congenital cataract, retinal detachment, persistent fetal vasculature and severe refractive error. Retinoblastoma is the reason the pathway is urgent rather than routine, because it is the most common intraocular malignancy of childhood and outcomes track tightly with time to diagnosis. Parents frequently present with photographs, and a reproducible white pupil across multiple images taken at different angles is a genuine finding rather than an artefact. Normal fixing and following in a child with one unaffected eye is expected and is never reassuring.
key_points: An absent unilateral red reflex requires paediatric ophthalmology assessment within days, not weeks
Normal visual behaviour is preserved when one eye is unaffected and does not exclude serious pathology
Repeated white pupil across several photographs taken at different angles argues against flash artefact
Definitive assessment is dilated examination under anaesthesia, with imaging arranged by the eye service
The differential spans retinoblastoma, congenital cataract, retinal detachment and persistent fetal vasculature
explanation.pearls: Around one in ten children with retinoblastoma present with squint rather than leukocoria, so a new squint after six months of age earns the same dilated examination that a white pupil does.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

subtopic_detail: Profuse purulent eye discharge with marked lid swelling on day three of life after an unscreened pregnancy
stem:
You are the paediatric resident called to the postnatal ward to see a baby boy who is seventy hours old. The midwife reports that both eyes began weeping yesterday evening and that this morning she could barely part the lids to clean them.

He was born at term by normal vaginal delivery to a nineteen year old woman who booked late and declined the routine first trimester sexual health screen. He has fed hungrily throughout and has had six wet nappies in the past day. He is afebrile and handles normally when undressed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 142 beats per minute, blood pressure 64/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Marked bilateral lid oedema with thick yellow discharge reaccumulating within a minute of cleaning, conjunctival injection with chemosis, corneas clear to penlight, anterior fontanelle soft, no rash and no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Eye swab taken for Gram stain, bacterial culture and nucleic acid amplification testing, results pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence topical chloramphenicol drops two hourly and review the baby on the postnatal ward the following morning
options.rationale: Topical therapy alone does not reach the systemic reservoir and does not prevent the corneal perforation that makes this presentation an emergency. Chloramphenicol drops are reasonable for a mild sticky eye later in the neonatal period, which is a different clinical picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit for intravenous ceftriaxone and frequent saline eye irrigation, with maternal and partner contact tracing
options.rationale: Onset within the first five days with copious purulent discharge and marked lid oedema is managed as gonococcal ophthalmia until proven otherwise, which requires a systemic third generation cephalosporin plus mechanical clearance of the purulent load by irrigation. The mother and her partner need treatment and contact tracing because the baby is the sentinel case. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start oral azithromycin for fourteen days and arrange community midwife review of the eyes every second day
options.rationale: Oral azithromycin is the treatment for neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis, which typically appears between days five and fourteen with less dramatic lid swelling and often a cough. Choosing it here covers the wrong organism during the window in which corneal damage occurs. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

options.text: Observe with hourly saline cleaning alone and start antibiotics only once the swab results have become available
options.rationale: Irrigation is a necessary part of treatment but is not sufficient alone, and waiting for culture surrenders the day or two in which perforation can occur. Gram stain may return within hours but treatment starts on the clinical pattern rather than on the laboratory. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal conjunctivitis)

options.text: Perform a full septic screen including lumbar puncture and start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin
options.rationale: This is the empirical regimen for undifferentiated early neonatal sepsis, but the baby is afebrile, feeding and systemically well with a localised picture, and neither agent reliably treats the organism in question. A broader workup would be triggered by systemic signs rather than by the eye findings alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal conjunctivitis)

explanation.summary: Conjunctivitis in the first month of life is graded by time of onset and by the severity of the lid and discharge findings, because the two organisms that matter behave differently. Gonococcal disease presents hyperacutely in the first few days with copious pus and tense lid oedema, and it is the only cause that perforates the cornea within days. Chlamydial disease is commoner in Australia and presents in the second week with a more indolent watery then mucopurulent discharge, sometimes with an afebrile pneumonitis. Chemical irritation from birth prophylaxis and simple nasolacrimal duct obstruction make up most of the remaining presentations and need no antibiotics. Late booking with declined screening removes the antenatal safety net and shifts the pretest probability substantially.
key_points: Onset in the first five days with copious pus and tense lid oedema is treated as gonococcal until excluded
Systemic third generation cephalosporin plus saline irrigation is the treatment, not topical antibiotic alone
Chlamydial conjunctivitis appears from day five to fourteen and is treated with oral azithromycin
Corneal perforation is the complication that makes the gonococcal presentation a same day emergency
The neonate is the sentinel case, so maternal and partner treatment and contact tracing follow automatically
explanation.pearls: Neonatal chlamydial infection acquired at delivery can present as an afebrile staccato cough with tachypnoea at four to twelve weeks, long after the eyes have settled, so a past sticky eye is worth asking about in an afebrile infant with a persistent cough.

subtopic_detail: Painful restriction of eye movement with reduced colour vision emerging during treatment of a sinus infection
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a seven year old boy who has had a blocked nose and facial pain for eight days and was started on oral amoxicillin by his general practitioner three days ago. His mother brings him back because the swelling around his left eye has worsened since this morning and he now cries when he looks up.

He is alert, drinking and has had no vomiting. He has no history of trauma, insect bite or preceding skin lesion, and his immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tense left periorbital swelling with erythema extending to the brow, globe displaced forwards and laterally, pain and limitation on upgaze and abduction, red desaturation on comparing a red object between the two eyes, visual acuity 6/6 right and 6/12 left
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 17.8 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), C reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Change to oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for ten days and arrange a clinic review in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Oral therapy with review is the correct pathway for preseptal cellulitis, in which the globe moves freely and vision is normal. Painful restricted movement with reduced colour discrimination places this behind the orbital septum, where oral absorption and clinic follow up are both inadequate. (Source: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.text: Arrange contrast computed tomography of the orbits and sinuses and start intravenous antibiotics with eye review
options.rationale: Proptosis, painful ophthalmoplegia and red desaturation indicate post septal involvement, and contrast imaging is needed to identify a subperiosteal or orbital collection that would require drainage. Intravenous antibiotics and ophthalmology involvement begin immediately rather than after the scan. (Source: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.text: Apply warm compresses with topical chloramphenicol ointment and review in the short stay unit in six hours
options.rationale: Topical treatment addresses the conjunctival surface and has no effect on an infection sited within the orbit behind the septum. A six hour observation period also allows optic nerve compromise to progress unmonitored. (Source: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture to exclude meningitis before committing the child to any intravenous antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: There is no neck stiffness, altered conscious state or other feature pointing to meningeal involvement, and the localising signs all sit within the orbit. Lumbar puncture would delay treatment of the process that is actually threatening this child's vision. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer directly for urgent surgical drainage of the orbit without obtaining any cross sectional imaging beforehand
options.rationale: Many children with post septal infection settle on intravenous antibiotics alone, and imaging is what distinguishes those with a drainable collection from those without. Operating without knowing whether a collection exists commits a child to an avoidable procedure. (Source: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

explanation.summary: Infection around the eye divides at the orbital septum, and that division drives the entire management pathway. Preseptal disease produces lid swelling and erythema with a freely mobile globe, normal acuity and normal colour vision, and is treated orally in the community with review. Post septal or orbital disease adds proptosis, pain or restriction on eye movement, reduced acuity, an afferent pupillary defect or red desaturation, and is managed with admission, intravenous antibiotics, imaging and ophthalmology involvement. Ethmoid sinusitis is the usual source in school aged children because the lamina papyracea is thin and permits direct spread. The complications that justify urgency are optic nerve compromise, subperiosteal abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis and intracranial extension.
key_points: The septum divides preseptal disease, treated orally, from orbital disease, which needs admission and imaging
Proptosis, painful or restricted eye movement, reduced acuity and red desaturation all indicate post septal spread
Ethmoid sinusitis spreading through the lamina papyracea is the usual source in school aged children
Contrast computed tomography identifies a subperiosteal collection and guides whether drainage is needed
Intravenous antibiotics and ophthalmology review start before the scan rather than after the report
explanation.pearls: Red desaturation, tested by asking the child which eye sees a red object as brighter, becomes abnormal before visual acuity falls, so it is the earliest bedside sign that the optic nerve is under pressure.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

subtopic_detail: Pallor and irritability in a toddler taking nine hundred millilitres of cow milk daily with a normal ferritin during a viral illness
stem: An 18-month-old boy has become pale and less active over two months. He drinks about 900 mL of cow milk daily and eats little else. A viral illness three days ago has settled.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, soft flow murmur, no organomegaly or bruising
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L, MCV 64 fL, RDW 18.4% (11.5-14.5), ferritin 48 micrograms/L (15-200), CRP 22 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral iron 3 mg/kg daily and limit cow milk to 500 mL
options.rationale: The film, indices and raised red cell distribution width describe iron deficiency, and the normal ferritin is explained by the raised C reactive protein, since ferritin rises as an acute phase reactant during intercurrent illness. Replacement plus reduction of the milk volume that is both displacing iron rich food and causing occult gut losses addresses cause and deficit together. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Order haemoglobin electrophoresis before treatment
options.rationale: Thalassaemia trait is worth considering in a microcytic child, but it characteristically gives a normal or low red cell distribution width with a red cell count that is high for the haemoglobin, and the pencil forms here point elsewhere. Electrophoresis is also distorted by coexisting iron deficiency, so treating first and testing later is the better sequence. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Arrange an urgent bone marrow aspirate and film review
options.rationale: A flow murmur is an expected haemodynamic consequence of anaemia at this haemoglobin and is not itself a marrow indication. Normal white cells and platelets above the reference range, with no organomegaly or bruising, argue strongly against marrow infiltration. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

options.text: Reassure that the ferritin is normal and repeat after recovery
options.rationale: This is the specific trap the C reactive protein is there to expose, because inflammation lifts ferritin into the normal range while stores remain empty. A haemoglobin of 88 g/L with a symptomatic child is not a result to observe for several weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Refer for an intravenous iron infusion first line
options.rationale: Intravenous iron is reserved for malabsorption, ongoing losses that outstrip oral intake, or documented failure of an adequately taken oral trial. Starting there exposes a well toddler to an infusion reaction risk for a deficiency that usually corrects with drops and dietary change. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional deficiency in Australian toddlers, and excessive cow milk intake is the commonest driver, acting through three mechanisms at once. Milk is low in iron, it displaces iron rich solids by filling the child, and in large volumes it causes a low grade protein losing enteropathy with occult blood loss. Volumes above about five hundred millilitres a day in this age group are the practical threshold. The diagnostic trap is that ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so any concurrent infection lifts it into the normal range and a normal value cannot exclude deficiency unless inflammatory markers are also normal. Beyond the anaemia itself, sustained iron deficiency in the second year of life is associated with lasting deficits in cognition and behaviour, which is why treatment is not deferred.
key_points: Cow milk above roughly five hundred millilitres daily in a toddler is a leading cause of iron deficiency
Ferritin rises with inflammation, so a normal value alongside a raised C reactive protein does not exclude deficiency
A high red cell distribution width with pencil forms favours iron deficiency over thalassaemia trait
Oral elemental iron at three milligrams per kilogram daily is first line, with intravenous iron reserved for failure
A soft flow murmur is an expected consequence of anaemia rather than a separate cardiac problem
explanation.pearls: Recheck the haemoglobin four weeks after starting oral iron and expect a rise of at least 10 g/L; continue treatment for a further three months after normalisation to refill stores rather than stopping once the count corrects.

subtopic_detail: Witnessed breathing pauses and morning headache in a four year old with large tonsils and poor weight gain
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a four year old girl whose parents describe loud snoring on most nights since she was two. Her father has recorded a video on his phone in which she stops breathing for around twelve seconds, then gasps and rolls over.

She wakes unrefreshed, complains of headache on several mornings a week and falls asleep in the car on short trips. Her kindergarten teacher has raised concerns about inattention and oppositional behaviour in the afternoons. Her weight has drifted from the fiftieth to the tenth centile over eighteen months while her height has tracked steadily.

data_table.Examination: Mouth breathing at rest with hyponasal speech, tonsils meeting in the midline, no cervical lymphadenopathy, normal tympanic membranes, no adenoidal facies, cardiovascular and respiratory examination normal, body mass index on the tenth centile
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to an ear nose and throat surgeon for consideration of adenotonsillectomy as the definitive treatment
options.rationale: Habitual snoring with witnessed apnoea, unrefreshing sleep, daytime somnolence, neurobehavioural change and faltering weight in a child with obstructing tonsils is the clinical picture for which adenotonsillectomy is first line and curative in the large majority. Surgical referral does not require a preceding sleep study when the history and airway findings are this concordant. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

options.text: Start an intranasal corticosteroid spray for six weeks and review the symptoms at the end of that treatment period
options.rationale: Intranasal steroid has a modest role in mild disease or in children awaiting surgery, but it does not reduce tonsillar tissue meeting in the midline. Using it as the sole strategy here accepts six more weeks of fragmented sleep in a child already losing weight centiles. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

options.text: Arrange a trial of continuous positive airway pressure delivered overnight through a paediatric nasal interface
options.rationale: Positive airway pressure is reserved for children in whom surgery is contraindicated, has already failed, or who have craniofacial or neuromuscular disease, because adherence in preschoolers is poor. It treats the obstruction nightly rather than removing the tissue causing it. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

options.text: Refer for developmental assessment of attention difficulties before pursuing any investigation of the sleep symptoms
options.rationale: Inattention and oppositional behaviour are recognised daytime consequences of fragmented sleep in this age group and commonly improve once the obstruction is relieved. Assessing attention first risks labelling a sleep disorder as a primary behavioural one. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

options.text: Request overnight oximetry at home and treat only if the trace shows at least three clusters of desaturation below ninety
options.rationale: Oximetry has value when it is positive, since a positive trace confirms disease, but a negative study does not exclude it and would wrongly stand down a convincing clinical picture. Making treatment conditional on the trace inverts the relationship between a screening test and a strong history. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric sleep services)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric sleep services

explanation.summary: Obstructive sleep apnoea affects around two to four per cent of Australian children and peaks between two and six years, matching the period of greatest adenotonsillar hypertrophy relative to airway size. The daytime phenotype in children differs from adults, presenting as inattention, hyperactivity and oppositionality more often than as frank sleepiness, which is why it is regularly mistaken for a primary behavioural disorder. Untreated disease carries consequences across growth, cardiovascular function and learning, with faltering growth driven by increased work of breathing and disrupted growth hormone secretion during fragmented slow wave sleep. Polysomnography remains the reference standard but access is limited in Australia, and it is not required before referral when the history and examination agree. Adenotonsillectomy resolves symptoms in the large majority of otherwise healthy children.
key_points: Peak incidence is two to six years, matching maximal adenotonsillar size relative to the airway
Daytime presentation in children is inattention and oppositionality more often than overt sleepiness
Faltering growth reflects increased work of breathing and disrupted slow wave growth hormone release
Adenotonsillectomy is first line and curative in most otherwise healthy children with concordant findings
A negative overnight oximetry trace does not exclude the diagnosis and should not override a strong history
explanation.pearls: Children under three years, those with a body mass index above the ninety fifth centile and those with trisomy 21 or neuromuscular disease need postoperative overnight monitoring after adenotonsillectomy, as their risk of respiratory compromise in the first night is materially higher.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric sleep services

subtopic_detail: Bedwetting most nights in a seven year old who is dry by day and has never had a dry spell lasting six months
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a seven year old boy whose parents want help with bedwetting. He wets five or six nights a week and has never been reliably dry overnight for longer than a fortnight. He is dry during the day, does not rush to the toilet, passes urine four to five times a day and opens his bowels daily without straining.
