He has started avoiding school camps and a friend's sleepover, which is what prompted the visit. His parents have already tried lifting him at eleven each night and restricting drinks after dinner without benefit. There is no snoring and no daytime somnolence.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no palpable bladder or faecal loading, normal external genitalia, normal lower limb tone power and reflexes, no sacral dimple or hair tuft, spine straight, growth along the fiftieth centile
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for glucose protein leucocytes and nitrites, bladder diary shows age appropriate voided volumes with no urgency episodes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe oral oxybutynin at night and titrate the dose upwards over four weeks according to the response
options.rationale: Antimuscarinic therapy targets detrusor overactivity, which announces itself through daytime urgency, frequency and holding manoeuvres, none of which are present here. Using it for monosymptomatic bedwetting treats a mechanism this child does not have. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

options.text: Continue nightly lifting and fluid restriction after dinner, and reassure the family that this resolves with age
options.rationale: Spontaneous resolution does occur at around fifteen per cent per year, but this family has already trialled these measures without effect and the child is now declining social activities. Lifting also trains a child to void while asleep rather than to wake to a full bladder. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

options.text: Arrange a bedwetting alarm with structured family support and review the response after four to six weeks
options.rationale: An alarm is first line for monosymptomatic bedwetting in a child of this age, has the highest sustained success once treatment stops, and works by conditioning waking to the sensation of a full bladder. Success depends on the child waking fully and completing the routine, so structured support and a defined review point are part of the prescription. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

options.text: Prescribe oral desmopressin nightly as an ongoing treatment and continue it until he becomes reliably dry
options.rationale: Desmopressin works quickly but relapse on withdrawal is common, which is why it is best used for short term cover such as a camp or sleepover rather than as the primary long term strategy. It also requires evening fluid restriction to avoid hyponatraemia. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for renal tract ultrasound and urodynamic studies before committing the family to any specific treatment
options.rationale: Imaging and urodynamics are reserved for children with daytime symptoms, a history of urinary infection, abnormal voiding or neurological signs, all absent here. Investigating a normal examination with a normal bladder diary delays the treatment that works. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

explanation.summary: Nocturnal enuresis is defined as involuntary wetting during sleep in a child of five years or older, and the first branch point is whether it is monosymptomatic, meaning no daytime urinary symptoms at all. Monosymptomatic enuresis reflects a mismatch between overnight urine production, bladder capacity and arousal from sleep, and is treated with an alarm or desmopressin. Non monosymptomatic enuresis, signalled by urgency, frequency, holding manoeuvres or daytime wetting, points to bladder dysfunction and needs that treated first. Constipation is the single commonest reversible contributor across both groups and is specifically sought at every assessment. Secondary enuresis, meaning recurrence after six months of dryness, widens the differential to include diabetes, urinary infection, and psychosocial stressors including abuse.
key_points: Monosymptomatic enuresis means no daytime urgency, frequency, holding or wetting on careful history
The alarm is first line and has the best sustained response after treatment stops
Desmopressin acts rapidly but relapses on withdrawal, so it suits short term cover such as camps
Constipation is the commonest reversible contributor and is asked about at every assessment
Imaging and urodynamics are reserved for daytime symptoms, infection, or neurological findings
explanation.pearls: Alarm treatment is continued until the child achieves fourteen consecutive dry nights, and stopping earlier is the commonest reason for relapse, so set that endpoint with the family when you write the prescription.

subtopic_detail: Sudden painful clustered erosions of uniform size on eczematous skin with fever after contact with a relative with a cold sore
stem: A 2-year-old girl with eczema has a facial rash that changed over 24 hours. She is in pain and has stopped drinking. Her grandmother had a lip blister three days ago.

data_table.Examination: Clustered erosions of uniform size, no honey coloured crusting, eyelids involved to the lash line, fluorescein negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase to a potent topical corticosteroid with wet dressings
options.rationale: Escalating topical steroid is the correct response to an eczema flare but is the wrong response to this pattern, and unopposed potent steroid over these lesions can allow the infection to extend. The uniform punched out morphology is what separates the two situations. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema herpeticum)

options.text: Oral cefalexin for seven days with review by the general practitioner
options.rationale: Bacterial superinfection of eczema is common and produces honey coloured crusting and pustules rather than uniform monomorphic erosions, and it is absent on this description. Treating only the bacterial possibility leaves the driving process untreated for a further two days. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit for intravenous aciclovir with ophthalmology review
options.rationale: Widespread monomorphic punched out erosions on eczematous skin in a febrile unwell toddler after cold sore contact is treated as disseminated herpes simplex, and involvement above the lash line with systemic upset and poor oral intake makes the intravenous route appropriate. Ophthalmology review is needed because periocular disease can progress to keratitis even with a currently clear fluorescein examination. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema herpeticum)

options.text: Topical aciclovir cream five times daily with clinic review tomorrow
options.rationale: Topical antiviral has negligible penetration across a large disrupted surface and no effect on viraemia, so it does not treat disseminated disease. It is intended for a localised recurrent cold sore on intact skin in an otherwise well person. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Analgesia and oral rehydration while awaiting the viral swab result
options.rationale: Nucleic acid testing may take a day or more, and the recognised complications of untreated dissemination include keratitis, encephalitis and bacterial sepsis from the denuded surface. Treatment starts on the clinical pattern and is stopped later if the swab excludes the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema herpeticum)

explanation.summary: Eczema herpeticum is disseminated herpes simplex infection of skin whose barrier is already broken by atopic dermatitis, and it is a paediatric emergency because it can progress to keratitis, encephalitis and secondary bacterial sepsis. The discriminating morphology is monomorphic, meaning every lesion is a punched out erosion of roughly the same size and stage, which contrasts with the polymorphic pustules and honey crust of bacterial impetiginisation and with the ordinary excoriated plaques of a flare. Fever, pain out of proportion to the visible rash and a rapidly extending rash in a child with known eczema should all raise it. Contact with an active cold sore is supportive but often absent, since shedding occurs without visible lesions. Periocular disease requires ophthalmology review because herpetic keratitis threatens sight and may not be apparent on an initial examination.
key_points: Monomorphic punched out erosions of uniform size distinguish this from polymorphic bacterial impetiginisation
It is a paediatric emergency owing to risks of keratitis, encephalitis and secondary bacterial sepsis
Systemic aciclovir is the treatment, with the intravenous route for systemic upset or extensive disease
Potent topical corticosteroid is withheld over infected areas while emollients are continued
Periocular involvement mandates ophthalmology review even when fluorescein examination is initially clear
explanation.pearls: Pain is the symptom that separates eczema herpeticum from an ordinary flare: atopic dermatitis itches, while herpetic erosions hurt, so a child who resists any touch to previously itchy skin has changed diagnosis until proven otherwise.

subtopic_detail: Timing of a live attenuated vaccine after completing two months of high dose prednisolone for nephrotic syndrome
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a nephrology clinic reviewing a three year old boy who has just completed an eight week course of prednisolone at 2 mg/kg daily for his first episode of nephrotic syndrome. He is now in remission and off all treatment as of four days ago.

His mother asks about his overdue measles mumps and rubella and varicella vaccinations, which were deferred when he became unwell. His two year old sister is fully immunised and there are no household contacts who are immunosuppressed or pregnant. He has had no blood product or immunoglobulin exposure.

data_table.Examination: Weight tracking on the fiftieth centile, no periorbital or peripheral oedema, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, chest clear, abdomen soft with no ascites
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein creatinine ratio within normal limits, serum albumin 38 g/L (35-50), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about these two vaccines?

options.text: Give both vaccines today, since he is in remission and has been off corticosteroid therapy for several days
options.rationale: Immune reconstitution lags behind the clinical remission and the last dose by weeks, so vaccinating on the day treatment stops risks disseminated vaccine strain infection. Being off treatment is necessary but not on its own sufficient. (Source: NCIRS: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Give the measles mumps and rubella vaccine today and defer the varicella vaccine for a further twelve months
options.rationale: Both are live attenuated vaccines and share the same deferral rule after significant immunosuppression, so separating them in this way has no basis. Splitting them also leaves the child unprotected against the pathogen that causes more severe disease in this setting. (Source: NCIRS: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Withhold both vaccines permanently and rely on maintaining household and childcare contact immunity instead
options.rationale: Permanent contraindication applies to ongoing significant immunosuppression, not to a completed course in a child now in remission. Cocooning contacts is a useful adjunct but is not a substitute for direct protection in a child who can safely be vaccinated later. (Source: NCIRS: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Defer both live vaccines until at least one month after the last corticosteroid dose, then give them together
options.rationale: Prednisolone at 2 mg/kg daily for fourteen days or longer counts as significant immunosuppression, and live vaccines are deferred for at least one month after that course finishes to allow immune recovery. Both may then be given at the same visit, and if not given together they are separated by four weeks. (Source: NCIRS: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Check measles and varicella serology first and vaccinate only if the antibody titres return below protective levels
options.rationale: Serology is not used to decide whether to give routine childhood live vaccines in an unvaccinated child, since absent prior exposure makes a negative result the expected finding. It adds a blood test and a delay without changing the plan. (Source: NCIRS: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Live attenuated vaccines replicate in the recipient, so significant immunosuppression converts an intended mild exposure into a risk of disseminated vaccine strain disease. Australian practice defines significant corticosteroid immunosuppression as prednisolone equivalent at or above 2 mg/kg daily, or 20 mg daily in a child over ten kilograms, continued for fourteen days or more. After such a course, live vaccines are deferred for at least one month once treatment has stopped. Lower doses, alternate day regimens, inhaled or topical corticosteroid, and physiological replacement do not require deferral at all. Inactivated vaccines can be given at any time, although the response may be blunted during treatment, which is a reason to time them thoughtfully rather than to withhold them.
key_points: Significant immunosuppression is prednisolone at or above 2 mg/kg daily for fourteen days or longer
Live vaccines are deferred at least one month after that course stops, not from the date of remission
Measles mumps rubella and varicella follow the same deferral rule and may be given at the same visit
Inhaled, topical, alternate day and replacement dose corticosteroids do not require any deferral
Inactivated vaccines may be given during immunosuppression, though the response may be reduced
explanation.pearls: Two live vaccines not given on the same day must be separated by at least four weeks, because the interferon response to the first blunts the take of the second and can leave the child inadequately protected.

subtopic_detail: Disc battery seen below the diaphragm on radiograph in an asymptomatic four year old who swallowed it two hours earlier
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a four year old girl who was found with an opened remote control two hours ago, and her father is certain that the twenty millimetre disc battery it contained is missing. She has had no drooling, no vomiting, no chest or abdominal pain, and she drank a cup of juice in the waiting room without difficulty.

She has no previous gastrointestinal surgery and no known swallowing problem. A single radiograph of the neck chest and abdomen has been performed.

data_table.Examination: Handling the situation calmly, no drooling, chest clear with no stridor, abdomen soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: Radiograph shows a twenty millimetre disc shaped radio opaque foreign body with a double ring halo sign lying in the gastric antrum, with no free gas beneath either hemidiaphragm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange emergency endoscopic removal within two hours regardless of the position shown on the radiograph
options.rationale: The two hour rule applies to a battery lodged in the oesophagus, where mucosal contact generates a hydroxide burn that can perforate within hours. Once the battery has passed into the stomach that contact is lost and the urgency changes entirely. (Source: RCH CPG: Button battery ingestion)

options.text: Give a dose of oral honey now and discharge her with advice to return only if she develops abdominal pain
options.rationale: Honey is given in the prehospital and pre removal window for a suspected oesophageal battery, where it coats the mucosa and buffers hydroxide generation, and it has no role once the battery is gastric. Discharging without a planned radiograph also removes the safety net that confirms passage. (Source: RCH CPG: Button battery ingestion)

options.text: Admit for observation with four hourly abdominal examination and a repeat radiograph before any discharge home
options.rationale: An asymptomatic child with a gastric battery and a normal abdomen does not need inpatient observation, and admission consumes a bed without altering the outcome. Written return advice covers the small risk of later symptoms just as effectively. (Source: RCH CPG: Button battery ingestion)

options.text: Discharge with written return advice and arrange a repeat radiograph in ten to fourteen days to confirm passage
options.rationale: A battery that has reached the stomach in an asymptomatic child of this age passes spontaneously in the great majority of cases, so observation at home with a defined imaging endpoint is appropriate. The repeat film identifies the minority that fail to progress and therefore need endoscopic retrieval. (Source: RCH CPG: Button battery ingestion)

options.text: Prescribe a stimulant laxative and a high fibre diet to accelerate transit, with review by the local doctor next week
options.rationale: There is no evidence that promoting transit changes the outcome for a gastric battery, and a laxative adds cramping that may confuse later assessment of abdominal pain. The decision point is whether the battery moves, not how quickly. (Source: Poisons Information Centre Australia)

explanation.summary: Disc battery ingestion is dangerous because current flowing at the negative pole hydrolyses tissue fluid and generates hydroxide, producing a liquefactive burn rather than a pressure injury, and this begins within two hours of mucosal contact. The whole management algorithm therefore turns on location. A battery in the oesophagus is removed emergently, ideally within two hours, and honey may be given before removal in a child over twelve months who can swallow and has no perforation signs. A battery that has passed into the stomach in an asymptomatic child is managed expectantly with a repeat radiograph, usually at ten to fourteen days, because spontaneous passage is the rule. Batteries twenty millimetres or larger, children under five years, and any symptomatic child prompt a lower threshold for earlier imaging and for endoscopic retrieval.
key_points: The injury is a hydroxide burn from current at the negative pole, beginning within two hours of contact
An oesophageal battery is removed emergently, ideally within two hours of ingestion
The double ring or halo sign on a plain film distinguishes a disc battery from a swallowed coin
A gastric battery in an asymptomatic child is observed with a repeat radiograph at ten to fourteen days
Failure to progress, or any new symptom, converts expectant management into endoscopic retrieval
explanation.pearls: Delayed catastrophic bleeding from an aorto oesophageal fistula can occur up to four weeks after an oesophageal battery has been removed, so any haematemesis in that window is treated as a surgical emergency rather than as incidental.

subtopic_detail: Two witnessed breathing pauses at home in a seven week old with mild work of breathing and oxygen saturation of 94 per cent
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a seven week old boy, born at thirty five weeks gestation, on day three of a coryzal illness. His parents describe two episodes at home in which he went quiet, stopped breathing for what they estimate was fifteen seconds and looked dusky around the mouth, each ending when they picked him up and rubbed his back.

He has taken about two thirds of his usual feed volume over the past twelve hours. In the department he is alert between examinations and has had no further episode in the ninety minutes since arrival. His older sister has a cold.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 beats per minute, blood pressure 74/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 52 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 per cent in room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recession with no tracheal tug or head bob, widespread fine inspiratory crackles with scattered expiratory wheeze, anterior fontanelle soft, capillary refill two seconds, moist mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal swab positive for respiratory syncytial virus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Discharge home with written advice, as his oxygen saturation and work of breathing are both reassuring
options.rationale: This anchors on the respiratory parameters, which are indeed mild, and ignores the finding that actually predicts deterioration in this age group. Apnoea in a young ex preterm infant frequently precedes rather than follows respiratory decompensation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Discharge home after a four hour period of observation in the department with continuous saturation monitoring
options.rationale: A short observation window cannot exclude recurrence, since apnoeas in this illness cluster irregularly and often worsen around days three to five, which is where this infant sits. The absence of an event in ninety minutes carries little predictive value. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence high flow nasal cannula oxygen at two litres per kilogram per minute and admit to the ward for monitoring
options.rationale: High flow is reserved for infants failing low flow oxygen after a trial of around two hours, and this infant does not currently require any supplemental oxygen at a saturation of 94 per cent. Escalating support ahead of need adds feeding interference without treating the apnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Perform a full septic screen with lumbar puncture and start intravenous antibiotics pending the culture results
options.rationale: A positive viral swab in an afebrile infant with classical auscultatory findings makes concurrent serious bacterial infection unlikely, and apnoea is explained by the confirmed diagnosis. A septic workup would be driven by fever, toxicity or an unexplained picture rather than by apnoea alone in this context. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Admit for inpatient cardiorespiratory monitoring and feeding support, without supplemental oxygen at present
options.rationale: Witnessed apnoea is an admission criterion in its own right in an infant under about two months corrected, because it is the feature that most strongly predicts the need for respiratory support and is independent of saturation and recession. Prematurity at thirty five weeks and reduced feeding compound that risk, and monitoring rather than oxygen is what this infant currently needs. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is the commonest reason for infant admission in Australia, and most disposition decisions are correctly driven by feeding, work of breathing and oxygen requirement. The important exception is apnoea, which in young infants arises from immature central respiratory control responding to viral infection rather than from airway obstruction, and therefore occurs independently of how severe the chest findings look. Risk is concentrated in infants under six to eight weeks of age, those born preterm, and those with chronic lung or cardiac disease or neuromuscular conditions. Australian practice uses low flow nasal prong oxygen as first line when oxygen is needed, with a saturation target of ninety per cent, reserving high flow for failure of low flow after about two hours. Illness typically peaks on days three to five, so an infant presenting at day three is on the rising limb.
key_points: Witnessed apnoea is an independent admission criterion regardless of saturation or work of breathing
Apnoea reflects immature central respiratory control and is concentrated in young and ex preterm infants
Illness peaks at days three to five, so early presentation means the trajectory is still rising
Low flow nasal prong oxygen is first line with a target saturation of ninety per cent
High flow nasal cannula is reserved for failure of low flow oxygen after a trial of about two hours
explanation.pearls: Apnoea can be the presenting feature of respiratory syncytial virus infection before any cough or crackles appear, so a young infant with an unexplained apnoeic episode in winter warrants a viral swab even when the chest sounds clear.

subtopic_detail: Worsening stridor and high fever twelve hours after dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline produced no sustained improvement
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a three year old boy who was brought in last night with a barking cough and stridor, given oral dexamethasone and two doses of nebulised adrenaline, and admitted to the short stay unit when his stridor kept returning.

This morning he looks worse. He is sitting forward, is not interested in his mother's phone and has a weak cough that no longer sounds barking. He is fully immunised. Over the past six hours his temperature has climbed and he has become increasingly reluctant to swallow his own secretions, though he is not drooling.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 168 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute, SpO2 93 per cent in room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Biphasic stridor at rest with marked tracheal tug and intercostal recession, toxic appearance, no rash, chest sounds symmetrical with poor air entry throughout
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 22.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), C reactive protein 148 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give a second dose of oral dexamethasone at 0.6 mg/kg and repeat nebulised adrenaline every twenty minutes
options.rationale: Repeating the croup bundle treats subglottic oedema, and the failure of two previous doses to hold is itself the evidence that a different process is operating. Escalating a treatment that has already failed twice delays the airway plan this child needs. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Request an urgent lateral neck radiograph to look for a thumbprint sign before making any airway decision
options.rationale: Imaging a child with a threatened airway moves them away from staff and equipment and can precipitate obstruction through distress and positioning. Even when the film is abnormal it does not change the immediate need for a controlled airway assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Activate the difficult airway team for inspection in theatre and start intravenous flucloxacillin with ceftriaxone
options.rationale: High fever, toxicity, a leucocytosis and stridor unresponsive to steroid and adrenaline describe bacterial tracheitis, in which purulent membrane rather than oedema obstructs the airway and adrenaline therefore cannot work. Management is airway inspection and clearance under controlled conditions alongside antistaphylococcal cover with a third generation cephalosporin. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Start high flow humidified oxygen and observe for a further two hours before escalating care any further
options.rationale: Humidified oxygen has no effect on a membranous obstruction and a two hour observation period in a toxic child with biphasic stridor risks obstruction occurring without an airway plan in place. Deterioration in this condition is characteristically abrupt. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline for presumed anaphylaxis and commence intravenous hydrocortisone and antihistamine
options.rationale: Anaphylaxis produces urticaria, angioedema, wheeze or hypotension with a plausible exposure and evolves over minutes to hours, not across a night with rising fever and inflammatory markers. Fever and a C reactive protein at this level are not features of an allergic airway. (Source: ASCIA: Anaphylaxis guidelines)

explanation.summary: Viral croup is common, responds to corticosteroid within a few hours and to nebulised adrenaline within minutes, and the response to that bundle is diagnostically useful. A child whose stridor does not settle, who becomes toxic, and who develops high fever with a marked leucocytosis has moved outside that diagnosis, and bacterial tracheitis is the condition that occupies that space. It usually follows a viral illness, is most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus, and obstructs through thick purulent membrane that adrenaline cannot shrink. Epiglottitis remains the other differential but has become rare since Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccination, and characteristically produces drooling and a muffled voice with a shorter history. All of these children are managed by minimising distress and arranging airway inspection with senior anaesthetic and ear nose and throat involvement in theatre rather than by examining the throat at the bedside.
key_points: Failure to respond to dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline argues against simple viral croup
Toxicity, high fever and marked leucocytosis point to bacterial tracheitis with a purulent membrane
Adrenaline cannot relieve membranous obstruction, which is why repeat dosing fails
Management is controlled airway inspection in theatre plus antistaphylococcal and gram negative cover
Avoid throat examination, cannulation attempts and imaging trips in any child with a threatened airway
explanation.pearls: In croup the RCH dose of dexamethasone is 0.15 mg/kg for mild and moderate disease, with 0.6 mg/kg reserved for severe croup, and nebulised adrenaline is a flat 5 mL of 1:1000 rather than a weight based dose, with a minimum three hour observation after the last dose.

subtopic_detail: Quiet chest with a normalising respiratory rate and a rising carbon dioxide after an hour of continuous salbutamol
stem:
You are the emergency registrar managing a nine year old girl who arrived an hour ago with a severe asthma exacerbation. She has had continuous nebulised salbutamol, nebulised ipratropium and oral prednisolone since arrival.

The nurse calls you because the family think she looks calmer. She is no longer speaking in single words because she is not speaking at all, and she is slumped against her mother rather than sitting upright as she was on arrival. Her mother mentions that she was admitted to intensive care with asthma two winters ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 91 per cent on eight litres per minute of oxygen, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Minimal audible wheeze with markedly reduced air entry throughout both lung fields, poor respiratory effort with reducing accessory muscle use, drowsy but rousable to voice
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas shows pH 7.21 (7.32-7.42), carbon dioxide 68 mmHg (41-51), bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22-32), lactate 3.1 mmol/L (less than 2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue the current nebulised therapy and repeat the blood gas in thirty minutes to confirm the trend
options.rationale: This reads the falling respiratory rate and quieter chest as improvement when both are signs of exhaustion and critically reduced air movement. Waiting thirty minutes in a child with this gas invites respiratory arrest. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Reduce the oxygen to maintain saturations between 92 and 94 per cent to avoid suppressing respiratory drive
options.rationale: Hypercapnic drive dependence is a concept from chronic obstructive lung disease in adults and does not apply to acute paediatric asthma, where hypoxia is the immediate threat. Reducing oxygen here would worsen the situation without addressing the obstruction. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Arrange an urgent chest radiograph to exclude pneumothorax before escalating to any further pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: Pneumothorax is worth considering in deteriorating asthma, but breath sounds are symmetrically reduced rather than unilaterally absent and there is no tracheal shift or cardiovascular collapse. Sending an exhausted hypercapnic child to the radiology department delays definitive escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate and call the intensive care team for urgent review at the bedside
options.rationale: A quiet chest with a falling respiratory rate, drowsiness and a rising carbon dioxide describes imminent respiratory failure, not response to treatment, and this child needs second line intravenous bronchodilation with senior critical care input immediately. Intravenous magnesium sulfate is the first line intravenous agent in Australian paediatric practice for severe asthma failing inhaled therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Change the prednisolone to intravenous hydrocortisone and add a further dose of nebulised ipratropium bromide
options.rationale: Switching the corticosteroid route offers no additional benefit when oral prednisolone has already been absorbed and neither agent acts fast enough to alter the next fifteen minutes. Additional ipratropium adds little once the initial doses have been given. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: The most dangerous moment in acute paediatric asthma is the point at which the clinical picture appears to settle, because reduced wheeze, a falling respiratory rate and diminishing accessory muscle use can all mean either improvement or exhaustion. The two are separated by mental state, air entry and gas exchange, and a drowsy child with a quiet chest and a rising carbon dioxide is decompensating. Carbon dioxide in acute asthma normally falls because of hyperventilation, so a normal value is already concerning and a raised value indicates failure. Australian escalation moves from continuous inhaled beta agonist and ipratropium with systemic corticosteroid, to intravenous magnesium sulfate, then to intravenous salbutamol or aminophylline with intensive care involvement. A previous intensive care admission is one of the strongest predictors of a further life threatening episode and should lower the threshold for early escalation.
key_points: A quiet chest means reduced air movement, not resolved bronchospasm, until proven otherwise
Carbon dioxide normally falls in acute asthma, so a normal value is concerning and a raised value is failure
Drowsiness, poor effort and a falling respiratory rate in this setting indicate exhaustion
Intravenous magnesium sulfate is the first line intravenous escalation with intensive care involvement
A prior intensive care admission markedly raises the risk of a subsequent life threatening episode
explanation.pearls: Salbutamol drives potassium into cells and generates lactate through beta two stimulation, so a raised lactate during continuous nebulisation usually reflects the treatment rather than tissue hypoperfusion and is not by itself a reason to give fluid.

subtopic_detail: Doughy skin with preserved blood pressure and a sodium of 163 in an infant whose formula has been scooped incorrectly
stem: A five-month-old boy has four days of vomiting and loose stools. His formula has been made up with an unfamiliar scoop. He weighs 6.4 kg, down from 7.0 kg at four months.

data_table.Examination: Sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, doughy abdominal skin, capillary refill two seconds
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 163 mmol/L, venous pH 7.31, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate fluid management?

options.text: Repeated rapid 20 mL/kg sodium chloride boluses
options.rationale: Repeated boluses are the correct approach to shock, but this infant has a preserved blood pressure and a central capillary refill of two seconds, so he is dehydrated rather than shocked. Volume loading a child who is not shocked accelerates the fall in sodium and raises the risk of cerebral oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

options.text: 0.9 per cent sodium chloride with glucose over 48 hours
options.rationale: In hypernatraemic dehydration the brain has generated intracellular osmoles over days, so correcting the sodium faster than about 0.5 mmol/L per hour, or 10 to 12 mmol/L per day, draws water into brain cells and causes cerebral oedema and seizures. Spreading the deficit and maintenance over 48 hours with an isotonic fluid achieves that rate, with the sodium rechecked frequently. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

options.text: 0.45 per cent sodium chloride with glucose over 12 hours
options.rationale: This combines a hypotonic fluid with a short correction window, which is the fastest route to a dangerous fall in serum sodium. The tonicity of the fluid and the duration of the infusion both need to oppose rapid correction rather than accelerate it. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

options.text: Nasogastric oral rehydration solution at maintenance rate
options.rationale: Nasogastric rehydration is genuinely first line for mild to moderate dehydration failing oral intake, but a sodium of 163 mmol/L with altered conscious state needs the controlled, measurable correction rate that intravenous therapy provides. A 24 hour interval between electrolyte checks is also too long at this sodium. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: 3 per cent sodium chloride before any rehydration
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is used to raise sodium acutely in symptomatic hyponatraemia, which is the opposite disturbance to the one present here. Giving it would worsen an already dangerous hypernatraemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

explanation.summary: Hypernatraemic dehydration behaves differently from the isonatraemic form because water is drawn out of cells into the extracellular space, which preserves circulating volume and therefore masks the usual clinical signs. Children look less unwell than their deficit implies, with normal blood pressure and capillary refill, while carrying the characteristic doughy or velvety skin and a fluctuating conscious state. In Australia the commonest causes are gastroenteritis with inadequate free water replacement, and incorrectly reconstituted formula where too much powder is added to too little water. The danger lies in correction, not in the presentation, because the brain generates idiogenic osmoles over days and rapid lowering of serum sodium drives water into brain cells, producing cerebral oedema and seizures. Correction is therefore capped at about 0.5 mmol/L per hour or 10 to 12 mmol/L per day, with frequent electrolyte monitoring.
key_points: Extracellular volume is relatively preserved, so clinical signs underestimate the true fluid deficit
Doughy inelastic skin with fluctuating irritability and drowsiness is the characteristic picture
Lower the sodium by no more than about 0.5 mmol/L per hour or 10 to 12 mmol/L per day
Rehydrate over 48 hours with an isotonic fluid, rechecking electrolytes every four to six hours
Reserve fluid boluses for genuine shock, since volume loading accelerates the fall in sodium
explanation.pearls: A seizure occurring during treatment of hypernatraemic dehydration usually signals that the sodium has fallen too quickly rather than that it remains too high, so the response is to slow or increase the tonicity of the infusion rather than to give more free water.

subtopic_detail: Persisting jaundice at three weeks in a breastfed infant with pale stools and a conjugated fraction of 68 micromol/L
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a three week old girl brought in because she still looks yellow. She is exclusively breastfed, feeding eight times a day, and her mother is confident about attachment.

Her weight has regained birth weight and is now 200 g above it. Her mother has brought a photograph of this morning's nappy, which shows a putty coloured stool, and mentions that his nappies have looked darker than her older child's did at this age. She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy, received vitamin K at birth and passed meconium on day one.

data_table.Examination: Jaundiced to the abdomen, alert and vigorous, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin with a firm texture, spleen not palpable, no bruising or petechiae, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 212 micromol/L, conjugated fraction 68 micromol/L, alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 40), gamma glutamyl transferase 384 U/L (less than 50), albumin 36 g/L (35-50), international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.9-1.2), full blood count within normal limits, direct antiglobulin test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently to a paediatric liver service the same day for investigation of conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
options.rationale: A conjugated fraction above 25 micromol/L, or above about twenty per cent of the total, is never physiological and never due to breast milk, and with pale stools and a firm liver edge the priority is to exclude biliary atresia. Outcomes after the Kasai portoenterostomy fall sharply beyond sixty days of age, which is what makes the referral same day rather than routine. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Reassure the mother that this is breast milk jaundice and recheck the bilirubin level in a further two weeks
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is common and can persist for up to twelve weeks, but it is an unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia occurring in a thriving infant with normal stool colour. The conjugated fraction and the pale stool exclude it and a two week delay consumes the window in which surgery works best. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Commence intensive phototherapy and repeat the total serum bilirubin level in six hours to assess the response
options.rationale: Phototherapy isomerises unconjugated bilirubin and has no effect on the conjugated fraction, so it cannot treat this picture. It is also contraindicated in significant conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia because it can precipitate the bronze baby syndrome. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Advise a 24 hour trial of formula feeding and repeat the bilirubin to see whether the level falls appreciably
options.rationale: Interrupting breastfeeding was historically used as a diagnostic manoeuvre for breast milk jaundice and is no longer recommended, since it undermines feeding for a test with poor specificity. It has no role at all once the conjugated fraction is raised. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Arrange a urine sample for culture and treat for urinary tract infection while awaiting the laboratory result
options.rationale: Urinary infection genuinely causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in infancy and a urine culture forms part of the workup, but it does not explain acholic stools or a raised gamma glutamyl transferase of this magnitude. Treating it alone would leave the obstructive process unaddressed. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Jaundice persisting beyond fourteen days in a term infant, or beyond twenty one days in a preterm infant, requires a split bilirubin rather than reassurance, and that single test determines everything that follows. An unconjugated result in a thriving breastfed baby with normal stools is usually breast milk jaundice, which needs no treatment beyond confirming that the infant is growing and that thyroid screening was normal. A conjugated fraction above 25 micromol/L or above twenty per cent of the total defines neonatal cholestasis and is always pathological. Biliary atresia is the diagnosis that drives the urgency, because it is progressive and because success of the Kasai portoenterostomy declines steeply with age, with the best outcomes before about sixty days. Pale acholic stools and dark urine are the clinical hallmarks, and parents are often better at reporting stool colour than clinicians are at eliciting it.
key_points: Jaundice beyond fourteen days in a term infant requires a split bilirubin, not reassurance
A conjugated fraction above 25 micromol/L or twenty per cent of total is always pathological
Pale acholic stools with dark urine point to obstruction and to biliary atresia specifically
Kasai portoenterostomy outcomes decline sharply beyond about sixty days of age
Phototherapy does not treat conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and risks the bronze baby syndrome
explanation.pearls: A normal newborn screening test does not exclude biliary atresia, since the screen detects neither it nor most structural liver disease, so a pale stool at three weeks warrants a split bilirubin regardless of a reassuring heel prick result.

subtopic_detail: Refusal to weight bear with a C reactive protein of 62 after apparent improvement on ibuprofen for a presumed irritable hip
stem: A four-year-old boy diagnosed with an irritable hip three days ago improved at first on ibuprofen. Since yesterday he refuses to stand. His mother recorded temperatures of 38.2 and 38.5 degrees C at home.

data_table.Examination: Right hip held flexed and externally rotated, guarding on passive internal rotation
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, CRP 62 mg/L, ESR 48 mm/h, ultrasound shows a 9 mm right hip effusion, pelvic radiograph normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue ibuprofen, orthopaedic review in one week
options.rationale: This is the management of transient synovitis, which characteristically improves over a few days rather than progressing to refusal to weight bear with rising inflammatory markers. Anti inflammatory therapy also partially masks the early signs of infection, which is how these presentations are missed. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Urgent image guided aspiration before antibiotics
options.rationale: Refusal to weight bear, a documented fever above 38.5 degrees Celsius, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 mm/h and a significant effusion satisfy enough predictive criteria that septic arthritis must be excluded by aspirating the joint. Synovial fluid for Gram stain, cell count and culture is obtained before antibiotics because prior dosing reduces the culture yield that guides later therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic arthritis)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin, reviewing response tomorrow
options.rationale: Antibiotics before aspiration compromise the synovial culture and leave the team without an organism to guide a treatment course lasting weeks. A septic hip also needs joint decompression, which antibiotics alone do not provide. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic arthritis)

options.text: Magnetic resonance of both hips before aspiration
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable for suspected osteomyelitis or when the site is unclear, but here ultrasound has already localised a substantial effusion. In a preschooler it needs anaesthesia and would delay the intervention that is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Oral prednisolone, repeat inflammatory markers in 48 hours
options.rationale: Corticosteroid would suppress the inflammatory response and the fever while allowing an untreated joint infection to destroy articular cartilage. It has no place until infection has been definitively excluded. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

explanation.summary: The central task in the acutely limping child is separating transient synovitis, which is common and self limiting, from septic arthritis, which destroys the joint within days if untreated. The widely used predictive criteria are refusal to weight bear, fever above 38.5 degrees Celsius, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 mm/h and a white cell count above 12 x10^9/L, with probability of infection rising steeply as more are met. These criteria guide rather than decide, and C reactive protein has since proven the more responsive single marker. A trajectory that worsens after initial improvement on anti inflammatory therapy is a particularly important pattern, because partial treatment softens the early picture. Ultrasound confirms an effusion but cannot distinguish sterile from infected fluid, so aspiration remains the only test that answers the question.
key_points: Predictive criteria are non weight bearing, fever above 38.5, sedimentation rate above 40 and white cells above 12
Ultrasound demonstrates an effusion but cannot distinguish sterile fluid from infected fluid
Aspiration for Gram stain, cell count and culture precedes antibiotics to preserve the microbiological yield
Deterioration after initial improvement on anti inflammatory therapy argues against transient synovitis
Untreated septic arthritis of the hip destroys cartilage and threatens the femoral head blood supply
explanation.pearls: Kingella kingae is the leading cause of septic arthritis between six months and four years, grows poorly on solid media and is often missed unless synovial fluid is inoculated into blood culture bottles or sent for nucleic acid testing.

subtopic_detail: Headache with a pulse of 62 and a rising blood pressure six hours into treatment as the biochemistry improves
stem: An eleven-year-old girl is six hours into treatment for new onset diabetic ketoacidosis. Her glucose has fallen from 34 to 14 mmol/L. She now has a headache, has vomited, and is irritable and slow to answer.

data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 13, no focal weakness
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH improved from 7.02 to 7.28; corrected sodium 139 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Increase the insulin infusion rate and continue fluids
options.rationale: The biochemistry is in fact correcting steadily and the ketone fall is appropriate, so the deterioration is not explained by insufficient insulin. Raising the rate would accelerate the osmotic shift that is the likely driver of the neurological change. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Give a 10 mL/kg sodium chloride bolus now
options.rationale: Hypovolaemia produces tachycardia with a narrow pulse pressure, not bradycardia with hypertension, so the haemodynamic pattern points the opposite way. A fluid bolus would add to intracranial volume at precisely the wrong moment. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Give hypertonic saline and reduce the fluid rate
options.rationale: Headache with a falling conscious state, bradycardia and rising blood pressure occurring while the biochemistry improves is cerebral oedema, and the Cushing response means treatment cannot wait for imaging. Hyperosmolar therapy with reduction of the fluid infusion rate and immediate critical care involvement is the intervention that alters outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Arrange an urgent computed tomography of the brain
options.rationale: Imaging is frequently normal in the early hours of this complication and a transfer to the scanner delays treatment during the period when deterioration is fastest. The diagnosis in this setting is clinical and treatment precedes confirmation. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Add intravenous glucose to the current regimen
options.rationale: Glucose is added to the fluid once the level approaches 14 to 17 mmol/L so that insulin can continue to clear ketones, and that adjustment is indeed due here. It does not account for bradycardia and hypertension, and treating this as hypoglycaemia at a glucose of 14 mmol/L misreads the picture. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema complicates roughly one per cent of paediatric episodes of diabetic ketoacidosis but accounts for the majority of deaths and lasting neurological disability, and it characteristically appears four to twelve hours into treatment, when the numbers are improving and the team has begun to relax. Risk is concentrated in younger children, in new onset diabetes, and in those presenting with more severe acidosis and a higher urea. The warning features are headache, recurrent vomiting, irritability or drowsiness, incontinence, and specific cranial nerve palsies, with bradycardia and hypertension representing the late Cushing response rather than an early sign. A failure of the sodium to rise as the glucose falls is an important biochemical warning, since corrected sodium should climb during treatment. Because computed tomography is often normal early and transfer wastes time, treatment with hyperosmolar therapy is given on clinical grounds.
key_points: Onset is typically four to twelve hours into treatment, as the biochemistry is improving
Bradycardia with rising blood pressure is a late Cushing response, not a sign of hypovolaemia
Risk concentrates in younger children, new onset diabetes and more severe presenting acidosis
Treat clinically with hypertonic saline or mannitol and reduced fluid rate rather than awaiting imaging
A corrected sodium that fails to rise as glucose falls is an early biochemical warning sign
explanation.pearls: Corrected sodium rises by about 2.4 mmol/L for every 5.5 mmol/L fall in glucose, so plotting it hourly during treatment gives an objective early warning that precedes any change in conscious state.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Diabetes management

subtopic_detail: next investigation for a six week old with a raised conjugated bilirubin fraction after an ultrasound that failed to visualise the gallbladder
stem: A six-week-old breastfed girl is still jaundiced. She feeds well and is gaining weight on the tenth centile. Her nappies stain orange and her stools are putty coloured.

data_table.Examination: Firm liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 148 micromol/L with conjugated fraction 68, ALT 128 U/L, GGT 410 U/L
data_table.Imaging: Ultrasound after four hours fasting: gallbladder not visualised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Transfer to a paediatric liver unit for cholangiography
options.rationale: A conjugated fraction above 20 per cent with pale stools and a non-visualised gallbladder is obstructive cholestasis until disproven, and the definitive test is operative cholangiography with biopsy at a specialist centre. The urgency is driven by the fact that portoenterostomy performed before around sixty days of age gives far better bile drainage than surgery after that point. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound after a six hour fast before referral
options.rationale: Fasting technique does affect gallbladder visualisation and a repeat scan is sometimes useful, but a normal ultrasound never excludes the diagnosis and repeating it costs days inside a narrow surgical window. Ultrasound is best used to find the alternative lesions such as a choledochal cyst. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Iminodiacetic acid scan after phenobarbital pre-treatment
options.rationale: Radionuclide scanning has largely fallen out of favour because it is highly sensitive but poorly specific, and the phenobarbital priming period adds close to a week of delay. It cannot exclude the diagnosis when it is abnormal, so the patient ends up at cholangiography regardless. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Reassure as breast milk jaundice, review in two weeks
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and by definition has a conjugated fraction below 20 per cent with normal stool colour, so this infant fails both criteria. The near pair matters because a well feeding thriving baby looks reassuring and that is how the diagnosis is missed. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Ursodeoxycholic acid and fat soluble vitamins, weekly review
options.rationale: Supportive nutritional and choleretic therapy belongs after the cause is established, and fat soluble vitamin replacement is certainly needed in prolonged cholestasis. Beginning it alone treats the consequences of obstruction while the window for surgery closes. (Source: Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Prolonged Neonatal Jaundice)
source_refs: Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Prolonged Neonatal Jaundice

explanation.summary: Any infant still jaundiced at fourteen days of age needs a split bilirubin, and a conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of the total defines cholestasis that is never physiological. Pale acholic stools and dark urine point to obstruction, and a non-visualised gallbladder on a fasted ultrasound supports it although a normal scan would not exclude it. The definitive investigation is intraoperative cholangiography with liver biopsy at a paediatric liver centre, arranged without delay. Outcome after Kasai portoenterostomy falls sharply once the infant passes about sixty days, so referral is measured in days rather than weeks.
key_points: Jaundice persisting beyond fourteen days requires a split bilirubin, not observation
A conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of total bilirubin is always pathological
Pale stools with dark urine indicate obstruction until proven otherwise
A normal ultrasound does not exclude biliary atresia; cholangiography is definitive
Portoenterostomy before about sixty days gives markedly better bile drainage
explanation.pearls: Ask the parents to compare the nappy against a printed stool colour chart rather than asking whether the stools look pale, because parental description alone misses about a third of acholic stools. A normal coagulation profile is reassuring only transiently: vitamin K dependent factors fall within weeks in cholestasis, so give intramuscular vitamin K before any biopsy is contemplated.

sources.label: Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Prolonged Neonatal Jaundice

subtopic_detail: an adolescent with referred knee pain and an externally rotated leg whose frontal hip radiograph was reported as normal
stem: A 13-year-old boy has six weeks of dull left knee ache. A knee radiograph was normal and ibuprofen has not helped. He has limped for a fortnight. His body mass index is on the 97th centile.

data_table.Examination: Knee examination normal; left hip internal rotation 10 degrees versus 40 on the right, with obligatory external rotation on flexion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Screening bloods for juvenile arthritis, then review
options.rationale: An inflammatory arthropathy would be expected to produce joint swelling, morning stiffness or involvement elsewhere, none of which are present. Serology has no role in a mechanical presentation and delays the imaging that will make the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp)

options.text: Frog leg lateral hip views, non-weight-bearing meanwhile
options.rationale: A frontal film misses early posterior slip of the femoral epiphysis in a substantial minority of cases, and the lateral projection is where the displacement is seen. Non-weight-bearing begins immediately on clinical suspicion because continued loading can convert a stable slip into an unstable one with a much higher rate of avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Magnetic resonance of the left hip, weight bearing allowed
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance detects a pre-slip and is useful when plain films are genuinely normal, but it is not the immediate next test and permitting weight bearing while awaiting it is the part that causes harm. The lateral radiograph is faster and answers the question in most cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Ultrasound of the left hip and inflammatory markers
options.rationale: Ultrasound answers the question of joint effusion, which serves transient synovitis and septic arthritis, and he is afebrile with six weeks of symptoms rather than days. The distinguishing relationship is that synovitis restricts rotation in all directions while a slip produces the characteristic obligatory external rotation on flexion. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp)

options.text: Physiotherapy for patellofemoral rehabilitation, review in six weeks
options.rationale: Anterior knee pain in an adolescent is frequently patellofemoral, but a normal knee examination with restricted hip rotation relocates the problem to the hip entirely. Six weeks of loaded rehabilitation is exactly the interval in which a stable slip progresses. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

explanation.summary: Knee pain in an adolescent with a normal knee examination should always redirect attention to the hip, because the obturator nerve refers hip pathology to the medial knee. Loss of internal rotation with obligatory external rotation as the hip is flexed is close to specific for slipped capital femoral epiphysis, and the risk factors of adolescence and raised body mass index fit. A frontal pelvic radiograph alone misses early slips because the displacement is posterior, so frog leg lateral views of both hips are required. Weight bearing must stop the moment the diagnosis is suspected, since progression from a stable to an unstable slip sharply increases the risk of avascular necrosis.
key_points: Examine the hip in every adolescent presenting with knee pain
Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion is the characteristic bedside sign
Frontal radiographs alone miss early posterior slips; frog leg laterals are essential
Image both hips, since bilateral involvement occurs in a substantial minority
Make the child non-weight-bearing on suspicion, before imaging confirms the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Trace Klein's line along the superior femoral neck on the frontal film: it should intersect part of the epiphysis, and failure to do so indicates a slip even when the report reads as normal. Screen for hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency and renal osteodystrophy when a slip occurs outside the usual age band of ten to sixteen years or in a child of normal weight, since an endocrinopathy underlies a meaningful proportion of those cases.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

subtopic_detail: choice of imaging for suspected hip dysplasia first noticed at seven months when the femoral head has begun to ossify
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a seven month old girl for her routine check. Her mother has noticed that the creases on the back of the thighs do not match and that one leg seems shorter when she changes the nappy.

The pregnancy was complicated by breech presentation from 34 weeks, and she was born by elective caesarean at term. She has an older sister who wore a harness as a baby. On examination, with the hips and knees flexed and the feet together on the couch, the left knee sits visibly lower than the right. Abduction of the left hip is limited to 45 degrees compared with 75 degrees on the right. You feel no clunk on either side. Her tone, reflexes and spine are normal and she is meeting her developmental milestones.

data_table.Examination: Asymmetrical thigh creases, left knee lower than right on Galeazzi testing, left hip abduction 45 degrees versus 75 degrees on the right, no clunk elicited
data_table.Background: Breech from 34 weeks, first degree relative treated in a harness, normal neurological examination

lead_in: Which imaging would you request?

options.text: No imaging, because the absence of a palpable clunk makes significant dysplasia unlikely here
options.rationale: The Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres lose their sensitivity after about three months because the hip becomes fixed rather than reducible, so a negative clunk in an older infant is expected and reassures nobody. Limited abduction and apparent limb shortening become the reliable signs at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: A limited computed tomography of the pelvis, because it defines acetabular version most precisely
options.rationale: Computed tomography gives a high radiation dose to the gonads of an infant girl for information that a plain film provides adequately before treatment. It has a role in postoperative assessment, not in diagnosis. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists: Paediatric Imaging Referral)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists: Paediatric Imaging Referral

options.text: A frontal pelvic radiograph, because the femoral head ossifies by around four to six months
options.rationale: Ultrasound depends on the femoral head being cartilaginous, and once the ossific nucleus appears at roughly four to six months it casts an acoustic shadow that obscures the acetabulum. From this age onward the plain radiograph is the investigation of choice, assessed using the acetabular index and Perkin's and Hilgenreiner's lines. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: A static and dynamic hip ultrasound, because it avoids ionising radiation in a young infant
options.rationale: Avoiding radiation is a sound instinct and ultrasound is genuinely the right test under about four months of age, but after ossification begins the image quality collapses and the study becomes unreliable. The distinguishing factor is the age of the child rather than a preference for one modality. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: A magnetic resonance scan of both hips, because it images cartilage and bone simultaneously
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance does image both tissues but requires sedation at this age and is reserved for assessing reduction after closed or open treatment. It is not a screening or first line diagnostic study. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

explanation.summary: Breech presentation beyond 34 weeks and a first degree relative are the two strongest risk factors for hip dysplasia, and this girl has both. After about three months the reducible clunk disappears, so limited abduction and apparent femoral shortening on Galeazzi testing become the signs that matter. The imaging choice is governed purely by ossification of the femoral head, which occurs around four to six months: ultrasound before that point, plain radiography after it. At seven months the correct request is a frontal pelvic radiograph, with orthopaedic referral to follow because harness treatment is generally ineffective beyond six months.
key_points: Breech presentation after 34 weeks and a positive family history are the principal risk factors
Ortolani and Barlow testing loses sensitivity after about three months of age
Limited abduction and a positive Galeazzi sign replace the clunk in older infants
Ultrasound is the test under four months; plain radiography is the test after ossification
Pavlik harness treatment is generally ineffective beyond six months of age
explanation.pearls: Unilateral limitation of abduction to less than 60 degrees in an infant beyond three months should prompt imaging even when every other finding is normal, since it is the single most reliable late sign. Expect an acetabular index above 25 degrees at one year to indicate dysplasia, and remember that a hip which was normal on newborn ultrasound can still present late, so reassess abduction at every routine check until walking.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists: Paediatric Imaging Referral

subtopic_detail: ophthalmology surveillance interval for a young girl with persistent knee swelling and a positive antinuclear antibody who has no eye symptoms
stem: A 3-year-old girl has had a swollen right knee for four months, with an hour of morning stiffness and then normal activity. She has had no fever or rash.

data_table.Examination: Right knee effusion with 10 degree fixed flexion, small right ankle effusion, eyes white
data_table.Investigations: Inflammatory markers normal, antinuclear antibody positive, rheumatoid factor negative

lead_in: What eye care would you arrange?

options.text: Visual acuity at each visit, referring only if acuity falls
options.rationale: Acuity remains normal until the inflammation has already caused structural damage, so waiting for it to fall means referring after the harm is done. Acuity testing is a useful adjunct but cannot substitute for the slit lamp. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Paediatric Uveitis)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Paediatric Uveitis

options.text: Slit lamp examination now, repeated only if the arthritis remains active
options.rationale: Eye inflammation runs a course independent of joint activity and commonly flares while the joints are quiet, so tying surveillance to arthritis activity is unsafe. Screening continues for years after the arthritis settles. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

options.text: Dilated fundoscopy at each visit, referring if red reflex is lost
options.rationale: Fundoscopy examines the posterior segment, whereas this uveitis is anterior and its cells and flare are visible only through a slit lamp. Loss of the red reflex indicates established cataract, which is a late complication rather than a screening finding. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Paediatric Uveitis)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Paediatric Uveitis

options.text: Slit lamp examination now and then three monthly thereafter
options.rationale: Chronic anterior uveitis in this form of childhood arthritis is asymptomatic, produces no redness or pain, and is detected only on slit lamp examination, so screening intervals are set by risk rather than by symptoms. A girl under seven with oligoarticular disease and a positive antinuclear antibody sits in the highest risk band and is screened three monthly. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

options.text: Slit lamp examination now and then twelve monthly thereafter
options.rationale: Twelve monthly screening applies to the lowest risk groups such as older children with systemic onset disease, and using the absence of symptoms to set the interval defeats the purpose of screening. The whole reason this uveitis is dangerous is that it is silent until synechiae or cataract have formed. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

explanation.summary: Persistent arthritis of four or fewer joints for more than six weeks in a child under sixteen, with normal inflammatory markers and no systemic features, describes oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis. The complication that determines long term disability is chronic anterior uveitis, which is entirely asymptomatic with a white quiet eye and is detected only by slit lamp examination. Risk is stratified by age at onset, disease subtype and antinuclear antibody status, and a young girl with oligoarticular disease and a positive antibody falls into the highest risk band requiring three monthly screening. Eye disease flares independently of joint activity, so screening continues regardless of how the arthritis behaves.
key_points: Oligoarticular disease with a positive antinuclear antibody in a young child is the highest uveitis risk group
The uveitis is asymptomatic with a white eye and normal acuity until damage is established
Slit lamp examination is the only adequate screening test
Eye and joint activity are independent, so surveillance is not tied to arthritis control
Normal inflammatory markers do not argue against the diagnosis in oligoarticular disease
explanation.pearls: Screen three monthly for a girl under seven with oligoarticular disease and a positive antinuclear antibody, six monthly when the antibody is negative or onset is later, and twelve monthly for systemic onset disease, continuing for at least four years after arthritis remission. Intra-articular corticosteroid injection is the usual first treatment for a single persistently swollen joint and often achieves prolonged remission without any systemic agent.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Paediatric Uveitis

subtopic_detail: timing of a delayed live viral vaccine in a child who has just finished a prolonged high dose oral corticosteroid course
stem: A 2-year-old boy has finished an eight-week course of oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily for nephrotic syndrome, his last dose four days ago. His parents want the measles, mumps and rubella and varicella vaccines deferred at his 18-month visit. He takes no other immunosuppressant.

data_table.Examination: Well, no oedema, growth on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for protein for three weeks

lead_in: When should the live vaccines be given?

options.text: Now, since the course has finished and he is in remission
options.rationale: Clinical remission is not the same as restored cell mediated immunity, and vaccinating within days of stopping high dose steroid risks disseminated infection from the attenuated virus. The deferral is tied to the steroid, not to disease activity. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: After three months, giving both vaccines together
options.rationale: Three months is the interval used after more profound immunosuppression such as chemotherapy or biologic therapy, and applying it here delays protection unnecessarily. The distinguishing factor is the depth and type of immunosuppression rather than its duration alone. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: After one month, giving the vaccines four weeks apart
options.rationale: The timing is right but separating the two live vaccines unnecessarily is wrong, because they may be co-administered at different sites. The four week rule applies only when two live parenteral vaccines are not given on the same day. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Never, as nephrotic syndrome is a contraindication
options.rationale: Nephrotic syndrome is not a contraindication to any vaccine, and these children in fact need particular attention to pneumococcal and varicella protection because of their infection risk. The only contraindication relates to the timing of immunosuppressive therapy. (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Childhood Nephrotic Syndrome)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Childhood Nephrotic Syndrome

options.text: After one month, giving both vaccines together
options.rationale: A course of 2 mg/kg daily of prednisolone for more than fourteen days counts as high dose immunosuppression, and Australian practice is to defer live vaccines for one month after it stops so that immune competence is restored. Measles, mumps and rubella and varicella vaccines may be given on the same day at different sites, which is the efficient choice ahead of his travel. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Prednisolone at 2 mg/kg daily, or more than 20 mg daily in a child over 10 kg, given for fourteen days or longer is considered high dose immunosuppression for vaccination purposes. Live attenuated vaccines are deferred until one month after such a course finishes, whereas the three month deferral belongs to chemotherapy and biologic agents. Measles, mumps and rubella and varicella vaccines may be given on the same day at separate sites, and if they are not, they must be separated by at least four weeks. Nephrotic syndrome itself is never a contraindication, and these children benefit particularly from complete varicella and pneumococcal protection.
key_points: Prednisolone at or above 2 mg/kg daily for fourteen days or more counts as high dose immunosuppression
Defer live vaccines for one month after stopping high dose corticosteroid
Three month deferral applies after chemotherapy or biologic therapy, not after steroids alone
Two live parenteral vaccines are given the same day or separated by at least four weeks
Nephrotic syndrome is an indication for careful catch up, not a contraindication
explanation.pearls: Inactivated vaccines can be given at any point during or after immunosuppression, so never delay the influenza or pneumococcal dose while waiting out a steroid course, even though the response may be blunted. For a documented measles exposure in a susceptible immunosuppressed child, normal human immunoglobulin within six days is the protection strategy rather than vaccine, because the live vaccine is contraindicated during the deferral window.

sources.label: Kidney Health Australia: Childhood Nephrotic Syndrome

subtopic_detail: an adolescent with sudden scrotal pain whose ultrasound is reported as showing preserved arterial flow
stem: A 13-year-old boy woke at 7 am with sudden severe left scrotal pain and vomited twice. Too embarrassed to tell anyone until this evening, he now reports less pain.

data_table.Examination: Left hemiscrotum swollen, left testis high riding and transverse, absent cremasteric reflex, no relief on elevation
data_table.Imaging: Scrotal ultrasound: swollen testis, oedematous epididymis, arterial flow present

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate scrotal exploration with bilateral orchidopexy
options.rationale: A high riding transverse testis with an absent cremasteric reflex after abrupt onset pain and vomiting is a clinical diagnosis of torsion, and preserved flow on ultrasound does not exclude it because partial or intermittent torsion and residual capsular flow are both well described. Exploration with fixation of both sides is the only action that can salvage the testis. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain)

options.text: Oral antibiotics for epididymo-orchitis with urology review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Epididymo-orchitis is the near pair and would be supported by gradual onset, fever, pyuria and relief on elevation, none of which are present here. Treating him as an infection on the basis of an oedematous epididymis on ultrasound is how torsion is missed. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain)

options.text: Observe overnight with analgesia and repeat the ultrasound tomorrow
options.rationale: Salvage rates fall steeply beyond six hours and he is already fourteen hours in, so an overnight delay for a repeat scan effectively decides against the testis. Reducing pain over time reflects ischaemic nerve death rather than improvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain)

options.text: Attempt manual detorsion and discharge him if the pain settles
options.rationale: Manual detorsion is a reasonable temporising manoeuvre while theatre is prepared, but it is never definitive because the underlying bell clapper anomaly remains and retorsion is common. Discharge without fixation leaves him at immediate risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain)

options.text: Request a radionuclide scrotal perfusion scan to resolve the discrepancy
options.rationale: Nuclear imaging adds hours and its result would not override a bedside examination this characteristic. Imaging is for the equivocal presentation, and this one is not equivocal. (Source: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute Scrotum)
