explanation.pearls: Untreated anterior uveitis produces posterior synechiae that tether the iris to the lens, so an irregular or sluggishly reacting pupil found on routine examination in a child with arthritis means the disease has been active for months and needs same day ophthalmology assessment.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening

subtopic_detail: distinguishing a fused suture from a positional head shape in an infant with progressive skull asymmetry
stem: A 5-month-old boy has a head shape his parents say is worsening despite four months of alternating his sleeping position and daily tummy time. His development is age appropriate.

data_table.Examination: Skull long front to back and narrow side to side, firm midline ridge, small anterior fontanelle, full neck rotation
data_table.Growth: Head circumference on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue repositioning and tummy time, review in three months
options.rationale: Repositioning is the correct treatment for a deformational head shape, and four months of it with worsening rather than improvement is the history that argues against that diagnosis. Persisting with it here delays surgery past the age at which the simplest operations are possible. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

options.text: Refer to a craniofacial service and image the sutures
options.rationale: A ridged suture with a head that is long and narrow, symmetrical ears and a shape that has worsened despite repositioning indicates a fused sagittal suture rather than a positional moulding, and this requires surgical assessment. Referral is time sensitive because endoscopic strip craniectomy with helmeting is generally restricted to infants under about six months, after which open vault remodelling becomes necessary. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

options.text: Physiotherapy for neck tightness contributing to the asymmetry
options.rationale: Physiotherapy is central where torticollis drives a positional flattening, but his neck rotation is full and symmetrical in both directions, which removes the mechanism. The near pair distinction is that positional flattening produces an asymmetrical parallelogram shape with one ear pushed forward, whereas his skull is symmetrically narrowed. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

options.text: Arrange a moulding helmet and review after eight weeks
options.rationale: Helmet therapy redirects growth through open sutures and cannot reshape a skull whose suture has already fused, so it would waste the remaining months of rapid brain growth. Helmets have a defined role after endoscopic surgery but not as an alternative to it. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

options.text: Measure thyroid function and vitamin D before referral
options.rationale: Metabolic bone disease can distort the growing skull, but rickets softens bone and produces frontal bossing and craniotabes rather than a ridged fused suture. His growth and development are normal, which further argues against a systemic metabolic cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

explanation.summary: Most abnormal head shapes seen in infancy are deformational and follow sustained supine positioning, which is a tolerable trade against the large reduction in sudden infant death that back sleeping achieved. Deformational plagiocephaly produces an asymmetrical parallelogram when viewed from above, with the ipsilateral ear and forehead displaced forward, and it improves with repositioning, tummy time, and treatment of any coexisting torticollis. True suture fusion produces a characteristic symmetrical distortion determined by which suture is involved, with sagittal fusion giving a long narrow skull, and it worsens rather than improves as the brain grows. A palpable ridge, a shape that deteriorates despite conservative measures, or a head circumference crossing centiles all warrant craniofacial referral. The functional risks of untreated multi-suture disease include raised intracranial pressure and visual loss, while single suture disease is more often an issue of head shape and skull growth.
key_points: Viewed from above, positional plagiocephaly is a parallelogram whereas sagittal fusion is long and narrow.
A positional head shape improves with repositioning; a fused suture worsens as the brain grows.
A palpable ridge along a suture line with a small anterior fontanelle points to fusion.
Check neck rotation in every infant with an abnormal head shape, since torticollis drives positional flattening.
Endoscopic strip craniectomy with post-operative helmeting is generally limited to infants under about six months.
explanation.pearls: Sagittal synostosis is the commonest single suture fusion and the head circumference stays on its centile, because the skull compensates by growing front to back, so a normal head circumference offers no reassurance against it.

subtopic_detail: choosing between a surgical and an endocrine cause of vomiting in a second week infant when the electrolytes contradict the expected pattern
stem: A 12-day-old boy has vomited forcefully after feeds for four days and is hungry straight afterwards. He is lethargic, mottled and poorly perfused. There is no abdominal mass after a test feed.

data_table.Examination: Lethargic, mottled, capillary refill 4 s; normal male genitalia, testes descended
data_table.Investigations: Na 119 mmol/L; K 7.4 mmol/L; glucose 2.1 mmol/L; pH 7.19; bicarbonate 12 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Hypertonic saline 3 per cent 4 mL/kg before any other treatment
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for hyponatraemic seizures or obtundation attributable to cerebral oedema, and here the low sodium is a marker of aldosterone deficiency with salt wasting rather than a free water excess. Correcting the number without replacing the missing hormone leaves the underlying loss running. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis)

options.text: Saline 20 mL/kg with intravenous fludrocortisone and dextrose
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is the long term mineralocorticoid and has no parenteral form, and it is the wrong drug for an acute crisis in any case. Hydrocortisone is chosen precisely because at stress doses it delivers both glucocorticoid and sufficient mineralocorticoid effect, which is the near pair distinction being tested. (Source: APEG: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia)

options.text: Saline 20 mL/kg with intravenous hydrocortisone and potassium treatment
options.rationale: Hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and a metabolic acidosis in a collapsed second week infant is the biochemical signature of mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency, and hydrocortisone must be given at the same time as volume resuscitation rather than after it. Delaying steroid until a cortisol result returns is the error that turns a treatable crisis into an arrest, so the sample is drawn and the drug given without waiting. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis)

options.text: Saline 20 mL/kg and surgical referral for pyloromyotomy
options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from losing gastric acid, which is the exact inverse of his acidotic, hyperkalaemic, low chloride picture, and no mass was palpable after a test feed. The projectile vomiting and hungry rebound are genuine shared features, which is why the electrolytes rather than the history decide this. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Saline 20 mL/kg with intravenous cefotaxime after blood cultures
options.rationale: Late onset sepsis is a legitimate competing diagnosis in a collapsed neonate and antibiotics are commonly given alongside, but sepsis does not by itself explain the combination of a sodium of 119 mmol/L with a potassium of 7.4 mmol/L. Treating only the infection would leave the steroid deficiency uncorrected and the infant would not improve. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Sepsis)

explanation.summary: Salt wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia typically presents in the second week of life, once the protective effect of maternal and placental steroid has worn off, and boys are at particular risk because they have no ambiguous genitalia at birth to trigger earlier investigation. The presentation overlaps almost completely with the far commoner pyloric stenosis in its history, since both produce forceful non bilious vomiting in a hungry infant of the same age, and the separation is biochemical. Loss of aldosterone drives urinary sodium loss with potassium and hydrogen retention, producing hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and a metabolic acidosis, while cortisol deficiency adds hypoglycaemia and impaired vascular tone. Treatment is simultaneous volume expansion, glucose, and stress dose hydrocortisone, with the diagnostic samples for cortisol and 17 hydroxyprogesterone drawn before the first dose but never allowed to delay it. Newborn screening for this condition is not performed uniformly across all Australian jurisdictions, so a normal or pending card cannot be relied on to exclude it.
key_points: Pyloric stenosis gives a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis; adrenal crisis gives hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemic acidosis.
Male infants with salt wasting disease have normal genitalia and so are not detected at birth on examination.
Draw cortisol and 17 hydroxyprogesterone before the first hydrocortisone dose, but never delay the dose for the result.
Hydrocortisone at stress doses provides enough mineralocorticoid activity for the acute phase.
Hyperkalaemia in this setting warrants an electrocardiogram and treatment in its own right alongside volume expansion.
explanation.pearls: Hydrocortisone for an infant in adrenal crisis is given as 25 mg intravenously as the initial bolus, followed by 25 mg over the next 24 hours as a divided or continuous dose, with the same 25 mg figure used for children under three years.

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis oxygen escalation from low-flow nasal prongs
stem: A 5-month-old girl with respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis was started on nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min two hours ago for saturations of 88%.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 /min, RR 62 /min, SpO2 91% on 1 L/min nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, nasal flaring, no grunting

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Increase low-flow nasal prong oxygen to 2 L/min and reassess
options.rationale: Low-flow nasal prong oxygen up to 2 L/min is the first-line escalation for bronchiolitis; reassessment before moving to high-flow is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start high-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min, FiO2 0.4
options.rationale: High-flow nasal cannula is reserved for failure of low-flow therapy (persistent desaturation or worsening work of breathing at 2 L/min); premature escalation is not supported. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start mask continuous positive airway pressure at 6 cmH2O
options.rationale: CPAP is reserved for severe bronchiolitis with impending failure (grunting, apnoea, exhaustion, HFNC failure); not indicated at this severity. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Give nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and reassess at 20 minutes
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months; salbutamol has no benefit and may worsen ventilation-perfusion mismatch. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Add four-hourly nebulised 3 per cent hypertonic saline
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is not routinely recommended in Australian bronchiolitis pathways; escalation of oxygen is the priority when saturations remain below 92 percent. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis in children under 12 months with viral upper respiratory prodrome progressing to wheeze, crackles and increased work of breathing. RCH guidance targets oxygen saturation 90 percent or greater. Low-flow nasal prong oxygen (up to 2 L/min) is first line when supplemental oxygen is needed. High-flow humidified nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min is escalation after failure of low-flow for at least one to two hours. Bronchodilators, adrenaline, steroids, hypertonic saline and chest physiotherapy are not routinely indicated in bronchiolitis. Feeding via nasogastric tube or intravenous fluid at two-thirds maintenance is used when oral intake falls below 50 percent.
key_points: Oxygen target in bronchiolitis is SpO2 at or above 90 percent (RCH).
Low-flow nasal prong oxygen up to 2 L/min is first-line escalation before HFNC.
Salbutamol, adrenaline, steroids, hypertonic saline are not recommended routinely.
explanation.pearls: Titrate low-flow nasal prong oxygen up to 2 L/min in bronchiolitis before escalating to high-flow; SpO2 target is 90 percent or greater at RCH.

subtopic_detail: Dexamethasone dose selection in moderate croup at emergency department presentation
stem: A 2-year-old boy has a barking cough and noisy breathing that began this evening, after two days of coryza and low-grade fever. He has no asthma and has never been intubated.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 34 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, T 37.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Inspiratory stridor at rest that settles when he is calm, suprasternal recession, no drooling

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment now?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg as a single dose
options.rationale: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg is inferior to dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg in croup due to shorter half-life and higher relapse rate; RCH prefers dexamethasone. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single dose
options.rationale: 0.6 mg/kg is the higher dose reserved for severe croup or those receiving nebulised adrenaline; not required for moderate croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline with oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup (stridor at rest with marked respiratory distress) or failure of steroid; not indicated when stridor settles at rest. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as a single dose
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is a second-line option when oral dexamethasone cannot be tolerated; oral dexamethasone is preferred first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose
options.rationale: RCH recommends dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally for mild or moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg is only for severe croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Croup is a viral laryngotracheobronchitis with barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor, typically age 6 months to 6 years. RCH severity grades on the Westley score: mild (score 0-2), moderate (3-5), severe (6-11). Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg is first line for mild and moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe croup. Nebulised adrenaline (5 mL of 1:1000 as a flat dose, not per kilogram) is used for severe croup or failure to improve; minimum three-hour observation is required after the last adrenaline dose. Nebulised budesonide 2 mg is an alternative when oral steroid cannot be tolerated.
key_points: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg is first line for mild and moderate croup at RCH.
0.6 mg/kg dexamethasone is reserved for severe croup or with nebulised adrenaline.
Nebulised adrenaline is a flat 5 mL of 1:1000, three-hour minimum observation after.
explanation.pearls: Moderate croup at RCH gets oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once; reserve 0.6 mg/kg and nebulised adrenaline for severe croup with stridor and marked distress at rest.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing functional constipation from organic disease requiring investigation in a toddler
stem: A 20-month-old boy passes one hard pellet-like stool every four to five days, and has done for six months, with visible straining. There has been no soiling. He passed meconium within 12 hours of birth.

data_table.Growth: Weight and height on the 25th centile, stable
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no mass; anus normally sited; normal lower limb neurology and spine
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and coeliac serology normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Anorectal manometry and rectal suction biopsy
options.rationale: Meconium in first 24 hours, normal growth, normal exam and no failure of oral laxatives make Hirschsprung very unlikely; biopsy is not first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Oral macrogol disimpaction then titrated maintenance
options.rationale: This is functional constipation (Rome IV) without red flags; RCH recommends osmotic laxative disimpaction and maintenance with behavioural advice. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Abdominal radiograph and thyroid function tests
options.rationale: Plain radiograph is not recommended for diagnosis or severity of constipation; thyroid screening not indicated without other features of hypothyroidism. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Cow milk protein exclusion diet for four weeks
options.rationale: Cow milk protein trial is considered when standard laxative treatment has failed for 4 weeks; not first line without a trial of osmotic laxative. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Daily sodium citrate enema for one week
options.rationale: Rectal disimpaction is reserved for oral disimpaction failure; oral macrogol (Movicol Junior) is first line and better tolerated than enemas. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation is diagnosed by Rome IV criteria (two or more of: two or fewer defecations per week, one or more episodes of incontinence per week after toilet training, history of retentive posturing, history of painful or hard bowel movements, presence of a large faecal mass in the rectum, history of large-diameter stools that may obstruct the toilet). Red flags mandating investigation include failure to pass meconium in first 48 hours (Hirschsprung), failure to thrive, abnormal lower limb neurology or spine, palpable abdominal mass extending past umbilicus, and failure of standard laxative therapy. Management is oral osmotic disimpaction (Movicol Junior four sachets escalating over four days) then maintenance titrated to soft daily stools, with behavioural and dietary advice.
key_points: Rome IV criteria and absence of red flags define functional constipation.
Osmotic macrogol (Movicol Junior) oral disimpaction is first line; enemas rarely needed.
Meconium within 48 hours effectively excludes Hirschsprung as a cause.
explanation.pearls: Toddler with hard pellet stools, normal exam and meconium in first 24 hours is functional constipation - start Movicol Junior disimpaction then maintenance, no imaging or biopsy needed.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and treatment of incomplete Kawasaki disease in a young infant with prolonged fever
stem: A 9-month-old girl has seven days of fever with irritability and poor feeding. Her parents report red eyes and cracked lips.

data_table.Examination: T 39.4 degrees C, non-purulent conjunctivitis, cracked lips, strawberry tongue, 2 cm cervical node, no rash
data_table.Investigations: CRP 148 mg/L, platelets 620 x10^9/L, Hb 96 g/L, albumin 28 g/L, ALT 78 U/L, sterile pyuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone with blood cultures repeated at 48 hours
options.rationale: Bacterial infection alone does not explain sterile pyuria plus coronary dilatation plus classical features; delaying IVIG risks coronary aneurysm. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin with high-dose aspirin, admit to cardiology
options.rationale: Incomplete Kawasaki (4 days fever + coronary z-score >2.5 + supportive labs) meets AHA treatment criteria; IVIG plus aspirin is standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: High-dose oral prednisolone for two weeks with low-dose aspirin
options.rationale: Adjunctive corticosteroids may be added for high-risk Kawasaki or IVIG failure; corticosteroid alone without IVIG is not first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Intravenous infliximab with low-dose aspirin and cardiology review
options.rationale: Infliximab is reserved for IVIG-resistant Kawasaki (persistent fever after second IVIG); it is not first-line therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone and vancomycin pending cultures
options.rationale: Antibiotic monotherapy delays definitive treatment; the coronary z-score of 3.2 with supportive features requires immediate IVIG. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a self-limited medium-vessel vasculitis of childhood; the major complication is coronary artery aneurysm. Classical criteria require fever for five or more days plus four of five: bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, cervical lymphadenopathy above 1.5 cm (usually unilateral), oral mucosal changes (strawberry tongue or cracked lips), and peripheral extremity changes. Incomplete Kawasaki is diagnosed when fever plus fewer criteria is combined with supportive laboratory or echocardiographic findings: raised CRP or ESR, platelets above 450 after seven days, anaemia, raised ALT, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria, or a coronary z-score above 2.5. Treatment is intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg single infusion plus aspirin (30-50 mg/kg/day) until afebrile 48-72 hours then low-dose 3-5 mg/kg/day for 6-8 weeks.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: fever plus 2-3 criteria plus supportive labs or echo (coronary z-score >2.5).
Treatment: IVIG 2 g/kg single dose plus aspirin (high then low dose).
Steroids adjunctive for high-risk; infliximab for IVIG resistance.
explanation.pearls: A febrile infant with two Kawasaki features plus raised CRP plus coronary z-score above 2.5 meets AHA criteria for incomplete Kawasaki: give IVIG 2 g/kg without waiting for classical criteria.

sources.label: AHA Scientific Statement: Diagnosis Treatment and Long-term Management of Kawasaki Disease 2017

subtopic_detail: Cyanosis with normal pulse oximetry saturation and normal arterial oxygen tension in a neonate
stem: A 4-week-old boy has had intermittent perioral cyanosis for two days. He started home-prepared vegetable puree this week, from a garden irrigated with well water. Central cyanosis persists on 15 L/min oxygen.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148 /min, RR 46 /min, SpO2 87% on 15 L/min, T 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Arterial blood gas pH 7.36, PaO2 240 mmHg, PaCO2 34 mmHg, chocolate-brown blood; echocardiogram structurally normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Intravenous cefotaxime and amoxicillin with a fluid bolus
options.rationale: The picture is refractory cyanosis with normal PaO2 not septic shock; antibiotics do not address the methaemoglobin. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Cyanosis)

options.text: Prostaglandin E1 infusion and urgent cardiology transfer
options.rationale: Cyanotic congenital heart disease is excluded by structurally normal echocardiogram with normal outflow tracts; prostaglandin is not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Cyanosis)

options.text: Intravenous methylene blue and stop the vegetable puree
options.rationale: Chocolate-brown blood with PaO2 240 mmHg and refractory cyanosis is methaemoglobinaemia; methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV is the antidote. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Exchange transfusion via an umbilical venous catheter
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is reserved for severe methaemoglobinaemia unresponsive to methylene blue or when methylene blue is contraindicated (G6PD deficiency). (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Intravenous ascorbic acid with continued high-flow oxygen
options.rationale: Ascorbic acid is a slow reducing agent used only when methylene blue is contraindicated; methylene blue is first line. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: Methaemoglobinaemia occurs when haem iron is oxidised from ferrous to ferric form, unable to bind oxygen and shifting the oxygen dissociation curve. In neonates, sources include high-nitrate well water used in home-prepared vegetable puree, topical anaesthetics (benzocaine, prilocaine) and dapsone. The pathognomonic finding is cyanosis with normal arterial PaO2 and chocolate-brown blood; pulse oximetry reads falsely between 82 and 88 percent. Co-oximetry measures true methaemoglobin. Treatment above 20 percent methaemoglobin or with symptoms is methylene blue 1 to 2 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes. Methylene blue is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (haemolysis risk); ascorbic acid or exchange transfusion is the alternative.
key_points: Chocolate-brown blood with high PaO2 and refractory cyanosis is methaemoglobinaemia.
Methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV is first-line antidote (5-minute infusion).
Contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (haemolysis risk); use ascorbic acid instead.
explanation.pearls: A neonate with cyanosis on oxygen, PaO2 above 200 mmHg and chocolate-brown blood has methaemoglobinaemia; give methylene blue 1 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes and screen for G6PD deficiency.

subtopic_detail: Choice of induction therapy in newly diagnosed paediatric Crohn disease with terminal ileal and colonic involvement
stem: A 14-year-old boy has two months of abdominal pain and non-bloody diarrhoea four to six times daily. Perianal examination is normal.

data_table.Growth: Weight fallen from the 50th to the 10th centile, height velocity reduced
data_table.Investigations: Terminal ileal cobblestoning, patchy colitis, non-caseating granulomas; no stricture, fistula or perianal disease on MR enterography

lead_in: What is the most appropriate induction therapy?

options.text: Intravenous infliximab at weeks zero, two and six with weekly methotrexate
options.rationale: Biologic first-line induction is reserved for aggressive disease with penetrating or stricturing phenotype, perianal disease, or growth failure with prior treatment failure. (Source: ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Disease Guidelines 2021)

options.text: Oral prednisolone tapered over eight weeks with azathioprine maintenance
options.rationale: Corticosteroids suppress linear growth in paediatric Crohn; enteral nutrition avoids this and is preferred first line for luminal disease. (Source: ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Disease Guidelines 2021)

options.text: Exclusive enteral nutrition with polymeric formula for six to eight weeks
options.rationale: Exclusive enteral nutrition is first-line induction in paediatric luminal Crohn without perianal or fistulising disease, equivalent to steroids for mucosal healing without growth suppression. (Source: ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Disease Guidelines 2021)

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone for five days, then oral prednisolone
options.rationale: IV steroids are reserved for severe acute colitis with systemic upset; not indicated for stable luminal ileocolonic Crohn without severe systemic features. (Source: ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Disease Guidelines 2021)

options.text: Oral mesalazine in divided doses with colonoscopy review at twelve weeks
options.rationale: 5-ASA has minimal role in Crohn induction; benefit is limited to mild colonic disease and it does not induce mucosal healing here. (Source: ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Disease Guidelines 2021)

explanation.summary: Paediatric Crohn disease often presents with abdominal pain, diarrhoea, weight loss and growth failure. Ileocolonoscopy with biopsy plus MR enterography is standard workup. For induction of remission in luminal ileocolonic Crohn without perianal, fistulising or severe systemic disease, exclusive enteral nutrition (polymeric formula as sole nutrition for 6-8 weeks) is first line and equivalent to corticosteroids for symptom relief with superior mucosal healing and no growth suppression. Corticosteroids are reserved for EEN failure or intolerance. Anti-TNF (infliximab, adalimumab) first-line induction is reserved for aggressive phenotype (penetrating or stricturing disease, extensive small bowel disease, perianal disease, severe growth failure). Maintenance is typically azathioprine 2-2.5 mg/kg/day or methotrexate 15 mg/m2 weekly.
key_points: Exclusive enteral nutrition is first-line induction in paediatric luminal Crohn.
Steroids suppress linear growth and are second line.
First-line biologic induction is reserved for penetrating, fistulising, perianal or severe growth failure phenotypes.
explanation.pearls: Newly diagnosed paediatric Crohn with luminal ileocolonic disease and growth failure but no fistula or perianal disease gets exclusive enteral nutrition for 6-8 weeks as first-line induction, not oral steroids.

subtopic_detail: Tachypnoea and poor feeding at seven weeks
stem: A 7 week old boy has had 10 days of cough, poor feeding and sweating during bottles. He was born at term and has gained 80 g since his 4 week check.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 176, RR 70, SpO2 95 percent in room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Fine crackles, subcostal recession, liver 4 cm below the costal margin, harsh pansystolic murmur

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Chest radiograph with transthoracic echocardiography
options.rationale: Hepatomegaly, a pansystolic murmur, sweating with feeds and poor weight gain at the age a left to right shunt unmasks point away from a viral illness, and imaging of the heart is the discriminating test. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs; RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Nasopharyngeal aspirate for respiratory viral testing
options.rationale: Viral testing is used for cohorting infants admitted with typical bronchiolitis, which runs over days rather than a fortnight and does not cause hepatomegaly or a murmur. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Full blood count with blood cultures and urine culture
options.rationale: A septic screen is indicated for a febrile infant under 3 months or one who looks unwell with unexplained tachypnoea; this boy is afebrile with localising cardiac findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Sweat chloride test with a faecal elastase level
options.rationale: These tests pursue cystic fibrosis, which would be suggested by faltering growth with greasy stools and recurrent chest infection, and newborn screening makes it an unlikely first line here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Twenty four hour oesophageal pH and impedance study
options.rationale: Reflux studies are reserved for infants with suspected complicated reflux after conservative measures fail, and reflux does not produce hepatomegaly or a pansystolic murmur. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary:
Tachypnoea with crackles in a small infant is usually bronchiolitis, but several features here do not fit: the illness has run for 10 days rather than peaking at day 3 to 5, there is no fever, weight gain has almost stopped, feeding provokes sweating, the liver is enlarged and there is a pansystolic murmur. That combination at 6 to 8 weeks is the classic timing for a left to right shunt to declare itself as pulmonary blood flow rises with falling pulmonary vascular resistance. A chest radiograph and echocardiogram answer the question directly.

In context: bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis, which makes it important to know which findings should stop you making it. Poor weight gain, sweating or breathlessness with feeds, hepatomegaly, a murmur, an illness that does not follow the expected trajectory, or symptoms from birth all warrant a different line of thought. The cost of anchoring is high, because untreated heart failure in infancy deteriorates while the team waits for a viral illness to turn the corner.
key_points: Left to right shunts declare at 6 to 8 weeks as pulmonary resistance falls
Sweating with feeds, poor weight gain and hepatomegaly suggest heart failure
Bronchiolitis peaks around day 3 to 5 and does not enlarge the liver
Echocardiography with a chest radiograph is the discriminating investigation
explanation.pearls: An infant who is breathless doing the one thing that matters most, feeding, and who is not gaining weight, has a cardiac problem until the echocardiogram says otherwise.

subtopic_detail: Paediatric DKA fluid rate with cerebral oedema risk balance
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 9 year old boy with new-onset type 1 diabetes. He presented with 2 weeks of polyuria and polydipsia and a 4 kg weight loss. He has been vomiting for 12 hours and is drowsy but rousable. His mother reports no headache and no visual complaints before arrival.

Weight today is 28 kg. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.14, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L (22 to 32), glucose 26 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.4), sodium 132 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), and beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.6 mmol/L. Vital signs: pulse 130/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min with Kussmaul pattern, SpO2 100 percent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill is 3 seconds and mucous membranes are dry. GCS is 14.

data_table.Weight and vitals: 28 kg; HR 130; BP 96/58; RR 34 Kussmaul; SpO2 100 percent; T 36.9
data_table.VBG: pH 7.14; HCO3 8 mmol/L (22 to 32); glucose 26 mmol/L; Na 132 mmol/L; K 4.8 mmol/L; beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.6 mmol/L
data_table.Neurology: GCS 14; drowsy but rousable; no headache or visual complaints

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial intravenous fluid regimen?

options.text: 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus over 15 minutes, then deficit plus maintenance over 24 hours
options.rationale: A 20 mL/kg rapid bolus and 24 hour rehydration is deprecated in paediatric DKA because faster fluid delivery is associated with cerebral oedema; RCH and ISPAD both cap the initial bolus at 10 mL/kg in the absence of shock (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis).

options.text: Commence intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/h before starting any intravenous fluid replacement
options.rationale: Insulin is deferred by 1 hour after fluid resuscitation begins because starting insulin before restoring intravascular volume drives potassium intracellularly and worsens hypovolaemia and cerebral oedema risk (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis).

options.text: 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus over 30 minutes, then deficit plus maintenance evenly over 48 hours
options.rationale: APEG and RCH paediatric DKA guidance sets an initial isotonic bolus of 10 mL/kg over 30 minutes for haemodynamically stable moderate to severe DKA, followed by rehydration of the assumed 7 to 10 percent deficit plus maintenance evenly across 48 hours to reduce cerebral oedema risk (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis).

options.text: Give oral rehydration solution with subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin for 4 hours before intravenous access
options.rationale: Oral rehydration and subcutaneous insulin are not appropriate for moderate to severe DKA with drowsiness and vomiting; delaying intravenous rehydration risks progression to shock and cerebral oedema (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis).

options.text: 5 mL/kg 0.45 percent sodium chloride bolus over 60 minutes with an 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate infusion
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid is avoided in the resuscitation phase and bicarbonate is contraindicated in paediatric DKA except in life-threatening hyperkalaemia because it worsens cerebral oedema and paradoxical CNS acidosis (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis).

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA management deliberately uses smaller boluses (10 mL/kg over 30 minutes) and longer rehydration (48 hours) than adult protocols because cerebral oedema is the leading cause of death. Insulin infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/h starts an hour after fluid begins, never before. Bicarbonate is reserved for cardiac-arrest-level acidosis. Hypotonic fluids are avoided during resuscitation because they worsen the drop in serum osmolality that drives cerebral oedema.
key_points: 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus over 30 minutes for non-shocked moderate to severe DKA
Deficit plus maintenance replaced evenly over 48 hours
Insulin infusion starts 1 hour after fluid; bicarbonate almost never indicated
explanation.pearls: In children with DKA, keep the fluid slow: rapid rehydration and hypotonic fluids are the two biggest reversible cerebral oedema risks.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines: DKA and HHS

subtopic_detail: Preventing fever after meningococcal B vaccination in a young infant
stem: You are seeing a healthy 6-week-old boy for his scheduled immunisations, which include the meningococcal B vaccine. His mother is anxious because his older sister had a high fever after that vaccine.

data_table.Growth: Born at term, thriving, weight on the 50th centile
data_table.Examination: Afebrile and well; chest and abdomen normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Give paracetamol 15 mg/kg with the vaccine, then six-hourly twice
options.rationale: Meningococcal B vaccine causes fever in more than half of infants, and the Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends prophylactic paracetamol 15 mg/kg given with or just before the vaccine and repeated six-hourly for two further doses in children under two years. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Give ibuprofen 10 mg/kg with the vaccine, then six-hourly twice
options.rationale: Ibuprofen is not recommended under three months of age and has not been studied for this indication; paracetamol is the agent with the supporting evidence. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

options.text: Give paracetamol 15 mg/kg only if a fever develops after the vaccine
options.rationale: Reactive dosing is the standard advice for every other vaccine on the schedule, where routine prophylaxis is not recommended. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Give prednisolone 1 mg/kg on the morning of the vaccination only
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have no role in vaccine reaction prophylaxis and may blunt the immune response to the vaccine. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Give paracetamol 15 mg/kg the evening before the vaccination only
options.rationale: A single dose the night before has worn off by the time fever appears, which is typically within six hours of the injection. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Meningococcal B vaccine is markedly more pyrogenic than the rest of the infant schedule, producing fever above 38 degrees in over half of infants when given with the other routine vaccines, usually within six hours and settling within two days. The Australian Immunisation Handbook therefore makes an explicit exception to the general rule against prophylactic antipyretics: children under two years receiving this vaccine are given paracetamol 15 mg/kg with or shortly before the dose, then two further doses six hours apart. This reduces both the rate and the height of the fever without meaningfully reducing the antibody response. Routine prophylaxis is not recommended for any other vaccine because it may slightly blunt immunogenicity for no clinical gain. In context, fever after immunisation in an infant under three months still needs clinical judgement, because a recent vaccine does not exclude a concurrent serious bacterial infection in an unwell or poorly perfused baby.
key_points: Meningococcal B vaccine causes fever in over half of infants under two years.
Prophylactic paracetamol 15 mg/kg with the vaccine then two six-hourly doses.
Routine antipyretic prophylaxis is not recommended for other vaccines.
Post-immunisation fever does not exclude serious bacterial infection in an unwell infant.
explanation.pearls: Write the three paracetamol times on the vaccination record: families who are told to give it only if fever appears usually start too late to prevent the peak.

subtopic_detail: Simple febrile seizure workup and disposition
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 18 month old girl in the emergency department 90 minutes after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 3 minutes at home. She has been coryzal for 2 days and reached a temperature of 39.2 degrees Celsius shortly before the seizure. She returned to her baseline within 20 minutes and has since been playing with a toy at triage. Her immunisations are up to date and there is no family history of epilepsy.

On examination she is alert and interactive with clear rhinorrhoea, red pharynx without exudate, and no rash. Neurological examination including tone, gait, and cranial nerves is normal. Vital signs: pulse 130/min, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill is under 2 seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130; BP 98/62; RR 28; SpO2 99 percent; T 38.4
data_table.Seizure: Generalised tonic-clonic, 3 minutes, single, resolved 90 minutes ago
data_table.Examination: Alert, interactive; normal neurology; coryzal features; no rash
data_table.Background: Immunisations up to date; no family history of epilepsy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange lumbar puncture and empirical intravenous ceftriaxone before considering discharge
options.rationale: LP is not indicated for a simple febrile seizure in a well child aged 18 months without meningism; the RCH criteria specifically identify this presentation as low risk and mandate no lumbar puncture (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

options.text: Order an urgent outpatient EEG within 1 week to exclude an underlying epilepsy syndrome
options.rationale: EEG has no role after a first simple febrile seizure; it does not change management and has a false-positive rate that generates unnecessary anxiety (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

options.text: Commence daily oral sodium valproate 20 mg/kg/day as long-term seizure prophylaxis
options.rationale: Prophylactic anticonvulsants are not recommended after simple febrile seizures; the modest reduction in recurrence does not justify long-term drug exposure in a benign self-limiting condition (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

options.text: Prescribe rectal diazepam for the family to give at the onset of any future febrile illness
options.rationale: Prophylactic benzodiazepines at fever onset are not routine after a first simple febrile seizure and expose the child to sedation without changing meaningful outcomes; rescue midazolam is reserved for prolonged or recurrent complex seizures (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

options.text: Give antipyretic advice, reassure the family, and discharge with GP review
options.rationale: This meets RCH criteria for a simple febrile seizure (generalised, under 15 minutes, single in 24 hours, age 6 months to 5 years, back to baseline); no bloods, no imaging, no LP, no EEG is indicated and safe discharge with parental education is the standard (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

explanation.summary: A simple febrile seizure in a child aged 6 months to 5 years is generalised, under 15 minutes, single in 24 hours, and followed by return to baseline. RCH policy is no bloods, no imaging, no LP, and no EEG for children meeting these criteria who look well. Discharge with antipyretic advice and a written safety net is the standard. Rescue medication is reserved for children with prolonged or recurrent complex febrile seizures. Long-term prophylaxis is not warranted.
key_points: Simple febrile seizure: generalised, under 15 minutes, single in 24 hours, baseline return
No LP, EEG, imaging, or prophylactic antiepileptic required
Discharge with education about recurrence and antipyretic use
explanation.pearls: Recurrence of febrile seizures is common (about 1 in 3) but does not increase epilepsy risk enough to warrant prophylaxis.

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease supplemental criteria and IVIG threshold
stem: A 2-year-old boy is on day 6 of fever above 39 degrees C, fractious and inconsolable. His parents describe a truncal rash that resolved on day 3.

data_table.Examination: Non-purulent conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, cracked lips, palmar erythema, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L, WCC 18 x10^9/L, platelets 480 x10^9/L, CRP 92 mg/L, ESR 68 mm/h, albumin 28 g/L, ALT 74 U/L, sterile pyuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone alone as first-line therapy
options.rationale: Corticosteroid monotherapy is not first-line; steroids are added to IVIG only in high-risk children (Kobayashi score suggestive of IVIG resistance) and never replace IVIG in initial treatment (Source: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease).
source_refs: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

options.text: Blood and urine culture and chest radiograph, deferring therapy 24 hours
options.rationale: The child meets incomplete Kawasaki criteria today; withholding IVIG for 24 hours of culture surveillance costs a treatment window that reduces coronary aneurysm risk and does not add diagnostic information the current data does not already give (Source: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease).
source_refs: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

options.text: Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone with immunoglobulin deferred
options.rationale: The clinical picture with sterile pyuria and mucocutaneous features fits Kawasaki not bacterial sepsis; antibiotics without IVIG leave the coronary risk untreated and can be given alongside IVIG when infection is a genuine competing possibility (Source: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease).
source_refs: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

options.text: Echocardiography with intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin now
options.rationale: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed when fever for at least 5 days is accompanied by 2 to 3 clinical criteria plus supportive laboratory findings (CRP 30 mg/L or above, ESR 40 mm/h or above, and 3 or more of anaemia, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminaemia, elevated ALT, sterile pyuria, leucocytosis); this child meets both and IVIG should not wait for confirmation to minimise coronary aneurysm risk (Source: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease).
source_refs: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

options.text: Observation with paracetamol and repeat markers on day 10
options.rationale: Delaying IVIG past day 10 substantially increases coronary aneurysm risk; a child meeting incomplete Kawasaki criteria on day 6 needs treatment now, not further observation (Source: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease).
source_refs: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease requires fever for at least 5 days plus 2 to 3 clinical criteria and supportive laboratory findings. The AHA algorithm activates when CRP is at least 30 mg/L or ESR at least 40 mm/h plus three of anaemia, thrombocytosis above 450, albumin below 30, ALT above the reference range, leucocytes above 15, or sterile pyuria. This 2 year old satisfies both the clinical and laboratory arms. Coronary aneurysm risk is minimised when IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin is given before day 10, so delay for further culture or observation is unsafe.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: fever plus 2 to 3 criteria plus supportive labs triggers immediate treatment
IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg/day reduces coronary aneurysm risk when given before day 10
Steroids are adjunct in high-risk children (Kobayashi score), never a replacement for IVIG
explanation.pearls: Sterile pyuria, thrombocytosis, and hypoalbuminaemia are the three most useful Kawasaki labs that support an incomplete presentation; a normal ESR does not exclude Kawasaki when CRP is high.

sources.label: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

subtopic_detail: Late preterm hypoglycaemia intervention threshold and glucose gel first-line
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the postnatal ward reviewing a 36 plus 4 week baby girl born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery 3 hours ago. Birthweight is 2450 g. Her mother has type 2 diabetes managed on metformin during pregnancy. The baby is skin-to-skin, has latched but only briefly, and looks pink and settled. The midwife has performed the routine pre-feed heel-prick glucose per the trust pathway.

On examination she is alert, well perfused, and euvolaemic. There is no jitteriness, tone is normal, and the cry is strong. Vital signs: pulse 148/min, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 98 percent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. The pre-feed heel-prick blood glucose is 2.2 mmol/L (above 2.6). Umbilical cord pH was 7.32 with base excess minus 2.

data_table.Baby: 36+4 weeks; 2450 g; 3 hours old; skin-to-skin; alert and pink; no jitteriness
data_table.Risk factor: Mother with type 2 diabetes on metformin during pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give a single formula top-up feed of 15 mL/kg and defer repeat glucose testing until the next routine 3 hour check
options.rationale: Formula alone without dextrose gel takes longer to correct the glucose and dextrose gel with breastfeeding is proven to reduce NICU admission; deferring repeat testing to the next 3 hour check misses a rebound below 2.6 (Source: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).
source_refs: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

options.text: Give buccal 40 percent dextrose gel 200 mg/kg, feed at the breast, and repeat the blood glucose in 30 minutes
options.rationale: The ANZ Neonatal Network hypoglycaemia pathway makes 40 percent dextrose gel 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) plus a feed the first-line response to asymptomatic hypoglycaemia (BSL under 2.6) in an at-risk late-preterm baby, with repeat glucose in 30 minutes to guide escalation (Source: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).
source_refs: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

options.text: Transfer to the neonatal unit for an intravenous 10 percent glucose infusion at 4 mg/kg/min
options.rationale: Intravenous glucose is reserved for symptomatic hypoglycaemia, glucose under 1.5 mmol/L, or failure of dextrose gel plus feed to correct the BSL; separating this baby from the mother now is disproportionate to a single asymptomatic pre-feed reading of 2.2 mmol/L (Source: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).
source_refs: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

options.text: Reassure the mother, encourage continued skin-to-skin, and repeat the glucose after the next feed in 3 hours
options.rationale: A late-preterm infant of a diabetic mother with a documented BSL of 2.2 mmol/L requires active correction, not observation for 3 hours which risks progression to symptomatic hypoglycaemia and neurodevelopmental harm (Source: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).
source_refs: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

options.text: Administer intramuscular glucagon 0.2 mg/kg and continue routine breastfeeding on the postnatal ward
options.rationale: Intramuscular glucagon is reserved for refractory or symptomatic hypoglycaemia where intravenous access is delayed; it is not the initial response to an asymptomatic BSL of 2.2 mmol/L when dextrose gel and a feed will correct most episodes (Source: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).
source_refs: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

explanation.summary: The AU pathway for asymptomatic at-risk neonatal hypoglycaemia (late preterm, infant of diabetic mother, macrosomia, or small-for-gestational-age) starts with 40 percent dextrose gel 200 mg/kg buccally with a supported breastfeed, then repeats the glucose in 30 minutes. This protocol reduces NICU admission and preserves breastfeeding and skin-to-skin. Intravenous glucose is reserved for symptomatic infants, a BSL under 1.5 mmol/L, or a failed gel-plus-feed trial. Glucagon is a niche rescue for refractory hypoglycaemia awaiting intravenous access.
key_points: Asymptomatic at-risk baby with BSL under 2.6 mmol/L: dextrose gel 200 mg/kg plus feed first
Repeat glucose 30 minutes after gel to guide escalation
Intravenous 10 percent dextrose only for symptomatic, BSL under 1.5, or gel-and-feed failure
explanation.pearls: Dextrose gel has been shown to reduce NICU admission when used first-line in asymptomatic neonatal hypoglycaemia; it does not replace a feed but keeps mother and baby together.

sources.label: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia
Australian and New Zealand Neonatal Network Clinical Practice Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Duct-dependent congenital heart disease and prostaglandin E1
stem: A 3-day-old term boy went grey during feeds. He was discharged well on day 1 and the 20 week morphology scan was normal.

data_table.Saturations: Pre-ductal 96 per cent; post-ductal 82 per cent
data_table.Blood pressure: 62/38 mmHg right arm; 44/26 mmHg right leg
data_table.Examination: Pale and cool with reduced femoral pulses; soft systolic murmur

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial drug?

options.text: Prostaglandin E1 at 10 to 20 ng/kg/min with urgent cardiology transfer
options.rationale: The saturation and blood pressure splits with metabolic acidosis point to a duct-dependent systemic circulation such as coarctation or interrupted arch; prostaglandin E1 maintains ductal patency and buys time for cardiac assessment and surgical planning (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

options.text: Adrenaline infusion at 0.1 microgram/kg/min for cardiogenic shock
options.rationale: Inotropic support without opening the duct addresses the wrong physiology; adrenaline may increase myocardial oxygen demand and worsen ischaemia in a duct-dependent lesion before prostaglandin restores systemic flow (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

options.text: Intravenous furosemide 1 mg/kg with oral captopril to reduce afterload
options.rationale: Furosemide and afterload reduction do not maintain ductal patency and worsen perfusion in a duct-dependent circulation before echocardiography and surgery; prostaglandin is the immediate stabilising drug (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

options.text: A 20 mL/kg saline bolus with ceftriaxone for suspected sepsis
options.rationale: Volume loading a duct-dependent systemic circulation can precipitate pulmonary oedema and cardiovascular collapse and antibiotics without prostaglandin do not address the anatomical driver of the shock (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

options.text: 100 per cent oxygen by facemask with continued ward observation
options.rationale: High-flow oxygen can accelerate ductus arteriosus closure, worsening a duct-dependent lesion; the pre-post ductal split needs prostaglandin, not more oxygen, and this baby requires transfer not ward observation (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

explanation.summary: A well-appearing term newborn presenting on day 2 to 3 with poor feeding, pre-post ductal saturation split, reduced femoral pulses, and metabolic acidosis has a duct-dependent systemic circulation until proven otherwise. The single stabilising drug is prostaglandin E1 at 10 to 20 nanograms/kg/min, which maintains patency of the ductus arteriosus and restores systemic flow. Antibiotics may run in parallel if sepsis is a competing possibility but should not delay prostaglandin. Volume loading and high-flow oxygen are actively harmful in this setting.
key_points: Pre-post ductal saturation split plus reduced femoral pulses suggests duct-dependent systemic circulation
Prostaglandin E1 10 to 20 ng/kg/min stabilises before echocardiography and transfer
Avoid high-flow oxygen and large volume loading before ductal patency is secured
explanation.pearls: Duct closes physiologically around day 2 to 5, which is when duct-dependent lesions unmask; a pre-post ductal saturation difference of at least 3 percent flags urgent cardiology assessment.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

subtopic_detail: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia salt-losing crisis in a neonate
stem: A 12-day-old term boy has vomited for three days and lost 12 percent of his birthweight, with no diarrhoea or fever. Newborn screening results are pending.

data_table.Examination: Lethargic, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 4 seconds, hyperpigmented but normal male genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Na 122 mmol/L, K 6.8 mmol/L, glucose 2.4 mmol/L, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: A 20 mL/kg saline bolus with intravenous ceftriaxone
options.rationale: Missing steroid replacement in a salt-losing crisis is a fatal omission even with fluid and antibiotics; sepsis may coexist but hydrocortisone must not wait, and 20 mL/kg initial bolus is larger than the RCH neonatal pathway recommends in the absence of overt shock signs (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis).

options.text: Oral fludrocortisone 100 microgram daily with oral rehydration
options.rationale: Oral fludrocortisone alone acts too slowly to reverse a salt-losing crisis and this shocked vomiting neonate cannot rely on oral rehydration; intravenous fluid and parenteral hydrocortisone are needed first (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis).

options.text: A 10 mL/kg saline bolus, dextrose and hydrocortisone 25 mg
options.rationale: This picture of hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and shock in a term male neonate on day 12 fits a salt-losing crisis in classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia; RCH pathway is fluid and glucose resuscitation with parenteral hydrocortisone as a stat 25 mg dose in neonates, and blood for 17-hydroxyprogesterone before ongoing hydrocortisone is essential to lock in the diagnosis (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis).

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate and salbutamol for the hyperkalaemia
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia treatment without addressing the underlying adrenal insufficiency does not correct the driving pathology; hydrocortisone plus saline and dextrose start the definitive treatment and typically bring potassium down without calcium or nebulised beta-agonist (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis).

options.text: Hypertonic saline 3 percent 3 mL/kg to raise sodium 8 mmol/L hourly
options.rationale: Rapid correction of hyponatraemia in a hypovolaemic child risks central pontine myelinolysis; the driver is aldosterone deficiency and sodium corrects gradually once fluid and hydrocortisone are given (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis).

explanation.summary: A 2 week old boy with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and shock has a salt-losing crisis of 21-hydroxylase deficiency until proven otherwise, because male infants have no ambiguous genitalia to flag the diagnosis earlier. The immediate treatment is fluid and glucose correction with parenteral hydrocortisone (25 mg stat in neonates), then continued hydrocortisone at stress dose. Blood for 17-hydroxyprogesterone must be drawn before the second hydrocortisone dose so newborn-screen confirmation is possible. Hyperkalaemia rarely needs additional treatment once hydrocortisone and volume are given.
key_points: Hyponatraemia plus hyperkalaemia plus hypoglycaemia plus shock in a 2 week old male = CAH salt-losing crisis
Hydrocortisone 25 mg stat and saline resuscitation are the immediate steps
Draw serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone before continuing hydrocortisone
explanation.pearls: Male CAH typically presents around day 7 to 14 as a salt-losing crisis because there is no genital ambiguity to prompt earlier diagnosis; newborn screening turnaround in Australia is usually about 1 week.

sources.label: APEG Position Statement on Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia

subtopic_detail: Croup severity assessment and dexamethasone dosing
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a metropolitan emergency department. A 2 year old boy is brought in by his mother at 2 am with a 1 day history of a barking cough and a hoarse voice.

On arrival he is alert and consolable in his mother's arms. He has a barking cough but no stridor when calm. Stridor becomes audible when he cries during examination. There is mild suprasternal recession only when upset, no tracheal tug at rest, and air entry is equal with no wheeze. He has taken a small amount of oral fluid in the last hour.

Pulse rate 128/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees C. His immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128/min; BP 100/60 mmHg; RR 32/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 37.6 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; barking cough; hoarse voice; stridor only when crying; mild suprasternal recession when upset; air entry equal; no wheeze
data_table.History: 1 day symptoms; immunisations up to date; taking small oral fluids

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose, and discharge home once settled and tolerating fluids
options.rationale: This child has mild croup: stridor only when upset, no stridor at rest, no significant recession at rest. Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once is first line for mild and moderate croup and discharge is safe once the child is settled and taking fluids (Source: RCH CPG: Croup; TG Respiratory).

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose, and observe for 30 minutes before discharge
options.rationale: The dose is correct for mild croup, however observation for 30 minutes only applies when nebulised adrenaline has been given; for children receiving oral steroid alone the practice is to observe until settled and confirm oral tolerance (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days, and review with the general practitioner in the morning
options.rationale: Prednisolone is an alternative when dexamethasone is unavailable, however a single dexamethasone dose has a longer duration of action and is preferred; a 3 day course of prednisolone is not required and adds risk without benefit (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single dose, and nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 immediately
options.rationale: The higher 0.6 mg/kg dose and nebulised adrenaline are reserved for severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession; using them for mild croup exposes the child to unnecessary tachycardia and mandates 3 hours of observation for rebound (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as a single dose, and admit for overnight observation of the airway
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is used only when the child cannot tolerate oral dexamethasone; it is second line to oral steroid, and admission for mild croup without stridor at rest is not indicated (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

explanation.summary: Mild croup is defined by a barking cough with no stridor at rest and no significant chest recession at rest, with the child alert. The Royal Children's guideline first line is a single oral dose of dexamethasone at 0.15 mg/kg with disposition home once the child is settled and tolerating oral fluids. The higher 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup, and nebulised adrenaline is added only for severe presentations. Any child who has received nebulised adrenaline requires a minimum of 3 hours of post administration observation before discharge to detect rebound obstruction.
key_points: Mild croup: dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally once.
Severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000.
Observe 3 hours after any nebulised adrenaline before discharge.
explanation.pearls: In Australian paediatric practice a single 0.15 mg/kg oral dexamethasone dose provides 72 hours of anti-inflammatory effect and covers the natural history of most croup without needing repeat dosing.

subtopic_detail: Rehydration route in paediatric gastroenteritis
stem: An 18-month-old boy weighing 12 kg has 24 hours of profuse watery diarrhoea and vomiting. A supervised trial of oral rehydration solution by syringe in triage failed after two vomits.

data_table.Examination: Rousable and interactive, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, capillary refill 2 sec, warm peripheries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg over 15 minutes
options.rationale: A 20 mL/kg bolus is indicated for shock or severe dehydration with poor perfusion; this child has capillary refill 2 seconds, warm peripheries and no hypotension, so full bolus resuscitation is not required and risks unnecessary sodium load (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

options.text: Nasogastric oral rehydration solution 20 mL/kg over the first hour
options.rationale: The child has mild to moderate dehydration with failure of a supervised oral trial; the RCH pathway is nasogastric rapid rehydration with oral rehydration solution as first line before moving to intravenous fluids, with equivalent efficacy and lower cost (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

options.text: Oral ondansetron 4 mg wafer and continued syringe feeds
options.rationale: Ondansetron 4 mg is the correct wafer dose for a 12 kg child and it does help vomiting, however after two vomits during a supervised oral trial the delivery route should be escalated rather than continued (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

options.text: Intravenous 5% dextrose with 0.45% sodium chloride at 46 mL/hour
options.rationale: Intravenous fluids are second line to nasogastric rapid rehydration for mild to moderate dehydration; a maintenance only rate at 46 mL per hour also fails to address the fluid deficit and delays correction (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

options.text: Admit and offer oral rehydration solution ad libitum at the bedside
options.rationale: Ad libitum offering already failed at the point of care and admission without an active rehydration strategy is not appropriate; a structured nasogastric or intravenous regimen is required in the setting of ongoing vomiting (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis).

explanation.summary: For a child with mild to moderate dehydration from gastroenteritis who fails a supervised oral trial, nasogastric rapid rehydration with oral rehydration solution is preferred before intravenous fluids. Nasogastric administration achieves comparable rehydration to intravenous fluids with fewer complications and shorter emergency stays. A single dose of ondansetron may reduce vomiting during the first hour. Intravenous fluids are reserved for severe dehydration, shock, ileus, or nasogastric failure.
key_points: Failed oral trial with mild to moderate dehydration: escalate to nasogastric before intravenous.
Ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg once reduces vomiting in the first hour.
Reserve intravenous fluids for severe dehydration, shock, or nasogastric failure.
explanation.pearls: Nasogastric rapid rehydration delivers oral rehydration solution at 20 mL/kg in the first hour and completes replacement over 4 hours, matching intravenous outcomes at lower cost for children with ongoing vomiting.

subtopic_detail: Serious bacterial infection workup in neonates
stem: A 25-day-old girl born at term has six hours of poor feeding and felt hot to her mother two hours ago. Her older brother has a runny nose.

data_table.Examination: Alert, fontanelle soft and flat, no rash
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, CRP 8 mg/L, urine dipstick negative; nasopharyngeal aspirate pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Admit for observation, starting antibiotics only if she deteriorates
options.rationale: Any infant under 4 weeks old with a fever above 38 degrees receives a full septic workup and empirical intravenous antibiotics without waiting for clinical deterioration because bacterial meningitis at this age presents with subtle signs (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

options.text: Await the nasopharyngeal aspirate before doing a lumbar puncture
options.rationale: Identification of a viral cause does not exclude concurrent invasive bacterial infection in an infant under 4 weeks old; the septic workup and empirical antibiotics remain required (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

options.text: Lumbar puncture, blood and urine cultures, then cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin
options.rationale: Any infant under 4 weeks old with a fever above 38 degrees requires a full septic workup including lumbar puncture followed by empirical broad spectrum antibiotics; cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin covers the neonatal group of organisms including group B streptococcus, Listeria and Escherichia coli (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child; TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Give intramuscular ceftriaxone and discharge for review tomorrow
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin and is avoided in neonates under 1 month; more importantly no infant under 4 weeks with a fever is discharged without a full workup and inpatient antibiotic completion (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child; AMH Neonatal).

options.text: Take a catheter urine specimen and observe her for four hours
options.rationale: A negative dipstick does not exclude urinary tract infection in young infants and observation only delays treatment; the required approach is lumbar puncture plus urine plus blood cultures followed by empirical antibiotics (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

explanation.summary: An infant under 4 weeks old with a temperature above 38 degrees Celsius receives a full septic workup including blood culture, urine by suprapubic aspirate or catheter, and lumbar puncture, then empirical intravenous antibiotics without waiting for deterioration. Cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin covers neonatal pathogens including group B streptococcus, Listeria monocytogenes and Escherichia coli. Ceftriaxone is avoided during the first month because it displaces bilirubin from albumin. A viral illness in an older sibling does not remove the need for the neonatal septic workup because concurrent bacterial infection remains possible.
key_points: Under 4 weeks and fever above 38 C: full septic workup plus empirical antibiotics.
Cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin covers group B streptococcus, Listeria and Escherichia coli.
Avoid ceftriaxone under 1 month due to bilirubin displacement risk.
explanation.pearls: In an infant under 28 days old use cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin rather than defaulting to ceftriaxone; the 28 day threshold is driven by the risk of kernicterus with ceftriaxone during the neonatal jaundice window.

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis oxygen escalation and admission decision
stem: A 3-month-old boy born at 38 weeks has four days of coryza and two days of wet cough, with one apnoea during a feed this morning.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168/min, RR 62/min, SpO2 88 per cent in air, 92 per cent on 2 L/min prongs after 20 minutes
data_table.Examination: Recession and tracheal tug persisting on prongs
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate: respiratory syncytial virus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate respiratory support?

options.text: Continue 2 L/min nasal prongs and reassess in two hours
options.rationale: Low flow nasal prong is the correct first line oxygen delivery, however this infant is still tachypnoeic with recession and has already had an apnoea at home; a further 2 hour delay before escalation is inappropriate given the risk profile (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Back to back nebulised salbutamol, then reassess
options.rationale: Salbutamol is not recommended in infants under 12 months with bronchiolitis; there is no evidence of benefit and it may cause tachycardia and tachyphylaxis (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Nebulised 3 per cent sodium chloride, then reassess
options.rationale: Nebulised hypertonic sodium chloride has been removed from the RCH pathway; systematic reviews do not show meaningful benefit in bronchiolitis (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: High flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min, target SpO2 90
options.rationale: High flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg per minute is appropriate for a bronchiolitic infant who has failed low flow oxygen with ongoing work of breathing, with an SpO2 target of 90 percent to avoid oxygen toxicity; admission to a monitored bed is required given the reported apnoea (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis; PREDICT bronchiolitis guideline 2022).

options.text: Intubate and ventilate now for the reported apnoea
options.rationale: Intubation is not first line here; the infant is oxygenating adequately on low flow oxygen and non invasive support with high flow has not been trialled, so early intubation is not indicated (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

explanation.summary: In bronchiolitis with hypoxia the Royal Children's approach is to start with low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L per minute and escalate to high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg per minute if low flow fails after around 2 hours or the child has red flag features. The SpO2 target on the guideline is 90 percent to avoid hyperoxia and unnecessary escalation. Salbutamol, hypertonic sodium chloride and nebulised adrenaline are not routinely recommended in infants under 12 months old. A history of apnoea, prematurity or feeding failure lowers the threshold for admission and closer monitoring.
key_points: Low flow oxygen first, high flow at 2 L/kg per minute if failing.
SpO2 target 90 percent for bronchiolitis at RCH.
Salbutamol, hypertonic saline and nebulised adrenaline not recommended in under 12 months.
explanation.pearls: A reported apnoea in a young infant with bronchiolitis mandates a monitored bed and lowered SpO2 target of 90 percent, even when the child appears clinically stable at triage.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and reporting of suspected non-accidental injury
stem: A 5-month-old boy has reduced right arm movement noticed at a nappy change. No fall is reported. An older half-sibling is in out of home care.

data_table.Examination: Bruising right upper arm, three circular bruises left cheek, healing linear mark left thigh; weight fallen to the 3rd centile
data_table.Investigations: Right humerus radiograph: mid shaft spiral fracture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Refer to the community child health nurse for a home visit
options.rationale: This is a red flag presentation for physical abuse with a spiral fracture in a non ambulant child, unexplained bruising in different sites, and faltering growth; a community follow up alone would leave the child at ongoing risk (Source: RACGP guide to non accidental injury).
source_refs: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

options.text: Immobilise the arm and discharge with the mother's partner
options.rationale: Discharge before a child protection workup risks further harm; a suspected non accidental injury requires admission and formal safeguarding assessment before disposition (Source: RACGP guide to non accidental injury).
source_refs: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

options.text: Order a skeletal survey and coagulation screen, then discharge
options.rationale: Ordering the tests without safeguarding action is inadequate; mandatory notification to child protection services and involvement of paediatric team are required whenever non accidental injury is suspected in a child under 2 years (Source: RACGP guide to non accidental injury).
source_refs: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

options.text: Consult orthopaedics and defer safeguarding until the plan is set
options.rationale: Fracture management does not take priority over safeguarding; the safeguarding pathway runs in parallel and is a mandatory reporting obligation for the doctor at the point of suspicion (Source: RACGP guide to non accidental injury).
source_refs: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

options.text: Admit for a child protection workup and notify child protection
options.rationale: A spiral humeral fracture in a non ambulant infant with additional unexplained bruises and faltering growth is highly suggestive of physical abuse; an admission for a skeletal survey, retinal examination, coagulation screen and social assessment, mandatory notification to child protection services, and paediatric team involvement is the correct standard of care (Source: RACGP guide to non accidental injury; RCH CPG: Child abuse).
source_refs: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

explanation.summary: A spiral long bone fracture in a non ambulant infant, together with bruises on multiple non bony sites and faltering growth, is a classic non accidental injury pattern that requires admission for a full child protection workup and mandatory notification to child protection services. The workup includes skeletal survey, retinal examination for haemorrhages, coagulation screen and social assessment. Mandatory notification obligations for doctors apply once there is a reasonable suspicion of harm, not once harm is proven. Delaying disposition until the fracture is orthopaedically fixed is not appropriate because safeguarding runs in parallel with medical care.
key_points: Spiral fracture in a non ambulant child: mandatory child protection referral.
Full workup: skeletal survey, retinal examination, coagulation screen, social assessment.
Reasonable suspicion, not proof, triggers the mandatory notification duty.
explanation.pearls: Bruising in a pre cruising infant (less than about 9 months old) is uncommon from normal activity, so any bruise in a non ambulant infant warrants a low threshold for a safeguarding assessment before discharge.

sources.label: RACGP guide to non accidental injury

subtopic_detail: Prolonged neonatal jaundice with pale stools
stem: A 4-week-old exclusively breastfed girl remains jaundiced since discharge. Her stools have been pale for 10 days and her urine dark. She is alert, feeding well and back to birth weight.

data_table.Examination: Icteric to the mid abdomen, abdomen soft, liver not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 148 micromol/L, direct bilirubin 62 micromol/L (<20), ALT 78 U/L, thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that this is breast milk jaundice and review in two weeks
