options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and resolves without pale stools; a direct bilirubin fraction above 17 micromol/L or above 20 percent of total in a 4 week old requires urgent workup for cholestasis and cannot be reassured (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice; NASPGHAN cholestasis guideline).

options.text: Arrange urgent same-day admission for hepatology assessment
options.rationale: A conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in a 4 week old with pale stools and dark urine is a surgical emergency until biliary atresia is excluded; the Kasai portoenterostomy outcome is much better if performed before 60 days of age, so same day paediatric admission for urgent workup and hepatology review is required (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice; NASPGHAN cholestasis guideline).

options.text: Commence phototherapy and repeat the bilirubin in 24 hours
options.rationale: Phototherapy treats unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; it is ineffective and inappropriate for conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and delays definitive workup (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Give intramuscular vitamin K and repeat coagulation studies
options.rationale: While correcting vitamin K status is part of cholestatic workup, a single injection alone without paediatric referral misses the time critical requirement to exclude biliary atresia within the first 60 days (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Trial formula feeding for 48 hours and repeat the bilirubin
options.rationale: A formula trial is used only in stable unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; it has no place when the direct fraction is elevated and there are pale stools, and it delays the diagnosis of biliary atresia (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

explanation.summary: A conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in an infant beyond 2 weeks old with pale stools and dark urine must be treated as a surgical emergency until biliary atresia is excluded. Urgent same day admission for hepatology review, imaging including hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid scan and possibly cholangiography allows the Kasai portoenterostomy to be performed before 60 days of age when outcomes are markedly better. Phototherapy is only useful for unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and does not treat the biliary obstruction. A formula trial is appropriate only for stable unconjugated jaundice and should not delay workup in a cholestatic infant.
key_points: Direct bilirubin above 17 micromol/L or above 20 percent of total is always abnormal.
Pale stools plus dark urine in an infant is biliary atresia until proven otherwise.
Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days gives the best outcomes.
explanation.pearls: In any infant beyond 2 weeks of age with persistent jaundice, always split the bilirubin; a conjugated fraction over 17 micromol/L makes biliary atresia the working diagnosis until same day imaging and hepatology review say otherwise.

subtopic_detail: Post UTI imaging decision at 20 months per RCH
stem: A 20-month-old girl is reviewed six weeks after her first febrile urinary tract infection, treated orally for Escherichia coli. She was well throughout and defervesced within 24 hours. Her antenatal morphology scan was normal and there is no family history of vesicoureteric reflux.

data_table.Examination: Well grown, normal examination; repeat urine culture negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging plan?

options.text: No imaging, with prompt culture and treatment of any future febrile illness
options.rationale: RCH advises no imaging after a single typical febrile UTI in a well thriving child aged 6 months to less than 3 years with normal antenatal monitoring; parents are counselled to seek review with any future febrile illness (Source: RCH CPG Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Dimercaptosuccinic acid renal scan at six months for cortical scarring
options.rationale: Dimercaptosuccinic acid scanning is a NICE construct and is not part of the RCH imaging cascade; it should not be requested after a single typical UTI (Source: RCH CPG Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Micturating cystourethrogram to grade reflux and guide prophylaxis
options.rationale: Micturating cystourethrogram is invasive, involves radiation and catheterisation, and is not in the RCH cascade after a single typical UTI in a child with normal antenatal imaging (Source: RCH CPG Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound this week to exclude obstruction and dilatation
options.rationale: Ultrasound is only indicated for atypical UTI features, recurrent UTI, or infants under 6 months without antenatal monitoring; a single typical UTI in a well thriving girl with a normal antenatal scan does not need ultrasound (Source: RCH CPG Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Continuous low-dose trimethoprim prophylaxis with imaging if UTI recurs
options.rationale: Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended after a single typical UTI in this age group; the PRIVENT trial and RCH guidance restrict prophylaxis to selected recurrent UTI or dilating reflux (Source: RCH CPG Urinary tract infection).

explanation.summary: The RCH imaging cascade after urinary tract infection reserves renal tract ultrasound for atypical UTI, recurrent UTI, infants under 6 months without antenatal monitoring, or when there is a family history of significant renal tract disease. A single typical UTI in a well thriving child between 6 months and 3 years with a normal antenatal morphology scan needs no imaging. Dimercaptosuccinic acid scanning and micturating cystourethrogram are NICE constructs and are not part of the RCH cascade. Parents are safety netted for prompt review and culture of any future febrile illness.
key_points: Single typical UTI plus normal antenatal scan plus well child equals no imaging.
Ultrasound only for atypical, recurrent, under 6 months, or absent antenatal monitoring.
DMSA and MCUG are not part of the RCH cascade.
explanation.pearls: Confirm the antenatal morphology scan was actually done and normal before deciding not to image; a missed antenatal scan converts a first typical UTI in an infant under 6 months into an indication for renal tract ultrasound.

subtopic_detail: First line oxygen delivery in moderate bronchiolitis per RCH
stem: A 7-month-old boy born at term has three days of coryza and 24 hours of cough, tachypnoea and feeds at half his usual intake.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158 /min, RR 62 /min, SpO2 89% in room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, mild subcostal recession, widespread wheeze and crackles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial oxygen delivery?

options.text: High flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min, target saturations 94 to 98 percent
options.rationale: High flow is reserved for failure of low flow after a trial of 2 hours; using it up front increases admissions to higher care beds without reducing intubation (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis; PARIS trial).

options.text: Nasal prong oxygen 1 to 2 L/min, target saturations at least 90 percent
options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis guidance recommends low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min as first line, with an SpO2 target of at least 90 percent; higher targets and high flow are not first line (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Hudson mask oxygen 6 L/min, target saturations 94 to 98 percent
options.rationale: A Hudson mask at this flow is not first line and blunts assessment of respiratory effort and feeding; low flow nasal prongs are preferred (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg before any supplemental oxygen is given
options.rationale: Salbutamol is not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months; RCH advises against routine bronchodilators regardless of wheeze (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with three hours observation
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is not routinely used in bronchiolitis and does not alter admission or length of stay; oxygen and feeding support are the mainstays (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis).

explanation.summary: RCH bronchiolitis guidance is deliberately conservative on oxygen delivery: start with low flow nasal prongs at 1 to 2 L/min and titrate to an SpO2 target of at least 90 percent. High flow nasal cannula is reserved for failure of low flow after at least 2 hours. Bronchodilators and adrenaline are not routinely recommended. Feeding support, hydration and time are the other pillars of care.
key_points: First line oxygen is nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min.
SpO2 target is 90 percent, not 92 to 94.
High flow reserved for failure of low flow after 2 hours.
explanation.pearls: Reassess at 2 hours after starting low flow; a persistent SpO2 under 90 on 2 L/min, sustained tachypnoea over 60 with recessions, or feeding failure defines low flow failure and is the trigger for high flow escalation rather than the initial choice.

subtopic_detail: Dexamethasone dosing in mild to moderate croup per RCH
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 2 year old boy brought in overnight with a 1 day history of coryza, hoarse voice, and a barking cough. He is settled on his mother's lap and has stridor only when upset. There is no drooling and he has been drinking sips of oral fluid.

He has no chronic respiratory disease, no cardiac disease, and no history of intubation. Immunisations are up to date. Older siblings have had similar symptoms this week.

Pulse rate 128/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 37.9 degrees C. Weight today is measured at 13 kg. He has mild suprasternal recession at rest and a barking cough on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128/min; BP 96/58 mmHg; RR 34/min; SpO2 97% RA; T 37.9 C
data_table.Examination: Settled on lap; mild suprasternal recession at rest; barking cough; stridor only when upset
data_table.Investigations: None indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid regimen?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days as an outpatient course of steroids with a review by the general practitioner in 48 hours
options.rationale: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg for 3 days has been shown to have higher representation rates than dexamethasone in croup and is not first line at RCH (Source: RCH CPG Croup; Cochrane).

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single stat dose in the department and reassess symptoms after 2 hours before discharge
options.rationale: 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe croup with stridor at rest and marked respiratory distress; using it in mild to moderate cases overtreats without added benefit (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single stat dose in the department and reassess symptoms after 2 hours before discharge
options.rationale: RCH advises oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild or moderate croup, with 3 hours of observation after any nebulised adrenaline; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe croup (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as a single dose in the department and reassess symptoms after 2 hours before discharge
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is an alternative when oral intake is not tolerated; this child is tolerating oral fluid so dexamethasone orally is preferred and cheaper (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

options.text: Intramuscular dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single stat dose in the department and reassess symptoms after 2 hours before discharge
options.rationale: Intramuscular dexamethasone is reserved for children who cannot tolerate oral intake; oral dose at 0.15 mg/kg is equivalent and less distressing (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

explanation.summary: RCH advises oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild or moderate croup with 2 hours of observation before discharge. Reserve 0.6 mg/kg for severe croup with stridor at rest and marked respiratory distress. Prednisolone is not first line because of higher representation rates. Nebulised or intramuscular routes are alternatives only when the oral route is not tolerated. Nebulised adrenaline is added for severe cases and mandates 3 hours of post dose observation.
key_points: Mild or moderate croup: dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally.
Severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000.
Observe 3 hours after last nebulised adrenaline; 2 hours after steroid alone.
explanation.pearls: Croup severity is scored on stridor at rest, retraction and air entry; if a child has only intermittent stridor when upset with mild recession at rest, that is moderate and 0.15 mg/kg is enough.

subtopic_detail: First line adrenaline dosing in anaphylaxis in a 4 year old per ASCIA
stem: A 4-year-old girl with known peanut allergy developed generalised urticaria, facial swelling, wheeze and a hoarse cry ten minutes after eating a peanut butter sandwich. Her autoinjector was left at home.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148 /min, BP 88/54 mmHg, SpO2 93% in room air
data_table.Examination: Audible stridor with diffuse wheeze
data_table.Growth: Weight 16 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first adrenaline dose?

options.text: Adrenaline 100 microgram intravenously by slow bolus with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Intravenous adrenaline bolus in anaphylaxis is reserved for cardiac arrest or refractory shock and only in a monitored setting; the initial route is always intramuscular (Source: ASCIA Acute management of anaphylaxis).

options.text: Adrenaline 160 microgram intramuscularly into the mid anterolateral thigh
options.rationale: Weight based arithmetic is discouraged for anaphylaxis in AU; ASCIA banded dosing avoids error under time pressure and matches the EpiPen strengths available in community use (Source: ASCIA Acute management of anaphylaxis).

options.text: Adrenaline 300 microgram intramuscularly into the mid anterolateral thigh
options.rationale: The 300 microg dose is reserved for children 20 kg and over; using this dose in a 16 kg child over doses her by a factor of about 2 (Source: ASCIA Acute management of anaphylaxis).

options.text: Adrenaline 150 microgram intramuscularly into the mid anterolateral thigh
options.rationale: ASCIA uses banded intramuscular adrenaline dosing: 150 microg for children 10 to 20 kg; a 16 kg child sits in this band and the IM thigh is preferred over any weight based arithmetic (Source: ASCIA Acute management of anaphylaxis).

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with high flow oxygen
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema but is not a substitute for intramuscular adrenaline in anaphylaxis; delaying IM adrenaline increases the risk of biphasic and fatal reactions (Source: ASCIA Acute management of anaphylaxis).

explanation.summary: ASCIA uses banded intramuscular adrenaline dosing to remove drug arithmetic errors under time pressure: 150 microg for 10 to 20 kg (EpiPen Jr band), 300 microg for over 20 kg (EpiPen band), and 500 microg for adults. The intramuscular anterolateral thigh is the first route in every case. Intravenous adrenaline is reserved for cardiac arrest or refractory shock in a monitored setting.
key_points: 10 to 20 kg equals 150 microg IM.
Over 20 kg equals 300 microg IM.
Repeat every 5 minutes while symptoms persist.
explanation.pearls: Do not use 10 microg/kg calculations for community or emergency anaphylaxis dosing; the banded table gives an equivalent effective dose without arithmetic and mirrors the EpiPen strengths.

subtopic_detail: Full septic workup in an unwell 6 week old with normal inflammatory markers
stem: A 6-week-old boy has 8 hours of poor feeding, one bilious vomit and reduced tone. He was born at term and had been gaining weight well.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 188/min; BP 62/38 mmHg; RR 62/min; T 36.2 C
data_table.Examination: Poorly rousable; mottled; delayed central capillary refill
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.28, lactate 4.9 mmol/L; WCC 6.2 x10^9/L; CRP 8 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral paracetamol and ward admission, with cultures reviewed overnight
options.rationale: An unwell shocked infant under 3 months needs immediate resuscitation and empirical antibiotics; awaiting cultures overnight without intervention delays sepsis treatment (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis; RCH CPG The febrile child).

options.text: Adrenaline infusion first, then cultures, cefotaxime and a fluid bolus
options.rationale: Inotropes are added AFTER adequate fluid resuscitation (up to 60 mL/kg) fails to restore perfusion; using adrenaline before fluids and antibiotics inverts the sepsis pathway (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis).

options.text: A 20 mL/kg bolus first, then cultures, then benzylpenicillin and gentamicin
options.rationale: Sequence at RCH is IV access, blood cultures, first antibiotic dose, then fluid bolus; cefotaxime is preferred under 2 months because gentamicin monotherapy misses Listeria and dosing is more forgiving than penicillin plus gentamicin (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis).

options.text: Withhold antibiotics because the inflammatory markers are normal
options.rationale: Inflammatory markers are insensitive in early sepsis in this age group and are not used to justify withholding empirical antibiotics in an unwell infant under 3 months; delay is a preventable cause of death (Source: RCH CPG The febrile child).

options.text: Access, cultures, cefotaxime, then 20 mL/kg saline over 5 minutes
options.rationale: RCH sepsis pathway: IV or IO access, then blood cultures, then IV empirical antibiotic within the hour (cefotaxime for under 2 months to cover Listeria and Neisseria), then 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline over 5 to 10 minutes and repeat to 60 mL/kg total (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis; RCH CPG The febrile child).

explanation.summary: RCH sepsis pathway in a shocked infant is a fixed order: IV or IO access, blood cultures, first IV antibiotic within the hour, then 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline over 5 to 10 minutes, repeat to a total of 60 mL/kg before considering inotropes. Under 2 months the empirical antibiotic is IV cefotaxime to cover Neisseria and Listeria. Normal inflammatory markers do not exclude sepsis in early presentation and must not delay antibiotics in an unwell infant.
key_points: Order: access, cultures, antibiotics, fluid, then inotropes.
Under 2 months: IV cefotaxime empirically to cover Listeria.
Normal WCC and CRP do not exclude bacterial sepsis in early presentation.
explanation.pearls: A hypothermic infant with lactate over 4 and delayed capillary refill is in cold septic shock; treat with warm fluid boluses and expect adrenaline infusion to be needed once 60 mL/kg has been given, not before.

subtopic_detail: Choice of rehydration route in moderate paediatric gastroenteritis per RCH
stem: An 18-month-old girl has 3 days of vomiting and watery diarrhoea. She has vomited back most of an hour of syringe-fed oral rehydration solution and now refuses it.

data_table.Examination: HR 148/min; interactive; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 2 s
data_table.Investigations: Na 137 mmol/L; HCO3 18 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate rehydration plan?

options.text: Nasogastric rehydration solution at 25 mL/kg per hour for 4 hours
options.rationale: RCH advises rapid nasogastric rehydration as first line for mild to moderate dehydration when oral has failed; 25 mL/kg per hour for 4 hours is the standard rapid rehydration schedule and works well in gastroenteritis (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis).

options.text: Intravenous saline with glucose at maintenance plus 50 percent
options.rationale: IV fluids are reserved for severe dehydration, shock or NGT failure; using them first in a moderately dehydrated child unnecessarily cannulates her and increases hyponatraemia risk (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis).

options.text: Continue oral rehydration by syringe, reassessing in 4 hours
options.rationale: Oral rehydration by syringe has already failed at 1 hour with ongoing vomiting; continuing the same failed strategy risks worsening dehydration and delayed reassessment (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis).

options.text: A single oral dose of ondansetron, then retrial of syringe feeding
options.rationale: A single dose of ondansetron 2 mg for 8 to 15 kg body weight is a reasonable adjunct but the primary rehydration route is still NGT if oral has failed; this option undertreats a 6 percent dehydration episode (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis).

options.text: Intravenous saline 20 mL/kg over 30 minutes, then reassessment
options.rationale: A 20 mL/kg bolus is a resuscitation dose for shock; this child has no signs of shock and is not tachycardic beyond age norms, so a bolus is not indicated (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis).

explanation.summary: RCH gastroenteritis guidance recommends rapid nasogastric rehydration as first line for mild to moderate dehydration once oral rehydration solution has failed. The standard schedule is 25 mL/kg per hour for 4 hours of oral rehydration solution via nasogastric tube. Intravenous fluids are reserved for severe dehydration, shock or NGT failure. A single dose of ondansetron helps reduce vomiting and IV need in the moderately dehydrated child but is an adjunct rather than a substitute for enteral rehydration.
key_points: NGT rehydration is first line when oral has failed.
25 mL/kg per hour of ORS for 4 hours.
IV reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or NGT failure.
explanation.pearls: Weigh the child on presentation and again during rehydration; using acute weight change is the most reliable bedside measure of dehydration and of successful rehydration in a child with recent well child weights recorded.

subtopic_detail: Severe croup management with concurrent adrenaline and dexamethasone
stem: A 20-month-old boy weighing 12 kg has two days of coryza and a barking cough and now has stridor at rest.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 /min, RR 48 /min, SpO2 93% in air, T 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Agitated when disturbed, stridor at rest, intercostal and suprasternal recession, tiring between cries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 0.5 mg/kg of 1 in 1000 plus oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is a flat 5 mL of 1 in 1000 per RCH; a per kg calculation is not the RCH protocol and dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg undertreats severe croup (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 plus oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg
options.rationale: Severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession requires both nebulised adrenaline (flat 5 mL of 1 in 1000 by RCH; not per kg) and dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, with 3 hour observation after the last adrenaline (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg alone with two hours of observation
options.rationale: Steroid alone at 0.15 mg/kg without nebulised adrenaline is not adequate for severe croup with stridor at rest; risk of airway obstruction is not addressed (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

options.text: Rapid sequence intubation now under paediatric anaesthetic support
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for severe croup that fails medical therapy or shows impending respiratory failure; a trial of nebulised adrenaline and steroids is first (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

options.text: Heliox by loose fitting mask plus intravenous dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg
options.rationale: Heliox is not a substitute for nebulised adrenaline in severe croup at RCH; oral dexamethasone is equivalent to IV and less distressing than cannulation (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

explanation.summary: RCH severe croup pathway combines nebulised adrenaline (a flat 5 mL of 1 in 1000 per dose regardless of weight) with oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, with a minimum of 3 hours observation after the last adrenaline dose to detect rebound obstruction. Steroid alone is inadequate for severe croup; intubation is reserved for medical failure or impending respiratory failure. Do not use per kg adrenaline arithmetic for the nebulised dose.
key_points: Severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PLUS nebulised adrenaline.
Nebulised adrenaline is a flat 5 mL of 1 in 1000, not per kg.
Observe at least 3 hours after last adrenaline for rebound.
explanation.pearls: Rebound obstruction typically occurs 2 to 3 hours after nebulised adrenaline wears off; discharge before 3 hours risks readmission with worse airway compromise, so treat the 3 hour observation as a hard rule.

subtopic_detail: Complex early neonatal jaundice with disconfirming DAT and normal groups
stem: A term female neonate is jaundiced to the abdomen at 30 hours of age. She is exclusively breastfed and has lost 3 percent of her birthweight. Both parents are of northern European heritage; her maternal grandfather had a splenectomy in his thirties.

data_table.Examination: Alert, no cephalohaematoma or bruising
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 285 micromol/L (conjugated 10); Hb 152 g/L; reticulocytes 8 percent; film frequent spherocytes; DAT negative; maternal O positive, neonatal A positive; G6PD pending

lead_in: What is the most likely aetiology of this baby's jaundice?

options.text: ABO haemolytic disease of the newborn
options.rationale: ABO incompatibility would be expected to give a positive direct antiglobulin test in most clinically important cases and the film is more likely to show microspherocytes without polychromasia (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy).
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.text: Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
options.rationale: Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is X linked and rare in northern European girls; the film would typically show bite cells and hemighost cells rather than spherocytes with polychromasia (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy).
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.text: Hereditary spherocytosis causing haemolysis
options.rationale: Spherocytes on film with reticulocytosis, a negative direct antiglobulin test, and a family history of unexplained splenectomy is classic for hereditary spherocytosis presenting in the newborn period; DAT negativity is the key disconfirming finding for immune haemolysis (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy; HSANZ Australasian hereditary spherocytosis guideline).
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.text: Physiological jaundice with poor milk intake
options.rationale: Physiological jaundice does not present under 24 hours, does not cause reticulocytosis, and would not produce frequent spherocytes and polychromasia on film (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy).
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.text: Delayed jaundice from cephalohaematoma resorption
options.rationale: There is no cephalohaematoma on examination and cephalohaematoma resorption does not cause frequent spherocytes; it typically peaks after day 3 (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy).
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

explanation.summary: Hereditary spherocytosis is the leading cause of chronic congenital haemolytic anaemia in people of northern European heritage; presentation in the newborn period with early unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is common. The diagnostic triad is spherocytes on film with reticulocytosis, a negative direct antiglobulin test, and a family history of unexplained neonatal jaundice, splenectomy or gallstones. The negative direct antiglobulin test kills the immune haemolysis differentials of Rh and ABO incompatibility. Confirmatory testing is by eosin 5 maleimide binding by flow cytometry or by osmotic fragility.
key_points: DAT negative haemolysis with spherocytes points to intracorpuscular defect.
Family history of splenectomy or neonatal jaundice supports HS.
Confirm by eosin 5 maleimide binding by flow cytometry.
explanation.pearls: When bilirubin is over the exchange threshold with haemolytic features in the first 24 to 48 hours of life, start intensive phototherapy first and send for HS confirmatory testing; folate supplementation for the first year of life is standard and up to a third of infants with HS require transfusion in the newborn period.

sources.label: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

subtopic_detail: Initial treatment of steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome in a preschool child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 4 year old boy whose parents noticed his eyes were puffy in the mornings for the past week, and that his tummy now looks swollen. He is otherwise well, eating and playing normally.

He has had no fever, rash or joint swelling, and his urine has been pale rather than dark or tea coloured. He was born at term with no antenatal renal abnormality and has no family history of kidney disease. On examination he has periorbital oedema, mild ascites and pitting oedema to mid shin. His blood pressure is on the 50th centile for age and height. His urine microscopy shows no red cell casts.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 92/58, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein creatinine ratio 640 mg/mmol; urine microscopy no red cell casts; complement C3 and C4 within normal limits
data_table.Blood tests: Serum albumin 17 g/L (35-50); creatinine 32 micromol/L (25-55); total cholesterol 9.2 mmol/L (below 4.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Percutaneous renal biopsy before any treatment to establish the underlying histological diagnosis
options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for atypical features such as age under one or over twelve years, hypertension, haematuria with casts, low complement or renal impairment, none of which is present (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic Syndrome).

options.text: Oral prednisolone daily for four to six weeks followed by an alternate day tapering course
options.rationale: Typical childhood nephrotic syndrome between one and twelve years with normal blood pressure, normal complement and no active urinary sediment is treated empirically with corticosteroid without biopsy, since around 90 per cent are steroid sensitive minimal change disease (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic Syndrome).

options.text: Intravenous albumin infusion followed by intravenous furosemide to mobilise the accumulated oedema
options.rationale: Albumin with diuretic is reserved for symptomatic oedema such as respiratory compromise, scrotal or vulval oedema or skin breakdown, and it carries pulmonary oedema risk in a child who is well (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic Syndrome).

options.text: Oral furosemide with strict fluid restriction and daily weights until the oedema has resolved
options.rationale: Diuretics in an intravascularly depleted child risk hypovolaemia and thrombosis, and they do nothing to treat the underlying glomerular protein leak (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic Syndrome).

options.text: Oral enalapril to reduce proteinuria with monitoring of renal function and serum potassium
options.rationale: Angiotensin blockade is an adjunct in steroid resistant or persistently proteinuric disease rather than initial therapy in a previously untreated child (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic Syndrome).

explanation.summary: Childhood nephrotic syndrome is defined by heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema, and in the one to twelve year age group it is overwhelmingly steroid sensitive minimal change disease. Treatment is therefore started empirically without histology, and biopsy is reserved for atypical features or steroid resistance after four weeks of daily therapy. The important early complications are hypovolaemia, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis from urinary loss of immunoglobulin and complement factors, and venous thrombosis from loss of antithrombin III. Families are taught home urine dipstick monitoring because relapse is common and early detection shortens the treatment course.
key_points: Age one to twelve with normal blood pressure and no active sediment means treat without biopsy
Around 90 per cent of this group are steroid sensitive
Albumin with diuretic is reserved for symptomatic oedema, not routine treatment
Watch for peritonitis and thrombosis as the major early complications
explanation.pearls: Any child with nephrotic syndrome and abdominal pain needs spontaneous bacterial peritonitis excluded, with pneumococcus the commonest organism; ascitic tap and intravenous cefotaxime should not wait for a fever, which is often absent on corticosteroids.

subtopic_detail: Renal surveillance schedule after Henoch Schonlein purpura
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6 year old girl in the short stay unit. Over four days she has developed a rash over her buttocks and the backs of her legs that her mother describes as raised purple spots that do not fade when pressed, along with sore swollen ankles and intermittent tummy pain.

She is afebrile and looks well between episodes of pain. Her platelet count and coagulation screen are within normal limits, which excludes a bleeding disorder as the cause of the rash. Her abdomen is soft with no mass, guarding or rectal bleeding. Her blood pressure is on the 60th centile for age and height and her creatinine is within normal limits. Her urinalysis today shows blood 2+ and protein 1+.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 98/60, RR 20, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura over buttocks and extensor surfaces of both legs; bilateral ankle swelling; abdomen soft, no mass
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis blood 2+ and protein 1+; urine protein creatinine ratio 42 mg/mmol; platelets, coagulation screen and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow up plan?

options.text: No specific renal follow up is required, since the rash and joint symptoms resolve spontaneously
options.rationale: Nephritis is the complication that determines long term outcome and can appear or progress weeks after the rash has faded, so discharge without surveillance misses it (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

options.text: Renal biopsy arranged within the next fortnight to grade the severity of the glomerular involvement
options.rationale: Biopsy is indicated for nephrotic range proteinuria, impaired renal function or persistent significant proteinuria rather than for mild haematuria and proteinuria at presentation (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

options.text: Oral prednisolone for four weeks to prevent progression of the renal involvement over time
options.rationale: Corticosteroids shorten abdominal and joint pain but have not been shown to prevent or alter the course of nephritis, which is the widespread misconception this option tests (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

options.text: Weekly blood pressure and urinalysis for the first month, then at decreasing intervals to twelve months
options.rationale: Australian practice is structured surveillance with blood pressure and urinalysis, most intensively in the first one to two months when nephritis usually declares itself, continuing to six or twelve months (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound now and repeated at six months to assess for structural renal damage
options.rationale: Ultrasound assesses structure and is used to exclude intussusception in the abdominal form, but it does not detect the glomerular disease that surveillance is designed to find (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

explanation.summary: Henoch Schonlein purpura is the commonest childhood vasculitis and the diagnosis is clinical, requiring palpable purpura with lower limb predominance plus at least one of arthritis or arthralgia, abdominal pain, or renal involvement. The rash, joints and gut symptoms are self limiting over days to weeks, but nephritis determines long term outcome and develops in around a third of children, usually within the first two months. Because nephritis can appear after the child has apparently recovered, the follow up schedule of blood pressure and urinalysis is the single most important part of management. Corticosteroids reduce the duration of abdominal and joint pain but do not prevent renal disease, which is why they are not given routinely.
key_points: Nephritis develops in about a third of children and usually within the first two months
Surveillance is blood pressure and urinalysis, most frequent early then tapering to twelve months
Corticosteroids help abdominal and joint pain but do not prevent nephritis
Intussusception is the important acute abdominal complication and is ileoileal rather than ileocolic
explanation.pearls: Intussusception complicating this vasculitis is typically ileoileal, so it is missed by the air enema that reduces the usual ileocolic form; ultrasound is the diagnostic test and surgical reduction is usually required.

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia from excessive cow milk intake in a toddler
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 18 month old boy whose mother is worried he looks pale and has become fussy and less interested in playing over two months. He walks and has around ten words.

He drinks about 1200 mL of cow milk daily from a bottle and eats very little solid food, refusing meat entirely. He has no diarrhoea, no blood in his nappies and normal growth along the 50th centile for weight and height. He was born at term and has no family history of anaemia or bleeding disorders. His coeliac serology, taken with total immunoglobulin A, is negative and his stool testing shows no occult blood. His blood film shows hypochromic microcytic red cells with anisocytosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 92/56, RR 26, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Blood film: hypochromic microcytic red cells with anisocytosis; coeliac serology with total immunoglobulin A negative; faecal occult blood negative
data_table.Blood tests: Haemoglobin 84 g/L (105-135); mean cell volume 62 fL (73-85); ferritin 6 micrograms/L (15-150); C reactive protein within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Transfuse packed red cells and recheck the full blood count before discharge from the day unit
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for cardiovascular compromise or a much lower haemoglobin, and this child is well perfused with a haemoglobin that will respond to oral therapy (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency).

options.text: Intravenous iron infusion arranged at the paediatric day unit within the next two weeks
options.rationale: Parenteral iron is for malabsorption, intolerance of oral therapy or failure to respond, none of which has yet been established in an untreated child (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency).

options.text: Oral iron supplementation with cow milk reduced below 500 mL daily and iron rich solids introduced
options.rationale: Excessive cow milk causes iron deficiency by displacing iron rich solids, inhibiting absorption and causing occult enteric blood loss, so treatment pairs oral iron replacement with the dietary correction that prevents recurrence (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency).

options.text: Dietary advice alone with cow milk reduced below 500 mL daily and repeat blood testing in three months
options.rationale: Diet alone corrects the cause but replenishes stores far too slowly when the ferritin is already 6 micrograms per litre with symptomatic anaemia (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency).

options.text: Haemoglobin electrophoresis before any treatment to exclude an underlying thalassaemia trait
options.rationale: Electrophoresis is the near pair investigation for microcytosis, but a ferritin of 6 micrograms per litre already establishes iron deficiency, and iron deficiency itself distorts electrophoresis results (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency).

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional deficiency in Australian toddlers and excessive cow milk intake is the usual mechanism, operating through three routes at once: displacement of iron rich foods, calcium and casein inhibition of iron absorption, and occult gastrointestinal blood loss from cow milk protein induced enteropathy. Treatment always pairs replacement with correction of the cause, because iron given without reducing milk intake produces relapse once the course ends. Oral therapy is given for three months beyond haemoglobin normalisation to refill stores rather than stopped when the haemoglobin recovers. Neurodevelopmental effects of iron deficiency in this age group may be only partly reversible, which is the reason for treating rather than observing.
key_points: Cow milk above about 500 mL daily is the usual cause in Australian toddlers
Ferritin below 15 micrograms per litre confirms deficiency once inflammation is excluded
Continue oral iron for three months after the haemoglobin normalises to refill stores
Iron deficiency distorts haemoglobin electrophoresis, so treat first and test later if microcytosis persists
explanation.pearls: Recheck the full blood count after four weeks of oral iron and expect a haemoglobin rise of at least 10 g/L; failure to reach that mark points to adherence problems, ongoing blood loss or a wrong diagnosis rather than a need for a higher dose.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

subtopic_detail: Imaging choice for suspected developmental dysplasia of the hip at six weeks
stem:
You are the general practitioner performing a six week check on a baby girl. She was born at 38 weeks by caesarean section for breech presentation at term and her mother's sister was treated in a harness as an infant.

The baby is feeding well and gaining weight along the 50th centile. On examination the Ortolani and Barlow tests are both negative today, but abduction of the left hip in flexion is limited to 55 degrees compared with 80 degrees on the right, and there is an extra skin crease on the left thigh. Leg lengths appear equal with the knees flexed and the feet together. Her neonatal hip examination in the postnatal ward was documented as normal and her tone and reflexes are normal today.

data_table.Examination: Ortolani and Barlow negative; left hip abduction in flexion 55 degrees versus 80 degrees on the right; asymmetric left thigh skin crease; Galeazzi test negative
data_table.Investigations: Neonatal hip examination documented as normal in the postnatal ward

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Plain anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis arranged today with orthopaedic review of the films
options.rationale: The femoral head is largely cartilaginous before about four to six months, so radiography is unreliable at six weeks and is the wrong modality for this age (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Repeat clinical examination at the six month immunisation visit with no imaging in the interim
options.rationale: Delaying to six months forfeits the window in which harness treatment is highly effective, and limited abduction is a recognised sign of an established dislocation (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Commence a Pavlik harness now and arrange orthopaedic review within the following two weeks
options.rationale: Harness treatment is prescribed and monitored by orthopaedics on the basis of confirmed imaging, and applying one to a normal hip carries a risk of avascular necrosis (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of both hips under sedation to define the position of the femoral heads
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging requires sedation, is not the standard first line test in infancy, and adds nothing over ultrasound at this age (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Ultrasound of both hips arranged now with orthopaedic referral if the acetabular indices are abnormal
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the investigation of choice under about four to six months because it images the cartilaginous femoral head, and limited abduction with a breech history and a positive family history mandates imaging despite negative provocative tests (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

explanation.summary: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is screened for clinically at every infant check, and Australian practice adds selective ultrasound for babies with risk factors regardless of examination findings. The principal risk factors are breech presentation in the third trimester, a first degree family history and female sex, and breech alone is an indication for imaging even with a normal examination. Ortolani and Barlow tests lose sensitivity after about three months because a dislocated hip becomes fixed rather than reducible, at which point limited abduction, asymmetric thigh creases and apparent leg length inequality become the leading signs. Ultrasound is used under four to six months and radiography thereafter, once the femoral head ossific nucleus has appeared.
key_points: Ultrasound is the imaging modality under about four to six months, radiography after
Breech presentation and a first degree family history each independently warrant imaging
Ortolani and Barlow lose sensitivity after about three months as the hip becomes fixed
Limited abduction and asymmetric creases are the signs of an established dislocation
explanation.pearls: Ultrasound performed before six weeks of age generates false positives from normal neonatal ligamentous laxity, so a scan for risk factors alone is scheduled at six weeks rather than in the first days of life.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care neonatal hip guidance

subtopic_detail: Preventer initiation threshold in childhood asthma
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 7 year old boy who has attended three times this year for wheeze. He has a written asthma action plan and uses salbutamol through a spacer.

Over the last three months he has needed salbutamol three times most weeks for chest tightness during football training, and wakes coughing about twice a month. He has had no oral corticosteroid course and no emergency presentation this year. His inhaler technique with the spacer was checked by the practice nurse today and was correct, and his mother confirms he has no exposure to tobacco smoke at home. He has eczema and allergic rhinitis, both well controlled. His spirometry today shows a forced expiratory volume in one second of 88 per cent predicted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 100/62, RR 20, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation today; no accessory muscle use; growth along the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: forced expiratory volume in one second 88 per cent predicted; inhaler technique with spacer verified as correct

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence a low dose inhaled corticosteroid preventer through the spacer and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Reliever use on more than two days per week or night waking more than twice a month indicates poor control and triggers preventer therapy, with low dose inhaled corticosteroid the first line agent in this age group (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Commence oral montelukast at night as the preventer of choice given his coexisting allergic rhinitis
options.rationale: Montelukast is less effective than inhaled corticosteroid as a preventer and carries a neuropsychiatric warning, so it is a second line option rather than first choice (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Commence a combination inhaled corticosteroid and long acting beta agonist inhaler through the spacer
options.rationale: Combination therapy is the near pair but is reserved for children whose symptoms persist despite an adequate trial of inhaled corticosteroid alone, which has not yet been tried (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Increase salbutamol to a regular four times daily schedule through the spacer and review in one month
options.rationale: Regular short acting beta agonist use does not treat the underlying airway inflammation and is associated with worse asthma outcomes (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Commence a five day course of oral prednisolone and continue reliever therapy as currently prescribed
options.rationale: Oral corticosteroid treats an acute exacerbation rather than establishing long term control, and there is no exacerbation today (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

explanation.summary: Asthma control in children is assessed over the preceding four weeks using daytime symptoms, reliever use, night waking and activity limitation, and any one feature out of range means the asthma is not well controlled. Reliever use on more than two days per week is the threshold most often crossed and is the usual trigger for starting a preventer. Before escalating therapy the four checkable causes of apparent treatment failure are reviewed: inhaler technique, adherence, ongoing trigger exposure and comorbid conditions such as rhinitis or obesity. Low dose inhaled corticosteroid remains the first line preventer in school aged children, with a review at four to six weeks to confirm response before any step up.
key_points: Reliever use on more than two days per week signals poor control and triggers preventer therapy
Check technique, adherence, triggers and comorbidities before escalating
Low dose inhaled corticosteroid is first line preventer in school aged children
Combination inhalers are reserved for persistent symptoms despite adequate corticosteroid
explanation.pearls: Review any new preventer at four to six weeks, since inhaled corticosteroid takes two to four weeks to reach effect; escalating earlier because of no immediate benefit is the commonest reason children end up on combination therapy they do not need.

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic threshold in acute otitis media for an Aboriginal child
stem:
You are the general practitioner at a regional clinic seeing a 3 year old Aboriginal boy brought in by his grandmother. He has been pulling at his right ear, sleeping poorly and off his food for two days, and she says he has been grizzly and hot.

He has had two previous ear infections in the past year. On otoscopy the right tympanic membrane is bulging, opaque and red with loss of the light reflex, and there is no perforation and no discharge in the canal. The left drum is normal. He is alert, drinking well and has no neck stiffness, mastoid tenderness or facial weakness. He has had all scheduled immunisations including pneumococcal conjugate vaccine. He has no drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116, BP 96/58, RR 24, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 38.3
data_table.Examination: Right tympanic membrane bulging, opaque and erythematous with absent light reflex; no perforation or discharge; left drum normal; no mastoid tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Regular paracetamol with review in 48 hours and antibiotics only if he has not improved
options.rationale: Watchful waiting with delayed prescribing applies to otherwise low risk children, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children are specifically excluded from that pathway because of higher rates of suppurative complications (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media).

options.text: Topical ciprofloxacin ear drops with analgesia and review by the practice nurse in three days
options.rationale: Topical antibiotic drops are for a discharging perforated ear or otitis externa and do not penetrate an intact tympanic membrane (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Immediate oral amoxicillin with regular analgesia and clinical review to confirm resolution
options.rationale: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children receive immediate antibiotics for acute otitis media rather than delayed prescribing, and amoxicillin remains the first line agent (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media).

options.text: Immediate oral amoxicillin with clavulanate given his two previous episodes in the past year
options.rationale: The combination is the near pair reserved for treatment failure after 48 to 72 hours of amoxicillin or for recent amoxicillin exposure, and starting with it adds gastrointestinal adverse effects without benefit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Urgent same day referral to the ear nose and throat service for consideration of tympanostomy tubes
options.rationale: Tube insertion is considered for recurrent acute otitis media or persistent effusion with hearing loss, not for an acute episode that has not yet been treated medically (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media).

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in most Australian children is managed with analgesia and delayed prescribing, since the majority resolve without antibiotics and the benefit at 24 hours is small. That default is deliberately reversed for specific groups at higher risk of suppurative complications and chronic disease, namely Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, children under six months, children with a perforation or bilateral disease under two years, and those who are systemically unwell. In these children immediate amoxicillin is given, often at a higher dose and for a longer course, because chronic suppurative otitis media and the associated conductive hearing loss carry substantial developmental and educational consequences. Follow up is arranged to confirm resolution rather than left to the family to initiate.
key_points: Delayed prescribing is the default for low risk children but not for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children
Amoxicillin is first line; the clavulanate combination is for treatment failure or recent exposure
Other immediate antibiotic groups include infants under six months and bilateral disease under two years
Arrange review to confirm resolution given the risk of persistent effusion and hearing loss
explanation.pearls: Chronic suppurative otitis media is defined by persistent discharge through a perforation for more than six weeks and requires topical ciprofloxacin with regular dry mopping; it is the endpoint that immediate treatment of acute episodes is designed to prevent.

sources.label: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children

subtopic_detail: Choosing between enema reduction and laparotomy in intussusception
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a tertiary emergency department reviewing an 8 month old boy. His mother says that since yesterday he starts crying suddenly, draws his legs up, then settles and goes floppy between episodes, and he has vomited six times with the vomit now looking green.

Over the last two hours he has become harder to rouse and his nappies have been dry. On examination his abdomen is distended and he cries and tenses when you palpate anywhere, with guarding in all quadrants that persists between spasms. His capillary refill is four seconds centrally. Ultrasound performed 20 minutes ago shows a target lesion in the right upper quadrant with free fluid and absent colour Doppler flow within the intussuscipiens. Radiology and theatre are both immediately available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 186, BP 68/38, RR 48, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Examination: Abdominal distension with generalised guarding persisting between spasms; capillary refill 4 seconds; reduced responsiveness
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: target lesion right upper quadrant, free fluid, absent colour Doppler flow within the intussuscipiens; venous lactate 4.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Air enema reduction in the radiology department with a surgical team standing by in theatre
options.rationale: Peritonism, shock and absent Doppler flow indicate bowel ischaemia or perforation, which are absolute contraindications to enema reduction because insufflation risks perforation and worsens the shock (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception).

options.text: Fluid resuscitation and antibiotics with immediate transfer to theatre for operative reduction
options.rationale: With peritonism, shock, free fluid and absent Doppler flow, surgery is the only safe route, preceded by resuscitation and broad spectrum antibiotics rather than delayed for them (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception).

options.text: Hydrostatic contrast enema reduction under fluoroscopic guidance after a fluid bolus is completed
options.rationale: Hydrostatic and pneumatic reduction share the same contraindications, so changing the medium does not make reduction safe in the presence of peritonism (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception).

options.text: Nasogastric decompression with intravenous fluids and repeat ultrasound in four to six hours
options.rationale: Spontaneous reduction occurs in a minority of small bowel intussusceptions in a well child, but observation in a shocked infant with ischaemic bowel risks perforation and death (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception).

options.text: Computed tomography of the abdomen with contrast to define the lead point before any intervention
options.rationale: Computed tomography adds radiation and delay when ultrasound has already made the diagnosis, and a lead point is identified at operation in this age group (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception).

explanation.summary: Intussusception is the commonest cause of intestinal obstruction between three months and three years, and ultrasound has replaced contrast studies as the diagnostic test. Non operative reduction by air or hydrostatic enema succeeds in around 80 to 90 per cent of cases and is the default, which is why the exceptions matter so much. Peritonitis, perforation, shock and sonographic evidence of ischaemia such as free fluid or absent mural Doppler flow all mandate surgery instead. Resuscitation, nasogastric decompression and broad spectrum antibiotics run in parallel with the transfer to theatre rather than delaying it, and recurrence after reduction occurs in roughly one in ten, most often within the first 48 hours.
key_points: Enema reduction is the default and succeeds in 80 to 90 per cent of cases
Peritonism, perforation, shock and absent Doppler flow are absolute contraindications to reduction
Resuscitation and antibiotics accompany rather than delay transfer to theatre
Recurrence occurs in about ten per cent, usually within the first 48 hours
explanation.pearls: A pathological lead point such as a Meckel diverticulum, duplication cyst or lymphoma is found in under 10 per cent overall but in the majority of cases outside the three month to three year window, so age at presentation should drive how hard the lead point is sought.

subtopic_detail: Acute scrotal pain with coexisting urinary symptoms in an adolescent
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 14 year old boy who developed severe left scrotal pain five hours ago while sitting in class. He vomited twice on the way to hospital and has not been able to walk comfortably.

He reports stinging when passing urine over the last three days and his urine dipstick today shows leucocytes and nitrites. On examination the left testis sits higher than the right and lies transversely, the cremasteric reflex is absent on the left and present on the right, and elevating the testis does not relieve his pain. There is no scrotal erythema or fixed swelling and he is afebrile. Ultrasound is available but the sonographer is 45 minutes away from the hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 122/70, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Left testis high riding and transverse; cremasteric reflex absent on the left, present on the right; Prehn sign negative; no scrotal erythema
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick leucocytes and nitrites positive; urine culture sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim with analgesia and outpatient urology review once the urine culture returns
options.rationale: Treating the urinary findings as the whole explanation ignores the high riding transverse lie and absent cremasteric reflex, and a coexisting urinary infection does not exclude torsion (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain).

options.text: Urgent scrotal ultrasound with Doppler and surgical referral only if arterial flow is reduced
options.rationale: Imaging that delays exploration is the classic anti pattern here, and Doppler can show preserved flow in incomplete or intermittent torsion, producing false reassurance (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain).

options.text: Manual detorsion at the bedside with analgesia and discharge home if the pain settles completely
options.rationale: Manual detorsion is a temporising manoeuvre while theatre is prepared and never replaces exploration, since it frequently leaves residual twist and does not fix the underlying anatomy (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain).

options.text: Immediate urological referral for scrotal exploration with fixation of both testes if confirmed
options.rationale: Sudden severe pain with a high riding transverse testis and an absent cremasteric reflex is torsion until proven otherwise, and exploration within six hours of onset gives the best salvage rate, so it proceeds without imaging (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain; Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand guidance).
source_refs: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand guidance

options.text: Intravenous antibiotics with admission for observation and reassessment by the surgical team overnight
options.rationale: Overnight observation spends the salvage window, since testicular viability falls sharply beyond six hours and is largely lost by twelve (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain).

explanation.summary: Testicular torsion is a time critical diagnosis where salvage rates exceed 90 per cent within six hours, fall to around 50 per cent by twelve hours and approach zero beyond twenty four. The diagnosis is clinical, and the features that matter most are sudden severe onset, a high riding or transverse testis, an absent cremasteric reflex and pain unrelieved by elevation. Ultrasound has meaningful false negative rates in incomplete or intermittent torsion and its main role is in equivocal cases where it will not delay theatre. A coexisting urinary tract infection or epididymo-orchitis does not exclude torsion, and the presence of a plausible alternative diagnosis is one of the commonest reasons torsion is missed in adolescents.
key_points: Salvage exceeds 90 per cent within six hours and falls steeply thereafter
Absent cremasteric reflex and a high riding transverse testis are the strongest clinical signs
Doppler ultrasound can be falsely reassuring in incomplete or intermittent torsion
A coexisting urinary infection does not exclude torsion in an adolescent
explanation.pearls: Both testes are fixed at exploration because the bell clapper deformity that permits torsion is bilateral in most affected boys, so fixing only the affected side leaves a substantial risk of contralateral torsion later.

sources.label: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand guidance

subtopic_detail: Late presentation of a duct dependent systemic circulation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the emergency department for a 6 day old term baby girl. Her mother says she has gone off her feeds since yesterday, is breathing fast, and looked grey and mottled this morning.

She was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery with no antenatal concerns and was discharged at 36 hours of age. On examination she is pale and mottled with cool legs. Her right brachial pulse is easily palpable but both femoral pulses are impalpable. Pre-ductal saturation in the right hand is 96 per cent and post-ductal saturation in the right foot is 88 per cent. Her chest is clear on auscultation and her liver edge is 3 cm below the costal margin. Her venous blood gas shows pH 7.18 with a lactate of 7.4 mmol/L and her blood glucose is 4.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178, BP 62/34 right arm, RR 66, SpO2 96% right hand and 88% right foot, temperature 36.2
data_table.Examination: Pale and mottled with cool legs; right brachial pulse present, both femoral pulses impalpable; liver 3 cm below costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.18 (7.32-7.42); lactate 7.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.0); blood glucose 4.2 mmol/L (2.6-6.0); chest radiograph cardiomegaly with pulmonary plethora

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 per cent sodium chloride 20 mL/kg bolus with intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin
options.rationale: Sepsis is the correct parallel consideration and antibiotics should be given, but a large fluid bolus alone worsens pulmonary congestion here and leaves the duct closing (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate

options.text: Intubation with hyperventilation and high flow oxygen to correct the metabolic acidosis rapidly
options.rationale: High inspired oxygen and hypocapnia both reduce pulmonary vascular resistance, which diverts more blood into the lungs and further reduces systemic perfusion in a duct dependent systemic circulation (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline infusion titrated to restore blood pressure and peripheral perfusion
options.rationale: Inotropes may be needed as an adjunct but they cannot restore lower body flow while the arterial duct is closing, which is the mechanical problem to be reversed (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate

options.text: Urgent echocardiography to define the anatomy before commencing any cardiovascular treatment
options.rationale: Waiting for imaging is the near pair error, since the pre and post ductal saturation gradient with absent femoral pulses is already sufficient to act and the duct may close within hours (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate

options.text: Intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion with antibiotics and preparation for intubation and transfer
options.rationale: A pre to post ductal saturation gradient with impalpable femoral pulses and lactic acidosis at day 6 indicates a duct dependent systemic circulation, and prostaglandin reopens the duct while antibiotics cover the sepsis that cannot yet be excluded (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate

explanation.summary: Duct dependent systemic lesions such as coarctation, interrupted aortic arch, critical aortic stenosis and hypoplastic left heart present in the first two weeks as the arterial duct closes, and they are frequently mistaken for sepsis because both produce a shocked, mottled, tachypnoeic neonate. The findings that separate them are a pre to post ductal saturation gradient greater than 3 per cent, absent or weak femoral pulses, and a lactic acidosis out of proportion to the respiratory findings. Prostaglandin E1 reopens the duct and is started on clinical suspicion rather than after echocardiography, because the duct can close completely within hours. Apnoea is the main adverse effect and occurs in around 10 to 12 per cent, so the airway plan is made at the same time as the infusion is started.
key_points: A pre to post ductal saturation gradient above 3 per cent with weak femoral pulses points to a duct dependent systemic lesion
Prostaglandin E1 is started on clinical grounds without waiting for echocardiography
High inspired oxygen worsens systemic perfusion by lowering pulmonary vascular resistance
Give antibiotics in parallel, since sepsis cannot be excluded at the bedside
explanation.pearls: Apnoea complicates prostaglandin E1 infusion in roughly one in ten neonates and is dose related, so airway equipment and an intubation plan must be at the cot side before the infusion starts, particularly for a road or air transfer.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate

subtopic_detail: Femoral fracture in a pre-ambulant infant with a normal bone profile
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department seeing a 3 month old boy brought in because he cries whenever his left leg is moved and his mother's partner noticed his thigh looked swollen this morning.

The history given is that he rolled from a lounge onto a carpeted floor yesterday afternoon, a distance of about 40 cm. He is not yet rolling or crawling according to his developmental history taken separately. Radiography shows a mid shaft spiral fracture of the left femur. His sclerae are white, he has no joint hypermobility, his growth is along the 50th centile and there is no family history of fractures or hearing loss. His corrected calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone and 25 hydroxyvitamin D are all within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, BP 78/46, RR 40, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Swollen left thigh with pain on movement; white sclerae; no joint hypermobility; no bruising elsewhere on exposed skin
data_table.Investigations: Radiograph: mid shaft spiral fracture of the left femur; corrected calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone and 25 hydroxyvitamin D within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit, notify child protection services and arrange a skeletal survey with paediatric review
options.rationale: A femoral fracture in a pre-ambulant infant with a mechanism inconsistent with his developmental stage is highly suspicious for inflicted injury and mandates admission, statutory notification and a full skeletal survey (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse; Australian child protection mandatory reporting requirements).

options.text: Apply a hip spica cast and discharge with orthopaedic outpatient and general practitioner follow up
options.rationale: Treating the fracture alone returns the infant to an unassessed environment, and fracture management is never a substitute for the safety assessment (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse).

options.text: Arrange an outpatient skeletal survey next week with a scheduled paediatric clinic appointment
options.rationale: Deferring the survey to an outpatient appointment is the near pair error, since it delays detection of other injuries and leaves the child unprotected in the interval (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse).

options.text: Send genetic testing for osteogenesis imperfecta and defer notification until those results return
options.rationale: A normal bone profile with white sclerae, normal growth and no family history makes osteogenesis imperfecta unlikely, and genetic results take weeks while the statutory obligation to report a reasonable suspicion applies now (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse).

options.text: Discharge with analgesia and safety netting advice, with review by the child health nurse this week
options.rationale: Discharge without investigation or notification misses the substantial risk that further and more serious inflicted injury follows an unrecognised presenting injury (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse).

explanation.summary: Any fracture in a child who is not yet independently mobile carries a high probability of inflicted injury, and a femoral fracture in this age group is among the most specific presentations. The central assessment is whether the mechanism offered is plausible for the child's developmental stage and for the energy required to produce the injury, and a 40 cm fall onto carpet does not fracture a femur. Medical mimics such as osteogenesis imperfecta, rickets and metabolic bone disease are considered and are largely excluded here by normal biochemistry, normal sclerae, normal growth and an absent family history. Doctors in every Australian state and territory are mandated reporters, and the threshold for notification is a reasonable suspicion rather than diagnostic certainty.
key_points: Fractures in pre-ambulant infants are highly suspicious for inflicted injury
Assess whether the mechanism matches the child's developmental stage and the energy required
A skeletal survey is performed as an inpatient, not deferred to outpatients
The reporting threshold is reasonable suspicion, not diagnostic certainty
explanation.pearls: Repeat the skeletal survey at 11 to 14 days when inflicted injury is suspected; healing periosteal reaction and callus reveal rib and metaphyseal fractures that were invisible on the initial films.

sources.label: Australian Institute of Family Studies mandatory reporting guidance

subtopic_detail: Oxygen and feeding thresholds in bronchiolitis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4 month old boy admitted overnight on day three of a coryzal illness. He was born at term and has no cardiac or respiratory background.

His mother says he is taking about half his usual bottle volume and had four wet nappies in the past 24 hours instead of his usual seven. He is alert between feeds and settles when held. On examination he has moderate subcostal recession, a respiratory rate of 58 and widespread fine crackles with expiratory wheeze. He has had no apnoeic episodes witnessed by nursing staff or by his mother, and his oxygen saturation has been recorded between 91 and 93 per cent over the past four hours.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 152, BP 84/52, RR 58, SpO2 92% room air, temperature 37.4
data_table.Examination: Moderate subcostal recession, no tracheal tug, widespread fine crackles and expiratory wheeze, capillary refill 2 seconds, moist mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate positive for respiratory syncytial virus; no chest radiograph performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence high flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min and continue oral feeding
options.rationale: High flow therapy is reserved for infants who fail low flow oxygen, and low flow itself is not indicated while saturations remain at or above the accepted threshold (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Commence low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min and continue oral feeding as tolerated
options.rationale: Oxygen is started when saturations fall persistently below the accepted threshold, and treating a saturation of 92 per cent adds no benefit while making feeding and handling harder (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Commence a trial of nebulised salbutamol and reassess his work of breathing afterwards
options.rationale: Bronchodilators do not alter the course of bronchiolitis or reduce admission duration, and wheeze in this age group reflects small airway obstruction rather than reversible bronchospasm (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Commence nasogastric feeding at a reduced volume and continue observation on room air
options.rationale: His problem is inadequate intake rather than hypoxia, and nasogastric hydration is the first line support for an infant feeding under about half normal volumes whose saturations remain at the accepted threshold (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Commence intravenous maintenance fluid at full rate and withhold all oral intake
options.rationale: Intravenous fluid is reserved for severe dehydration, shock or failed nasogastric feeding, and it carries a greater risk of hyponatraemia from inappropriate antidiuresis than enteral hydration (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bronchiolitis).

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is managed with hydration and oxygen alone, and almost every other intervention that seems intuitively helpful has been shown not to work. Australian practice accepts an oxygen saturation threshold of 90 per cent rather than the 92 to 94 per cent used in other conditions, because treating higher figures prolongs admission without improving outcome. Feeding difficulty is the commonest reason for admission and is managed enterally first, with nasogastric feeding preferred over intravenous fluid because it is physiological, avoids cannulation and carries less risk of dilutional hyponatraemia. Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics, nebulised hypertonic saline and chest physiotherapy all lack evidence of benefit, and a chest radiograph is not routinely indicated because it changes management rarely while frequently prompting unnecessary antibiotics.
key_points: The Australian oxygen saturation threshold in bronchiolitis is 90 per cent
Low flow nasal prong oxygen is first line when oxygen is needed, with high flow for its failure
Nasogastric feeding is preferred over intravenous fluid for inadequate intake
Bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics and physiotherapy have no established benefit
explanation.pearls: Apnoea rather than hypoxia is the feature that changes disposition in infants under two months or those born preterm, so a witnessed apnoeic episode warrants closer monitoring even when saturations and feeding look acceptable.

sources.label: Paediatric Research in Emergency Departments International Collaborative bronchiolitis guideline

subtopic_detail: First line investigation of global developmental delay
stem:
You are the paediatrics registrar seeing a 26 month old boy referred by his child health nurse because he is not yet walking independently and says only four words. He sat unsupported at eleven months and crawled at sixteen months.

He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy with no perinatal concerns, and his newborn hearing screen and formal audiology testing were both normal. His parents are not related, there is no family history of developmental problems, and his growth is tracking along the 25th centile for length and weight. Examination shows mild generalised hypotonia with normal facial features and an otherwise normal neurological examination.

data_table.Examination: Head circumference on the 50th centile, mild generalised hypotonia, no dysmorphism, no hepatosplenomegaly, no neurocutaneous stigmata
data_table.Investigations: Formal audiology normal; full blood count, thyroid function and creatine kinase within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line investigation?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Neuroimaging has a higher yield with microcephaly, macrocephaly, focal signs, seizures or regression, none of which he has (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Delay).

options.text: Serum lead level with urine metabolic screening for organic acid disorders
