options.rationale: Aspiration follows a septic joint picture of fever, raised inflammatory markers and a hip held still in flexion and external rotation, and full painless hip range with a normal C-reactive protein argues against it (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp).

options.text: Discharge with paracetamol and advice to return if still limping in a week
options.rationale: Analgesia alone leaves an undisplaced spiral tibial fracture unprotected, and the child keeps loading a painful limb for the two weeks it takes periosteal reaction to appear (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler Fracture).

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin after blood cultures are collected
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics treat osteomyelitis, which would show fever, night pain and a raised C-reactive protein rather than an afebrile child with normal markers and a clear mechanism of injury (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Request urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the right tibia and knee
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging usually needs sedation at this age and adds nothing when the history, focal tibial tenderness and normal markers already define the management (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler Fracture).

options.text: Apply a below knee walking cast and arrange fracture clinic review
options.rationale: An undisplaced spiral tibial fracture in this age group is invisible on the initial film in a large proportion of cases, so a child with a twisting mechanism and focal tibial tenderness is immobilised and reviewed rather than cleared by the radiograph (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler Fracture).

explanation.summary: A toddler who will not weight bear needs the septic joint and osteomyelitis pathway considered first, and here the afebrile state, full painless hip range and normal inflammatory markers close that branch. What remains is an occult undisplaced spiral fracture of the tibial shaft, which frequently does not appear on the first radiograph and only becomes visible when periosteal new bone forms at one to two weeks. Treating the clinical picture rather than the film prevents a fortnight of pain and repeated presentations. These fractures are low energy, heal reliably, and do not require operative fixation.
key_points: Normal C-reactive protein with full painless hip movement makes septic arthritis very unlikely
A normal initial radiograph does not exclude an undisplaced spiral tibial fracture
Focal tenderness over the tibial shaft plus a twisting mechanism is enough to treat
Immobilisation with clinic review beats repeat imaging in the first week
Periosteal reaction confirming the fracture appears at about 10 to 14 days
explanation.pearls: Up to half of toddler fractures are radiographically occult on presentation, so a child who localises pain to the tibia after a twisting fall is immobilised on the clinical picture and the confirmatory periosteal reaction is looked for at 10 to 14 days.

subtopic_detail: Scarred preputial ring in a school aged boy versus physiological non retraction
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 9 year old boy whose father reports that the end of his penis puffs up like a balloon when he passes urine, and that this has been happening for about six months. Over that time the stream has become thin and sprays sideways, and twice the tip has been sore enough to keep him home from school.

He has never had a urinary tract infection and is otherwise well. On examination the foreskin will not retract at all. The tip is thickened into a firm pale ring that does not stretch when traction is applied, and the visible glans and surrounding skin are not red or inflamed.

data_table.Examination: Non retractile foreskin with a firm pale thickened preputial ring that does not stretch on traction, no erythema of the glans or shaft, no discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for leucocytes and nitrites

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure that separation is incomplete and review in twelve months
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is right for physiological non retraction, in which the preputial skin is soft and pink and there are no urinary symptoms, and it does not apply once there is scarring with an obstructed stream (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin Care).

options.text: Prescribe topical betamethasone twice daily to the tip for six weeks
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid with gentle stretching works well for a soft physiological ring, but a fibrotic pale scar does not soften with steroid and the delay prolongs obstructed voiding (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin Care).

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for circumcision on the elective list
options.rationale: A firm pale scarred preputial ring with ballooning, spraying and recurrent soreness is pathological rather than physiological phimosis, and it is one of the few absolute indications for circumcision in childhood (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin Care; RACP Circumcision Statement).

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days and daily saline soaks
options.rationale: Oral antibiotic treats balanoposthitis, whose near pair feature is a red swollen tender foreskin with purulent discharge rather than a pale avascular fibrotic ring (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Teach gentle daily retraction after a warm bath and review in three months
options.rationale: Retraction exercises are appropriate for the soft unscarred foreskin, and forcing a scarred ring risks splitting it and creating further cicatricial scarring (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin Care).

explanation.summary: Most non retractile foreskins in boys are physiological, reflecting incomplete separation of preputial adhesions that completes during the first decade or into adolescence. The distinction that matters is the appearance of the ring: soft, pink and pouting is physiological, while firm, pale and fibrotic is scar. Scarring with obstructed voiding, recurrent soreness or recurrent infection is the pathological form, and it is the setting in which circumcision is genuinely indicated rather than elective. Steroid and stretching should not be used to delay definitive treatment once the ring is fibrotic, because the outcome is repeated splitting and denser scar.
key_points: Physiological non retraction needs no treatment and no examination under anaesthesia
Ballooning alone in a soft unscarred foreskin is not an indication for surgery
A firm pale non stretching ring signals scarring rather than adhesion
Topical corticosteroid is for the soft ring, not the fibrotic one
Scarring with obstructed voiding is an accepted indication for circumcision
explanation.pearls: Topical betamethasone 0.05 per cent twice daily for four to six weeks resolves the majority of soft physiological phimoses, but a pale fibrotic ring predicts steroid failure and should be sent for surgical opinion at the first visit.

subtopic_detail: Radio-opaque foreign body ingestion where the number of objects changes the urgency
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 3 year old boy is brought in two hours after his mother saw him spit out and then swallow some of the small silver balls from his older brother's desk toy. She thinks he swallowed two or three.

He is playing in the cubicle, is not drooling, and has just finished a cup of juice without difficulty. His chest is clear and his abdomen is soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds. The abdominal radiograph shows two round radio-opaque objects lying in the gastric shadow, stacked against each other with a thin lucent line between them.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108, blood pressure 96/60, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: No drooling, tolerating oral fluids, chest clear, abdomen soft and non tender
data_table.Investigations: Abdominal radiograph shows two round radio-opaque objects in the gastric shadow, apposed with a thin lucent line between them and no free gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge home with advice to sieve the stools and repeat the film in a week
options.rationale: Watchful waiting with stool checking is the pathway for a single blunt object such as a coin in the stomach of a well child, and it is unsafe once more than one magnetic object is present (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Ingestion).

options.text: Give oral polyethylene glycol and repeat the abdominal film in 24 hours
options.rationale: Accelerating transit does not separate objects that are already held together across tissue, and the delay allows pressure necrosis of the bowel wall to progress (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Ingestion).

options.text: Arrange urgent upper endoscopy for retrieval of both objects tonight
options.rationale: Two or more magnets attract across loops of bowel and cause pressure necrosis, fistula and perforation, so while they remain within endoscopic reach in the stomach they are removed urgently even though the child is well (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Ingestion).

options.text: Observe on the ward with four hourly review and a film in the morning
options.rationale: Observation wastes the window in which the objects are still retrievable from above, and clinical signs of bowel injury appear only after necrosis is established (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Ingestion).

options.text: Refer for laparotomy and removal of both objects with bowel inspection
options.rationale: Open surgery is the answer once the objects have passed the duodenum and cannot be reached endoscopically, or when there are peritoneal signs, and neither applies while they sit in the stomach (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Ingestion).

explanation.summary: Ingested foreign bodies are triaged by what the object is, where it sits and whether the child has symptoms, and the number of objects is decisive when they are magnetic. A single blunt object in the stomach can be managed expectantly, whereas two or more magnets, or one magnet with another metallic object, can trap bowel wall between them and cause necrosis within hours. Button batteries lodged in the oesophagus form the other emergency, needing removal within two hours because of alkaline mucosal injury. The apposed pair with a lucent gap between them on the film is the radiographic signature that should trigger the call to the endoscopist.
key_points: One blunt object in the stomach of a well child can be managed expectantly
Two or more magnets are an emergency regardless of symptoms
Objects in the stomach are removed endoscopically, beyond the duodenum surgically
A lucent gap between apposed radio-opaque objects suggests interposed tissue
An oesophageal button battery needs removal within two hours
explanation.pearls: Two magnets anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract mandate removal on the day of presentation, and if they have already passed the ligament of Treitz the decision moves from endoscopy to surgical review rather than to observation.

subtopic_detail: Return to contact sport after concussion in a person under 19 years
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 14 year old boy eight days after he collided head to head in a junior rugby league match. He did not lose consciousness but was dazed on the field, was removed from play, and had headache and difficulty concentrating in class for four days.

He has now been free of headache, fogginess and light sensitivity for three full days, has returned to a full school day, and has completed light jogging and stationary cycling without symptoms. His neurological examination including balance testing is normal. His coach has asked you to sign him off for the semi final this Saturday, and his father says he has never had a previous head knock.

data_table.Examination: Normal cranial nerve, limb and cerebellar examination, tandem gait normal, no neck tenderness
data_table.Timeline: Injury day 0, symptoms resolved day 5, aerobic exercise tolerated days 6 to 8, currently day 8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about returning to play?

options.text: Allow return to contact training now with a full game on the weekend
options.rationale: Clearing him at day eight applies the adult community pathway, and the paediatric pathway is deliberately slower because of the longer physiological recovery in the developing brain (Source: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport).
source_refs: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography head scan before any return to training
options.rationale: Imaging answers the question of structural injury in the acute phase and has no role in return to play decisions in a boy who is now asymptomatic with a normal examination (Source: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport).
source_refs: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

options.text: Allow return once he completes a two day graded exercise progression
options.rationale: Tolerating the graded exercise stages is necessary but not sufficient in this age group, because a minimum calendar interval also applies before contact is resumed (Source: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport).
source_refs: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

options.text: Withhold competitive contact sport until at least 21 days after injury
options.rationale: The Australian youth pathway sets a floor of 21 days from injury before competitive contact or collision sport, with at least 14 symptom free days first, and non contact conditioning continues in the meantime (Source: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport).
source_refs: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

options.text: Refer for neuropsychological testing before clearing him to play again
options.rationale: Formal neuropsychological assessment is reserved for persisting symptoms beyond four weeks or repeated concussions, and it does not shorten the minimum interval in an uncomplicated first concussion (Source: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport).
source_refs: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

explanation.summary: Australian community and youth sport guidance deliberately separates the child and adolescent pathway from the professional pathway, because young athletes recover more slowly and repeat injury during the vulnerable window carries disproportionate risk. Return to learn comes before return to sport, and the graded exercise progression only starts once symptoms have settled. Even a straightforward recovery cannot compress the minimum calendar interval to competitive contact play. Any return of symptoms at a stage means dropping back to the previous stage rather than pushing through.
key_points: Return to learn precedes return to sport in school aged athletes
Symptom resolution alone does not authorise a return to contact
The Australian youth floor is 21 days from injury before competitive contact sport
At least 14 symptom free days are required before contact training
Neuroimaging has no role in return to play decisions
explanation.pearls: A community athlete under 19 cannot return to competitive contact sport sooner than 21 days after concussion in Australia, even with complete symptom resolution by day five, and non contact aerobic conditioning is what fills the interval.

sources.label: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

subtopic_detail: Choice of imaging for suspected hip dysplasia once the femoral head has begun to ossify
stem:
You are the paediatric outpatient registrar seeing a 6 month old girl referred because her mother noticed that the skin creases on her thighs do not match. She was born at term in the breech position and had a normal newborn hip examination documented in her blue book.

She is not yet crawling but rolls both ways and sits with support. On examination the left hip abducts to only 45 degrees while the right abducts fully, the left knee sits lower than the right when the hips and knees are flexed with the feet together, and there is no click or clunk on provocative testing. Her leg lengths and spine are otherwise normal.

data_table.Examination: Limited left hip abduction to 45 degrees, asymmetric thigh creases, positive Galeazzi sign on the left, no clunk on Ortolani or Barlow testing
data_table.History: Breech presentation at term, newborn hip examination recorded as normal, no family history of hip disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging investigation?

options.text: Arrange static and dynamic hip ultrasound of both hips this week
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the modality of choice under about four months, but from four to six months the ossifying femoral head casts an acoustic shadow over the acetabulum and makes measurements unreliable (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Arrange an anteroposterior pelvis radiograph and orthopaedic review
options.rationale: Once the femoral head ossifies at around four to six months the plain anteroposterior pelvis film becomes the reliable test, and limited abduction with a positive Galeazzi sign warrants orthopaedic assessment alongside it (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Apply a Pavlik harness and review in the orthopaedic clinic in three weeks
options.rationale: Harness treatment is applied after imaging confirms the diagnosis and its success falls sharply beyond six months of age, so it is not started blind at this visit (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Reassure and reassess the hips at the twelve month health check
options.rationale: Limited abduction is the most reliable sign of dysplasia after the newborn period, and deferring to twelve months risks presentation with an established dislocation and a limp (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of both hips under light sedation
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is used to assess reduction after closed or open reduction, not to make the initial diagnosis, and it requires sedation for no additional information here (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

explanation.summary: A normal newborn hip examination does not exclude dysplasia, because the acetabulum can become progressively dysplastic over the first months and breech presentation remains the strongest single risk factor. The physical signs shift with age: instability signs such as Ortolani and Barlow fade after about three months, and asymmetric abduction with a positive Galeazzi sign takes over. Imaging must follow the same clock, with ultrasound early and plain radiography once the ossific nucleus appears. Late diagnosis matters because harness treatment fails beyond six months and the child then faces closed or open reduction with a spica cast.
key_points: Breech presentation at term is the strongest risk factor even with a normal newborn examination
Ortolani and Barlow signs become unreliable after about three months
Limited abduction and a positive Galeazzi sign are the older infant signs
Ultrasound is the test under four months, plain radiography from about four to six months
Pavlik harness success falls away after six months of age
explanation.pearls: Hip ultrasound loses accuracy once the femoral ossific nucleus appears at around four to six months, so a six month old with asymmetric abduction is imaged with an anteroposterior pelvis radiograph rather than repeat ultrasound.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: DDH

subtopic_detail: Nocturnal events in a preschooler where the pattern separates seizure from parasomnia
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4 year old girl referred by her general practitioner with a working diagnosis of night terrors. Her parents have kept a two week diary and have filmed several events on a phone.

The diary records six to eight events on most nights, spread from shortly after she falls asleep through to the early morning. Each lasts about 30 seconds and looks identical to the last: she opens her eyes, stiffens her right arm, then cycles her legs and makes a grunting noise. Her parents can rouse her at the end and she talks to them normally before going back to sleep. She is tired and irritable during the day, and her development and examination are normal.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological and developmental examination, no neurocutaneous stigmata, head circumference on the 50th centile
data_table.Sleep diary: Six to eight stereotyped events per night lasting about 30 seconds, occurring throughout the night, with full alertness immediately afterwards

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure, advise a safe sleep environment, and review in three months
options.rationale: Reassurance suits a parasomnia, which occurs once or twice a night in the first third of sleep, varies between episodes and leaves the child confused rather than immediately alert (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep Problems).

options.text: Start melatonin 2 mg at bedtime and review the sleep diary in one month
options.rationale: Melatonin addresses delayed sleep onset rather than events arising out of established sleep, and it would delay recognition of an epilepsy syndrome (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep Problems).

options.text: Arrange overnight oximetry and refer for adenotonsillectomy assessment
options.rationale: Obstructive sleep apnoea causes snoring, witnessed pauses and restless sleep with daytime tiredness, but not brief identical motor events with preserved awareness afterwards (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea).

options.text: Refer for polysomnography to quantify arousals from slow wave sleep
options.rationale: Polysomnography maps sleep architecture and respiratory events, and while video is useful it is not the test that identifies interictal epileptiform discharges (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile Seizures).

options.text: Refer for a sleep deprived electroencephalogram and neurology review
options.rationale: High frequency, brief, stereotyped hypermotor events occurring throughout the night with rapid recovery of awareness point to a sleep related epilepsy, and the sleep deprived recording is the investigation that captures the discharges (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile Seizures).

explanation.summary: The nocturnal event history is discriminating if the right five questions are asked: how many per night, when in the night, how long, how similar to each other, and how the child behaves immediately afterwards. Parasomnias are infrequent, arise from slow wave sleep in the first third of the night, last minutes, vary between episodes and end in confusion with amnesia. Sleep related hypermotor seizures are brief, numerous, identical, distributed across the whole night and followed by preserved awareness. Daytime irritability from fragmented sleep is common to both and does not discriminate. Home phone video has become one of the most valuable pieces of evidence in this assessment.
key_points: Count the events per night and note their distribution across the night
Stereotypy between events is the single most useful feature for seizure
Immediate return of awareness after an event argues against a parasomnia
Parasomnias arise from slow wave sleep in the first third of the night
Home video should be actively requested and reviewed
explanation.pearls: More than two identical events in a single night, each under a minute and spread across the whole night, moves a child from the parasomnia pathway to a sleep deprived electroencephalogram rather than to reassurance.

subtopic_detail: Bowed legs with a metabolic bone profile that separates nutritional from inherited rickets
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 20 month old boy referred because his legs have become increasingly bowed since he started walking at 17 months. His family moved to Melbourne from a country with a warmer climate two years ago, his mother covers most of her skin outdoors, and he was breastfed without supplementation until 14 months.

He now drinks about 1.2 litres of cow milk each day and eats little else. He has no family history of bone disease and both parents have straight legs. On examination he has symmetrical bowing of both tibiae, widening at both wrists, and a normal chest and abdomen.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical genu varum, widened wrists, no frontal bossing, no proximal weakness, growth tracking on the 25th centile
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.15 mmol/L (2.20-2.60); phosphate 0.85 mmol/L (1.20-1.80); alkaline phosphatase 1180 U/L (100-400); parathyroid hormone 18.5 pmol/L (1.6-6.9); 25 hydroxyvitamin D 16 nmol/L (greater than 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start colecalciferol and oral calcium with repeat bloods in one month
options.rationale: A low 25 hydroxyvitamin D with a raised parathyroid hormone identifies nutritional deficiency, and a child on high milk intake with poor solid variety still needs calcium alongside replacement to avoid the hypocalcaemia that follows bone healing (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D Deficiency).

options.text: Start colecalciferol alone and repeat the bone profile in three months
options.rationale: Replacing vitamin D without calcium in a child with a poor dietary calcium intake risks symptomatic hypocalcaemia as remineralising bone takes up circulating calcium (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D Deficiency).

options.text: Refer for genetic testing for X linked hypophosphataemia before treating
options.rationale: Inherited phosphate wasting gives a low phosphate with a normal 25 hydroxyvitamin D and a normal or only mildly raised parathyroid hormone, so the markedly raised parathyroid hormone and deficient vitamin D here point elsewhere (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D Deficiency).

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for bracing of both legs and monitor his growth
options.rationale: The bowing is a consequence of soft undermineralised bone and straightens with medical treatment, so bracing addresses the deformity while leaving the cause untreated (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D Deficiency).

options.text: Advise increasing cow milk to two litres daily and review in one month
options.rationale: Cow milk is not fortified with vitamin D in Australia, and volumes at this level displace iron rich solids and cause iron deficiency anaemia (Source: NHMRC Infant Feeding Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Nutritional rickets remains common in Australian children with darker skin, limited sun exposure, prolonged unsupplemented breastfeeding and a monotonous diet. The biochemistry separates the causes efficiently: a low 25 hydroxyvitamin D with secondary hyperparathyroidism is nutritional, whereas a low phosphate with normal vitamin D and normal parathyroid hormone suggests renal phosphate wasting. Alkaline phosphatase is the most sensitive marker of active disease and is what falls first with successful treatment. The maternal vitamin D status should be checked at the same time, because the mother of an affected breastfed child is usually deficient herself.
key_points: Raised alkaline phosphatase with a raised parathyroid hormone signals active nutritional rickets
Give calcium with vitamin D when dietary calcium intake is poor
Cow milk in Australia is not fortified with vitamin D
Milk volumes above about 500 mL daily displace iron rich solids
Screen and treat the mother of an affected breastfed infant
explanation.pearls: Alkaline phosphatase falls before the radiographic changes resolve, so a repeat level at four weeks is the earliest objective sign that colecalciferol and calcium replacement is working.

subtopic_detail: Knee pain in an adolescent where the examination redirects the imaging
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 13 year old boy with three weeks of aching in the left knee that is worse after football training and eases with rest. There was no single injury and no swelling.

He weighs 78 kg and his body mass index sits above the 97th centile. He walks into the room with the left foot turned outwards. The left knee has full range of movement, no effusion, no joint line tenderness and stable ligaments. When you flex the left hip the thigh rolls into external rotation, and internal rotation of that hip is limited to 10 degrees compared with 40 degrees on the right. He is afebrile and systemically well.

data_table.Examination: Out toeing gait on the left, normal knee examination with no effusion, obligatory external rotation on left hip flexion, left hip internal rotation 10 degrees versus 40 degrees on the right
data_table.Growth: Weight 78 kg, body mass index above the 97th centile for age

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee within two weeks
options.rationale: Knee imaging follows a knee examination that is actually abnormal, and a full painless knee with restricted hip rotation makes the knee the referral site rather than the source (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Advise relative rest, ibuprofen and physiotherapy for the knee pain
options.rationale: Conservative management fits patellofemoral pain, which reproduces symptoms on patellar compression and squatting rather than restricting hip internal rotation (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Arrange left knee radiographs and review in the fracture clinic later
options.rationale: Films of the wrong joint are the usual reason for delayed diagnosis in this presentation, and the delay allows a stable slip to become unstable (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Order pelvis radiographs including frog leg views and refer urgently
options.rationale: Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion with loss of internal rotation in a heavy adolescent is the classical hip sign, and both anteroposterior and frog leg lateral views are needed because early slips are visible only on the lateral (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Check inflammatory markers and arrange an ultrasound of the left knee
options.rationale: Inflammatory markers and ultrasound target septic arthritis or an effusion, and three weeks of activity related pain in an afebrile boy with a dry knee does not fit that pattern (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp).

explanation.summary: Hip pathology in children and adolescents refers pain to the distal thigh and knee through the obturator nerve, and a substantial proportion of slipped capital femoral epiphysis presents with knee pain alone. The examination that redirects the diagnosis costs seconds: compare internal rotation of both hips with the patient supine and watch for obligatory external rotation as the hip is flexed. Delay converts a stable slip, in which the child can still weight bear, into an unstable slip with a markedly higher risk of avascular necrosis. Treatment is in situ screw fixation, and the contralateral hip is assessed at the same time because bilateral disease is common.
key_points: Examine the hips in every child or adolescent presenting with knee pain
Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion is the most specific bedside sign
Frog leg lateral views are required because early slips hide on the anteroposterior film
Keep the child non weight bearing once the diagnosis is suspected
Endocrine screening is considered in slips outside the usual age or weight range
explanation.pearls: Around one in five adolescents with a slipped capital femoral epiphysis presents with isolated knee or thigh pain, so a knee examination that is entirely normal should send the film request to the pelvis rather than the knee.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

subtopic_detail: Recognising a vascular birthmark in a location that threatens function
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 4 month old girl whose mother has brought her because of a lump on her eyelid. It appeared as a faint pink patch at about three weeks of age and has grown steadily since.

The lesion is a bright red raised swelling 25 mm across on the right upper eyelid that extends over the lid margin and pushes the lid down so that it covers the upper half of the pupil. It is soft, compressible and not tender, and there is no ulceration or bleeding. She is otherwise well, feeding and growing along the 50th centile, and has no other skin lesions.

data_table.Examination: Bright red compressible 25 mm lesion on the right upper eyelid overlying the lid margin and obscuring the upper half of the pupil, no ulceration, single lesion on full skin examination
data_table.Growth: Weight and length tracking along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently to ophthalmology and paediatrics for propranolol
options.rationale: A lesion obstructing the visual axis is a high risk infantile haemangioma that causes deprivation amblyopia within weeks, so it needs urgent specialist assessment and systemic propranolol after a cardiovascular check (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Haemangioma).

options.text: Reassure the parents and review the lesion at twelve months of age
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is correct for most infantile haemangiomas because they involute, but involution begins around 12 months and by then irreversible amblyopia will have developed (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Haemangioma).

options.text: Apply topical timolol maleate gel twice daily and review monthly
options.rationale: Topical beta blocker is effective for small superficial lesions of a few millimetres, and it penetrates too poorly to control a 25 mm periocular lesion (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Haemangioma).

options.text: Refer for pulsed dye laser treatment at the next available list
options.rationale: Pulsed dye laser is used for residual telangiectasia after involution or for ulcerated lesions, and it does not control the deep proliferative component causing the obstruction (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Haemangioma).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the orbit before treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is reserved for segmental facial lesions raising the possibility of an associated syndrome or for suspected deep orbital extension, and arranging it first would delay sight saving treatment (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Haemangioma).

explanation.summary: Infantile haemangiomas appear in the first weeks of life, proliferate rapidly until about five months, then involute slowly over years, and the great majority need no treatment at all. Treatment is reserved for lesions that threaten function, ulcerate, or will leave significant disfigurement, and the periocular site is the classic functional threat because occlusion of the visual axis for even a few weeks in infancy produces deprivation amblyopia. Astigmatism from pressure on the globe is a second mechanism of visual loss that persists even after the lesion shrinks, so ophthalmology follow up continues after treatment. Oral propranolol has replaced systemic corticosteroids and typically produces visible softening and colour change within days, with a pretreatment assessment for heart rate, blood pressure and any history suggesting airway or cardiac disease.
key_points: Proliferation peaks by about five months, before spontaneous involution begins
Periocular lesions cause deprivation amblyopia and astigmatism
Oral propranolol is first line for function threatening lesions
Topical timolol is limited to small superficial lesions
Five or more cutaneous haemangiomas prompts liver ultrasound
explanation.pearls: Five or more cutaneous infantile haemangiomas warrants abdominal ultrasound for hepatic haemangiomas, which can cause high output cardiac failure and consumptive hypothyroidism even when the skin lesions themselves are trivial.

subtopic_detail: Investigation after biochemistry confirms a central cause of early puberty
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a girl of 5 years and 6 months whose mother noticed breast development four months ago. Her height has crossed from the 50th to the 90th centile over the past year and her mother has noticed an adult body odour.

She has breast development to Tanner stage 3 and sparse pubic hair. She has no headache, no vomiting and no visual symptoms, and there are no cafe au lait macules on full skin examination and no history of unexplained laughing episodes. Her fundi are normal and her visual fields are full to confrontation.

data_table.Investigations: Luteinising hormone 4.2 IU/L after gonadotrophin releasing hormone stimulation indicating a pubertal response, oestradiol raised for age, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Bone age 9 years and 6 months against a chronological age of 5 years and 6 months, pelvic ultrasound shows an enlarged uterus with an endometrial stripe

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound and repeat the bone age in six months
options.rationale: The pelvic ultrasound has already been done and repeating a bone age adds nothing when the diagnosis is biochemically established and the priority is to find the cause (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and pituitary
options.rationale: A pubertal luteinising hormone response to stimulation confirms a central cause, and every girl under 6 years with central precocious puberty needs brain imaging because the likelihood of an intracranial lesion is highest in this age group (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

options.text: Measure adrenal androgens and image the adrenal glands with CT
options.rationale: Adrenal investigation is for virilisation with a suppressed luteinising hormone response, and the near pair distinction is that a peripheral cause suppresses gonadotrophins while a central cause raises them (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

options.text: Commence a gonadotrophin releasing hormone analogue immediately
options.rationale: Treatment to halt puberty and preserve adult height is appropriate but is not an investigation, and starting it without imaging risks missing a hypothalamic lesion (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

options.text: Reassure the family and repeat the growth measurements in a year
options.rationale: Isolated premature thelarche without growth acceleration or bone age advance can be observed, and this girl has both a markedly advanced bone age and an oestrogenised uterus (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

explanation.summary: Precocious puberty means secondary sexual characteristics before 8 years of age in girls and 9 years in boys, and the first branch point is whether the cause is central, meaning early activation of the hypothalamic pituitary gonadal axis, or peripheral, meaning autonomous sex steroid production. A stimulated luteinising hormone response separates them, since central causes give a pubertal rise while peripheral causes suppress gonadotrophins through negative feedback. Central precocious puberty is idiopathic in the majority of girls but the proportion with an intracranial lesion rises sharply as the age at onset falls, which is why imaging is mandatory under 6 years and considered between 6 and 8 years. In boys the calculus is reversed, with a much higher rate of underlying pathology at any age, so imaging is arranged for all of them. Treatment with a gonadotrophin releasing hormone analogue aims to preserve adult height and to allow psychosocial development to match chronological age.
key_points: A pubertal luteinising hormone response to stimulation indicates a central cause
Peripheral causes suppress gonadotrophins through negative feedback
Brain imaging is mandatory for central precocious puberty in girls under 6 years
All boys with central precocious puberty need brain imaging
Bone age advance and an oestrogenised uterus separate this from premature thelarche
explanation.pearls: A hypothalamic hamartoma is the commonest intracranial cause of central precocious puberty and may be signalled by gelastic seizures, which parents describe as unexplained bursts of laughing rather than as seizures, so ask about them directly.

subtopic_detail: Vaccinating a child whose food allergy is widely but wrongly assumed to be a contraindication
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 11 month old boy who is due his scheduled vaccines including measles mumps rubella, and whose mother also wants this season's influenza vaccine given.

At seven months of age he developed widespread hives, vomiting and wheeze within 15 minutes of one mouthful of scrambled egg and was given intramuscular adrenaline in the emergency department. He has avoided egg since. He has no asthma and has had no previous vaccine reaction, and he is well and afebrile today.

data_table.Examination: Well child with clear chest, no rash and no fever
data_table.Immunisation history: Up to date on the National Immunisation Program schedule with no previous adverse events following immunisation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach today?

options.text: Refer to a specialist allergy clinic for vaccination in hospital
options.rationale: Hospital vaccination is reserved for a previous anaphylaxis to a vaccine or to a vaccine component such as gelatin, not for food allergy to egg (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook; ASCIA).

options.text: Give the measles mumps rubella vaccine but omit the influenza one
options.rationale: Modern influenza vaccines contain ovalbumin below 1 microgram per dose and are given routinely to children with egg anaphylaxis, so omitting it withholds protection without reason (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Give both vaccines today with the standard 15 minute observation
options.rationale: Egg allergy of any severity is not a contraindication to measles mumps rubella or influenza vaccine, both of which are given in general practice with the routine 15 minute observation period (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook; ASCIA).

options.text: Arrange skin prick testing to each vaccine before administering it
options.rationale: Skin testing with vaccines has poor predictive value and is not recommended before routine immunisation of a child with food allergy (Source: ASCIA).

options.text: Give each vaccine in graded doses 30 minutes apart in the practice
options.rationale: Graded dosing is a specialist protocol used after a genuine vaccine reaction and has no role when the allergy is to a food rather than to a vaccine component (Source: ASCIA).

explanation.summary: Measles mumps rubella vaccine is grown in chick embryo fibroblast culture rather than in egg and contains no measurable ovalbumin, so egg allergy has never been a contraindication to it. Influenza vaccines are egg grown but modern manufacturing leaves ovalbumin content below 1 microgram per dose, a quantity well below any threshold for reaction, and large studies of children with egg anaphylaxis have shown no excess of reactions. Australian guidance is therefore that children with egg allergy of any severity, including anaphylaxis, receive both vaccines in the usual community setting with the standard 15 minute observation. The vaccine components that genuinely do warrant specialist assessment are gelatin and neomycin, and a previous anaphylactic reaction to a vaccine itself. Unnecessary referral is not neutral, because it delays immunisation and reinforces a family belief that vaccines are dangerous for their child.
key_points: Measles mumps rubella vaccine is not grown in egg and contains no ovalbumin
Influenza vaccines contain less than 1 microgram of ovalbumin per dose
Egg allergy of any severity is not a contraindication to either vaccine
Gelatin and neomycin allergy are the components that warrant specialist input
Unnecessary referral delays immunisation and reinforces vaccine anxiety
explanation.pearls: The one egg containing vaccine that still requires specialist assessment in Australia is yellow fever vaccine, which contains substantially more residual egg protein than influenza vaccine and is given under supervision in a designated travel clinic.

subtopic_detail: Applying low risk criteria to a transient event in a well infant
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 10 week old boy born at 39 weeks whose mother brought him in after an episode this afternoon. She says that while he was lying in his bouncer after a feed he went floppy and the skin around his lips turned blue for about 20 seconds, and that he came good when she picked him up and blew on his face.

Nobody gave rescue breaths or chest compressions. He has fed normally since and is now alert and interactive. He has had no fever, no cough and no vomiting, no similar episode before, and his immunisations are up to date. His examination including tone, fontanelle, femoral pulses and a full skin inspection is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138 beats per minute, respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, blood pressure within normal limits for age
data_table.Examination: Alert and interactive, normal tone, soft fontanelle, symmetrical femoral pulses, no bruising or petechiae on full skin inspection, normal cardiovascular and respiratory examination
data_table.Observation: Four hours of cardiorespiratory monitoring in the emergency department with no further events

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for 24 hours of cardiorespiratory monitoring and observation
options.rationale: Prolonged monitoring does not improve outcomes in an infant meeting every low risk criterion and generates false alarms that lead to further unnecessary testing (Source: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram and a brain scan before discharge
options.rationale: Neurological investigation is indicated when the history describes focal features or when the examination is abnormal, and it has a very low yield after a single brief event with a normal examination (Source: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event

options.text: Perform a full septic screen including lumbar puncture and admit
options.rationale: A septic screen is driven by fever or an unwell appearance, and this afebrile well appearing infant with a normal examination does not meet the threshold (Source: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event

options.text: Educate the parents, offer resuscitation training and discharge
options.rationale: He meets every low risk criterion of age over 60 days, born at 32 weeks or later, a single event lasting under one minute, no cardiopulmonary resuscitation by a trained provider and a reassuring history and examination, so the recommended course is education, an offer of resuscitation training and discharge with follow up (Source: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event

options.text: Arrange a 24 hour oesophageal pH study and start a proton pump drug
options.rationale: Reflux is frequently assumed to be the cause of these events but pH studies do not establish causation, and acid suppression in infants carries risks of gastroenteritis and pneumonia without demonstrated benefit here (Source: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event

explanation.summary: The term brief resolved unexplained event replaced apparent life threatening event because the older label implied a danger that the evidence does not support, and it applies only when an infant under one year has a sudden brief episode of altered colour, tone, breathing or responsiveness that has fully resolved and has no explanation after history and examination. The value of the definition is that it creates an explicitly low risk group in whom extensive investigation and admission cause more harm than benefit. The criteria are age over 60 days, gestational age of 32 weeks or more with a corrected age of at least 45 weeks, a first event lasting less than one minute, no cardiopulmonary resuscitation by a trained provider, and a reassuring history and physical examination. Any infant failing a criterion is higher risk and needs individualised assessment, and the history should always include a careful and non accusatory consideration of inflicted injury, which is why a full skin inspection for bruising is part of the examination.
key_points: The event must have fully resolved and remain unexplained after history and examination
Low risk requires age over 60 days and a single event under one minute
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation by a trained provider excludes the low risk group
Extensive investigation in low risk infants causes net harm
Always inspect the skin for bruising and consider inflicted injury
explanation.pearls: An electrocardiogram is the one investigation reasonable to consider even in a low risk infant, because a long QT syndrome is otherwise undetectable on examination and is a treatable cause of sudden death.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event
American Academy of Pediatrics Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Sequencing treatment against imaging after an abnormal newborn screening result
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 7 day old girl recalled after her newborn screening card taken on day three flagged a raised thyroid stimulating hormone. Confirmatory venous blood taken this morning has just been reported.

She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy, is breastfeeding slowly and sleeps through feeds. She is mildly jaundiced, has a large posterior fontanelle and mildly reduced tone, and no goitre is palpable. Her mother has no thyroid disease, has taken no antithyroid medication and has had no iodine containing contrast.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 92 mIU/L (1-20 in the first week), free thyroxine 6 pmol/L (10-26), total bilirubin below the phototherapy threshold for age
data_table.Examination: Posterior fontanelle admitting a fingertip, mildly reduced tone, no goitre palpable, umbilicus healing normally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Await the thyroid scan result before starting any thyroid hormone
options.rationale: Every day of untreated hypothyroidism in the newborn period costs cognitive outcome, and imaging is not required to make the biochemical diagnosis (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism).

options.text: Repeat the venous thyroid function tests in two weeks and review
options.rationale: A repeat is appropriate for a borderline screening result with normal free thyroxine, and this infant already has unequivocal biochemical and clinical hypothyroidism (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism).

options.text: Commence thyroxine only if the thyroid scan shows no gland present
options.rationale: Treatment is determined by the biochemistry rather than the anatomy, since dyshormonogenesis with a normally sited gland causes hypothyroidism just as severe as agenesis (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism).

options.text: Refer to paediatric endocrinology for review within four weeks
options.rationale: Endocrine involvement is appropriate but a four week wait squanders the window in which treatment preserves cognitive outcome, which closes at around two weeks of age (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism).

options.text: Commence thyroxine today and arrange thyroid imaging in parallel
options.rationale: A markedly raised thyroid stimulating hormone with a low free thyroxine confirms congenital hypothyroidism, and thyroxine is started the same day while imaging to determine the underlying cause proceeds without delaying treatment (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism; Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group).

explanation.summary: Congenital hypothyroidism affects about one in 2000 to 3000 births in Australia and is the commonest preventable cause of intellectual disability, which is why it has been part of newborn screening since the 1970s. Most affected infants have no clinical signs at birth because maternal thyroxine crosses the placenta, and the classic features of prolonged jaundice, a large posterior fontanelle, hypotonia, poor feeding, constipation and an umbilical hernia appear only as that supply is exhausted. Outcome depends almost entirely on how quickly treatment starts, with normal cognitive development expected when thyroxine begins within the first two weeks of life and a measurable loss of intelligence quotient for each week of delay thereafter. Imaging with ultrasound or a radionuclide scan distinguishes agenesis, an ectopic gland and dyshormonogenesis, which matters for genetic counselling and for deciding later whether a trial off treatment at three years is worthwhile, but it must never delay the first dose.
key_points: Most affected newborns appear normal because of transplacental maternal thyroxine
Treatment within the first two weeks of life preserves normal cognitive outcome
Imaging determines the cause but must not delay starting thyroxine
Dyshormonogenesis causes hypothyroidism as severe as glandular agenesis
Prolonged jaundice and a large posterior fontanelle are late clinical clues
explanation.pearls: The Australian starting dose is thyroxine 10 to 15 micrograms per kilogram daily, aiming to normalise the free thyroxine within two weeks, and the tablet is crushed in a small volume of water or breast milk rather than mixed into a full feed that the infant may not finish.

subtopic_detail: First line treatment of asymptomatic hypoglycaemia in an at risk newborn
stem:
You are the paediatric resident called to the postnatal ward to see a two hour old boy born at 39 weeks and 1 day to a mother whose gestational diabetes was managed with metformin. His birth weight is 4250 g and he had a good breastfeed at 40 minutes of age.

He is pink and alert with normal tone, is not jittery, and has no grunting, tachypnoea or recession. His axillary temperature is 36.9 degrees Celsius and he is rooting for a further feed. The routine pre feed blood glucose taken by the midwife is 2.2 mmol/L, confirmed on a laboratory sample.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138 beats per minute, respiratory rate 46 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 2.2 mmol/L on a laboratory confirmed sample, taken before the second feed
data_table.Examination: Alert, pink, normal tone, no jitteriness, anterior fontanelle soft, cardiovascular and respiratory examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give buccal 40 per cent dextrose gel and support a breastfeed
options.rationale: Buccal dextrose gel with a feed is first line for asymptomatic hypoglycaemia in an at risk newborn, reduces admission to special care and does not interfere with establishing breastfeeding (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).

options.text: Give a 2 mL/kg bolus of 10 per cent glucose intravenously now
options.rationale: An intravenous bolus is reserved for a symptomatic infant or one with a blood glucose below about 1.5 mmol/L, and it separates a well baby from his mother unnecessarily (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).

options.text: Give a formula top up by bottle and recheck the glucose in one hour
options.rationale: Feeding alone raises the glucose more slowly than gel plus a feed, and introducing a bottle at two hours of age undermines breastfeeding when an equally effective option exists (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).

options.text: Recheck the blood glucose before the next feed without treating now
options.rationale: A confirmed value below 2.6 mmol/L in an at risk infant requires treatment rather than observation, because neuroglycopenic injury can occur before clinical signs appear (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).

options.text: Admit to the special care nursery for an intravenous glucose infusion
options.rationale: Nursery admission with an infusion is for persistent or symptomatic hypoglycaemia that has not responded to gel and feeds, and it is not the first step in a well feeding baby (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).

explanation.summary: Newborns at risk of hypoglycaemia include infants of diabetic mothers, those who are large or small for gestational age, preterm infants and those who are unwell, and these babies are screened with pre feed glucose measurements in the first 24 hours. The Australian operational threshold is 2.6 mmol/L, chosen because it is the level below which neurophysiological changes have been demonstrated rather than because symptoms appear there. Dextrose gel changed practice because it treats effectively without separating mother and baby, and it is given at 0.5 mL per kilogram rubbed into the buccal mucosa, followed immediately by a feed and a repeat glucose 30 minutes later. Failure to respond after two doses, symptoms, or a very low reading move the infant onto the intravenous pathway, and hypoglycaemia persisting beyond 48 to 72 hours prompts investigation for hyperinsulinism or an endocrine cause.
key_points: The Australian operational threshold for newborn hypoglycaemia is 2.6 mmol/L
Dextrose gel 0.5 mL per kilogram buccally plus a feed is first line
Recheck the glucose 30 minutes after the gel is given
Intravenous glucose is for symptomatic infants or failure of gel and feeds
Hypoglycaemia persisting past 48 to 72 hours needs endocrine investigation
explanation.pearls: When hypoglycaemia persists beyond 72 hours, take a critical sample at the time of a low glucose for insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, ketones and free fatty acids, because the diagnosis of hyperinsulinism depends on measuring insulin while the glucose is actually low.

subtopic_detail: First line drug choice in a generalised epilepsy where one common agent is aggravating
stem:
You are the general paediatric registrar seeing a 6 year old girl whose teacher has recorded 20 to 30 episodes a day in which she stops mid sentence, stares, and does not respond for a few seconds before carrying on as if nothing happened. Her school work has fallen away this term.

She does not fall, does not jerk and is not drowsy or confused afterwards. When you ask her to blow on a paper windmill for two minutes in clinic she stops and stares for six seconds with fluttering eyelids and a brief upward eye movement. Her development, growth and neurological examination are normal, and an electroencephalogram shows generalised 3 Hz spike and wave discharges on a normal background.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium and glucose within normal limits
data_table.Electroencephalogram: Generalised symmetrical 3 Hz spike and wave discharges on a normal background, provoked by hyperventilation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Commence carbamazepine and review the seizure diary in four weeks
options.rationale: Carbamazepine aggravates absence seizures and can precipitate absence status, making it a specifically contraindicated choice in generalised epilepsies (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Commence ethosuximide and review the seizure diary in four weeks
options.rationale: Ethosuximide is first line for childhood absence epilepsy, with a comparative trial showing equal seizure freedom to valproate but less attentional impairment and fewer adverse effects (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; RCH CPG: Afebrile Seizures).

options.text: Commence levetiracetam and review the seizure diary in four weeks
options.rationale: Levetiracetam is markedly less effective for typical absence seizures than ethosuximide or valproate and is not a first line choice in this syndrome (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Commence lamotrigine and review the seizure diary in four weeks
options.rationale: Lamotrigine is effective in generalised epilepsy but requires slow titration over weeks and achieved lower seizure freedom rates than ethosuximide in the comparative trial (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange brain magnetic resonance imaging before starting treatment
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is not required when the clinical syndrome and electroencephalogram are typical, and is reserved for focal features, developmental regression or an abnormal examination (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile Seizures).

explanation.summary: Childhood absence epilepsy typically begins between four and ten years of age in a developmentally normal child and is defined by frequent brief staring episodes without postictal confusion, accompanied by generalised 3 Hz spike and wave activity. Hyperventilation for two to three minutes provokes an event in the great majority of untreated children, which makes it the single most useful bedside test and is often achieved by asking the child to blow a windmill or a tissue. The differential is inattention or daydreaming, which is not interruptible in the same way and does not stop mid activity, and focal impaired awareness seizures, which have an aura, automatisms and postictal drowsiness. Prognosis is good with around two thirds achieving remission by adolescence, though attentional difficulties can persist and warrant follow up even after seizures stop.
key_points: Hyperventilation provokes an absence in most untreated children
There is no aura and no postictal confusion in typical absence seizures
Carbamazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin and vigabatrin aggravate absence seizures
Neuroimaging is not needed when syndrome and electroencephalogram are typical
Attentional difficulties can persist after seizure remission
explanation.pearls: In the randomised comparison of the three first line agents, ethosuximide and valproate both achieved around 45 per cent freedom from failure at 12 months against 21 per cent for lamotrigine, and ethosuximide caused less attentional impairment than valproate.

subtopic_detail: Timing of referral for a palpable inguinal testis that has never been in the scrotum
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 14 month old boy for a routine check. His mother mentions that a doctor told her at the six week check that one of his testes was not down, and she was told it would probably sort itself out.

The right hemiscrotum is small and empty. You can feel a firm mobile testis in the right inguinal canal and can bring it as far as the neck of the scrotum, but it springs straight back when you let go. The left testis sits normally in the scrotum, the phallus is normal with a terminal meatus, and his growth and general examination are normal.

data_table.Examination: Empty right hemiscrotum with a palpable testis in the right inguinal canal that cannot be brought into the scrotum, normally descended left testis, normal phallus with terminal meatus
data_table.Growth: Weight and length tracking along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review the testis at his second birthday
options.rationale: Spontaneous descent essentially never occurs after six months of corrected age, so further waiting only delays surgery past the recommended window (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testis).

options.text: Arrange an ultrasound of the groin to locate the testis first
options.rationale: Imaging adds nothing when the testis is already palpable, and ultrasound has poor sensitivity for a truly impalpable testis so it does not change management either way (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testis).

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for orchidopexy without further delay
options.rationale: A testis that has never been in the scrotum and cannot be brought there requires orchidopexy, ideally completed between six and twelve months of age, so at 14 months referral should be immediate (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testis).

options.text: Arrange human chorionic gonadotrophin stimulation before referral
options.rationale: Hormonal treatment has low success rates, a high relapse rate and is not used in Australian practice for an isolated unilateral undescended testis (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testis).

options.text: Refer for karyotype and hormonal testing before any surgical opinion
options.rationale: Endocrine and genetic assessment is indicated for bilateral impalpable testes or for hypospadias with an undescended testis, because those combinations raise the possibility of a difference of sex development, and neither applies here (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testis).

explanation.summary: Around 3 per cent of term boys have an undescended testis at birth and most descend spontaneously by three months of corrected age, after which further descent is very unlikely. The main clinical task is distinguishing a true undescended testis from a retractile one, which can be brought into the scrotum and stays there until the cremasteric reflex fires again, and which needs annual review rather than surgery. Orchidopexy is recommended between six and twelve months of age because the germ cell population deteriorates from the second year, and earlier surgery is associated with better fertility outcomes and a lower risk of malignancy. Surgery does not abolish the increased risk of testicular cancer but does make the testis examinable, which is why these boys are taught testicular self examination from adolescence.
key_points: Spontaneous descent is very unlikely after six months of corrected age
A retractile testis stays in the scrotum once brought there and needs review only
Orchidopexy is recommended between six and twelve months of age
Ultrasound does not help for either a palpable or an impalpable testis
Bilateral impalpable testes or associated hypospadias warrant endocrine assessment
explanation.pearls: Examine for an undescended testis with warm hands and the child relaxed, sweeping from the anterior superior iliac spine along the inguinal canal towards the scrotum, because a cold room or a cold hand triggers the cremasteric reflex and turns a normal testis into an apparently undescended one.

sources.label: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: Selecting first line treatment for primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7 year old boy who wets the bed five or six nights a week and has never been dry for longer than a fortnight. He has started refusing invitations to sleep at his cousin's house and tells you he wants it to stop.

He is dry all day, has no urgency or frequency, and does not have to rush to the toilet. He opens his bowels once a day with a soft stool and has never soiled. His growth, abdominal examination, spine and lower limb neurological examination are normal, and his parents say they are willing to be woken at night and to keep a record.

data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis shows no glucose, protein, blood, nitrites or leucocytes
data_table.Examination: Normal abdominal examination with no palpable faecal loading, normal lumbosacral spine and normal lower limb neurological examination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe desmopressin each night and review him in three months
options.rationale: Desmopressin works quickly but relapse on stopping is common, so it is chosen for short term cover such as a camp or when alarm therapy is not feasible rather than as first line (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).

options.text: Advise no drinks after six in the evening and review in three months
options.rationale: Evening fluid restriction alone has not been shown to cure enuresis and can lead to daytime under drinking with reduced functional bladder capacity (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).

options.text: Prescribe oxybutynin twice daily and review him in three months
options.rationale: Anticholinergics are for overactive bladder with daytime urgency and frequency, and this boy has no daytime symptoms at all (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).

options.text: Arrange an enuresis alarm and review him after four to six weeks
options.rationale: Alarm therapy is first line for primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis in a motivated child over six years with engaged parents, achieving lasting dryness in around two thirds with a much lower relapse rate than drug treatment (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).

options.text: Prescribe imipramine at night and review him after four to six weeks
options.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressants are a last resort for refractory enuresis because of cardiotoxicity in overdose and a high relapse rate on cessation (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Nocturnal enuresis affects around 15 per cent of five year olds and resolves spontaneously in about 15 per cent of affected children each year, so treatment is offered when the child is bothered rather than at a fixed age. The first step is separating monosymptomatic enuresis from enuresis with daytime symptoms, since the latter points to bladder dysfunction and needs a different approach, and the second is excluding and treating constipation, which is the commonest reversible contributor. Urinalysis is done once to exclude diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus and urinary infection, and further imaging is not required in a child with a normal examination. Alarm therapy works by conditioning and takes several weeks to have effect, so families need to be told at the outset to persist for at least six weeks and to continue until 14 consecutive dry nights are achieved.
key_points: Separate monosymptomatic enuresis from enuresis with daytime symptoms
Exclude and treat constipation before starting specific treatment
Urinalysis is the only routine investigation needed
Alarm therapy is first line and has the lowest relapse rate
Desmopressin is useful for short term cover such as camps and sleepovers
explanation.pearls: Continue alarm therapy until the child has achieved 14 consecutive dry nights, usually around eight to twelve weeks in total, because stopping at the first run of dry nights is the commonest cause of relapse.

subtopic_detail: Follow up schedule for renal involvement after a childhood small vessel vasculitis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6 year old boy who has had a raised purple rash over his buttocks and the backs of both legs for five days, along with sore swollen ankles and tummy pain that comes and goes.

The rash does not fade when you press it and the spots stand up from the skin. His abdomen is soft with no guarding and no mass, his stool has tested negative for blood and his scrotum is not swollen or tender. He is eating and drinking, walking with a limp, and his parents want to know what happens next.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 380 x10^9/L (150-450), haemoglobin 124 g/L (110-145), international normalised ratio 1.0, activated partial thromboplastin time within normal limits, creatinine 34 micromol/L (20-60), albumin 38 g/L (35-50)
data_table.Urinalysis: Blood 1 plus, protein negative, no nitrites or leucocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing plan?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone for one week and then review him
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are used for severe abdominal pain or orchitis and do not prevent or treat the renal involvement, so they are not given for isolated haematuria (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

options.text: Refer for renal biopsy before the rash begins to resolve
options.rationale: Biopsy is indicated for nephrotic range proteinuria, impaired renal function or a rapidly progressive course, none of which is present with isolated microscopic haematuria (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

options.text: Commence an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor today
options.rationale: Angiotensin blockade is used for established persistent proteinuria rather than for haematuria alone, and starting it now would treat a complication that has not developed (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

options.text: Discharge with advice to return only if the rash worsens
options.rationale: Renal involvement can appear weeks after the rash has faded and is silent until it is advanced, so discharge without surveillance is the error that allows nephritis to be missed (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

options.text: Arrange weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for one month
options.rationale: Australian practice is weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for the first month, then at decreasing frequency for six to twelve months, because nephritis develops in around a third of children and almost always within the first six months (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

explanation.summary: Immunoglobulin A vasculitis is the commonest vasculitis of childhood and is diagnosed clinically on palpable purpura in a gravity dependent distribution with at least one of arthritis or arthralgia, abdominal pain, renal involvement or a compatible biopsy. A normal platelet count and normal coagulation are what separate it from thrombocytopenic and coagulopathic causes of purpura, and they should be checked in every child. The rash and joint symptoms settle over weeks, but renal involvement is the determinant of long term outcome and is the reason these children need structured follow up rather than simple discharge. Intussusception is the other complication to warn parents about, since it is typically ileoileal in this condition and may not be visible on the ultrasound views used for the usual ileocolic form.
key_points: Diagnosis is clinical, with palpable purpura in a gravity dependent distribution
Normal platelets and coagulation separate it from other causes of purpura
Nephritis develops in about a third and almost always within six months
Corticosteroids treat severe abdominal pain but do not prevent nephritis
Warn parents about intussusception, which is usually ileoileal in this condition
explanation.pearls: Continue urinalysis and blood pressure surveillance for at least six months after the rash resolves, because late nephritis presenting after the first month accounts for a substantial minority of cases and is entirely asymptomatic until proteinuria is heavy.

subtopic_detail: Managing blood streaked stools in a thriving exclusively breastfed infant without stopping breastfeeding
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 7 week old girl whose mother has noticed streaks of bright red blood and clear jelly like strings mixed through her nappies for the past four weeks.

She is exclusively breastfed, feeds hungrily every three hours and settles afterwards. Her mother reports no vomiting, no fever and no change in the number of nappies. She has dry rough patches on both cheeks that her mother has been treating with a moisturiser. Her weight has tracked steadily along the 50th centile since birth and her abdomen is soft with no distension or masses.

data_table.Examination: Alert and settled, weight on the 50th centile tracking along the same line since birth, soft non tender abdomen, mild dry eczematous patches on both cheeks, normal perianal appearance
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange flexible sigmoidoscopy before making any dietary change
options.rationale: Endoscopy is the near pair reserved for infants with faltering growth, systemic illness or failure to respond to exclusion, and it would subject a thriving infant to anaesthesia for a diagnosis better made by dietary challenge (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Exclude cow milk from the mother's diet and continue breastfeeding
options.rationale: Blood and mucus in the stool of a thriving, systemically well breastfed infant is most often a non immunoglobulin E mediated proctocolitis from maternally ingested cow milk protein, and a strict maternal exclusion trial of two to four weeks with calcium supplementation is the treatment while breastfeeding continues (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula and stop breastfeeding
options.rationale: A hydrolysed formula is the correct step for a formula fed infant with the same presentation, but stopping breastfeeding is not required and removes its protective benefit unnecessarily (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.text: Change to an amino acid based formula and stop breastfeeding now
options.rationale: Amino acid formula is reserved for infants who fail an extensively hydrolysed formula or who have faltering growth or severe disease, and this infant has neither (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.text: Start a proton pump inhibitor and continue breastfeeding as usual
options.rationale: Acid suppression treats a different problem, does not affect colonic mucosal inflammation, and in infants is associated with increased rates of gastroenteritis and lower respiratory infection (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Cow milk protein allergy in infancy divides into immunoglobulin E mediated disease, which produces urticaria, vomiting or anaphylaxis within minutes to two hours, and non immunoglobulin E mediated disease, which produces delayed gastrointestinal symptoms over hours to days and is not detectable by skin prick or specific immunoglobulin E testing. Allergic proctocolitis is the mildest form of the delayed group and characteristically occurs in a well grown, contented breastfed infant, which is why the visible blood alarms parents far more than it alarms the clinician.
